knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Legendre conjugacy for functions taking values in the full extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) with the Euclidean pairing \(\langle y,x\rangle\), and let \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}=[-\infty,+\infty]\). For a function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), its Fenchel–Legendre conjugate is the function \(f^*:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) defined by
\[
f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.
\]
The biconjugate is \(f^{**}:=(f^*)^*\). Two functions \(f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) form a conjugate pair when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let X be Euclidean n-space and let f take values in the full extended real line. The Fenchel–Legendre conjugate of f at y is the supremum, over x in X, of the Euclidean pairing of y and x minus f(x). Applying conjugation twice gives the biconjugate. Two functions f and g form a conjugate pair exactly when each is the conjugate of the other.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel conjugacy as a dual-geometric interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the Euclidean dual pair \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(X^*=\mathbb R^n\), with pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle\). Let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real Fenchel conjugacy; no smoothness or convexity of the input is required for the transform itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is \[f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\},\qquad y\in X^*.\] Its epigraph is the parameter set of all affine minorants of \(f\): \[\operatorname{epi}f^*=\{(y,\beta)\in X^*\times\mathbb R:\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\le f(x)\ \forall x\in X\}.\] Thus each \((y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\) represents the affine function \(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\) lying below \(f\). The associated biconjugate is \[f^{**}(x):=\sup_{y\in X^*}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\] For every \(x,y\), \(\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+f^*(y)\), and \(f^{**}\le f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real function on Euclidean space, its Fenchel conjugate at a dual vector is the supremum of the dual pairing minus the function. The epigraph of the conjugate consists exactly of the slope-offset pairs whose affine functions minorize the original function. Conjugating again takes the supremum of this complete family of encoded affine minorants. Fenchel's inequality holds for every primal-dual pair, and the biconjugate never exceeds the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\), with \((y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\iff \langle x,y\rangle-\beta\le f(x)\) for every \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^*(y)=-\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)-\langle x,y\rangle\}.\]
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-\beta:(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex, then \(f^{**}=f\).
If \(f=\delta_C\), then \(f^*\) is the support function of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The transform converts a function into a closed convex function whenever the conjugate is proper.
The inequality \(f_1\le f_2\) implies \(f_1^*\ge f_2^*\).
boundary_notes: The values \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) require the usual extended-real conventions; expressions of the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\) are excluded.
Infinite-dimensional dual pairs require a specified topology and continuous dual; that regime is not asserted here.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the extended-real function \(f\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and identify its algebraic and continuous dual with \(X^*=\mathbb R^n\) through the bilinear pairing \((x,y)\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real dual-pair viewpoint. The notation distinguishes primal and dual copies even though both are coordinatized by \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), its dual-pair conjugate is the function \(f^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\bigr).\] Conversely, for \(g:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \[g^*(x)=\sup_{y\in X^*}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-g(y)\bigr).\] A pair \((f,g)\) is a mutually conjugate dual pair precisely when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\). Equivalently, it is a minimal pair, under pointwise order, among those satisfying \[\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+g(y)\qquad\forall(x,y)\in X\times X^*.\] Mutual conjugacy therefore requires both members to be closed proper convex functions, apart from the two constant improper functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual spaces are treated as distinct copies of Euclidean space linked by their bilinear pairing. Conjugating a primal function takes a supremum over primal points and produces a dual function; the same formula with the variables reversed returns a primal function. Two functions form a mutually conjugate pair when each is the conjugate of the other. Equivalently, they give a pointwise-minimal valid decomposition of the pairing into a primal term plus a dual term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f,g)\) is mutually conjugate exactly when \(g(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f(x)=\sup_y(\langle x,y\rangle-g(y))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For closed proper convex \(f\), the pair is \((f,f^*)\) and \(f^{**}=f\).
The valid inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+g(y)\) is tight as a function pair exactly when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\).
special_cases_latex: Under the Euclidean identification \(X=X^*\), the self-conjugate quadratic \(x\mapsto\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is its own dual partner.
For a linear subspace \(L\), \(\delta_L^*=\delta_{L^\perp}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Fenchel's inequality is the universal pairing inequality associated with \((f,f^*)\).
The effective domain of \(f^*\) records the dual vectors for which \(f-\langle\cdot,y\rangle\) is bounded below.
boundary_notes: The Euclidean identification does not eliminate the directional distinction between primal and dual variables.
No locally convex infinite-dimensional topology or restricted continuous dual is specified.

notation.meaning: Dual copy of the primal Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Minorant Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function is the pointwise supremum of all its affine minorants; equivalently, its conjugate supplies every affine lower bound needed to recover it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in M_f}\{\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\}.
\]
Equivalently, the epigraph of \(f\) is the intersection of the closed half-spaces lying above its continuous affine minorants. Thus every value of \(f\) is recovered from the family of affine lower bounds encoded by its conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) equals the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine functions minorizing it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau representation by continuous affine minorants.

notation.meaning: Set of slope-intercept pairs defining affine minorants of f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Epigraph Parameterization of Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact slope-intercept parameterization of all finite continuous affine lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and set \(a_{u,\alpha}(x)=\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\). Then \[a_{u,\alpha}\le f\iff \alpha\ge f^*(u).\] Consequently, \[M_f=\{(u,\alpha):\alpha\ge f^*(u)\}=\operatorname{epi}f^*.\] If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous and convex, the pointwise supremum of the affine functions parameterized by this set equals \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the conjugate is precisely the parameter set of all finite affine minorants of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_f=\operatorname{epi}f^*\), and for closed convex f the associated affine minorants have supremum f.

notation.meaning: affine function with slope u and negative-intercept parameter alpha
parameter set of affine minorants of f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation by all continuous affine minorants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Write \(\mathcal A(f)\) for the family of finite affine functions majorized by \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise representation. Exact recovery applies to closed convex functions; arbitrary inputs are replaced by their lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the affine-minorant family \[\mathcal A(f):=\{a_{y,\beta}:a_{y,\beta}(x)=\langle x,y\rangle-\beta,\ (y,\beta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R,\ a_{y,\beta}\le f\}.\] Its pointwise envelope is \[M_f(x):=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}a(x),\] with the supremum of the empty family interpreted as \(-\infty\). Then \[M_f=f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f),\] where the right side denotes the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Hence a function \(f\) is closed and convex exactly when \[f(x)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-\beta:(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\}\qquad\forall x.\] For proper convex \(f\), at least one finite affine minorant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine-minorant family contains every finite affine function lying pointwise below the given extended-real function. Its pointwise supremum is the biconjugate, equivalently the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of the input. Therefore a closed convex function is recovered exactly as the supremum of all its affine minorants. Each such minorant is parametrized by a point in the epigraph of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}a=f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\), and this envelope equals \(f\) when \(f\) is closed and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[a_{y,\beta}\in\mathcal A(f)\iff \beta\ge f^*(y).\]
\[\operatorname{epi}M_f=\bigcap_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}\operatorname{epi}a.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is finite affine, its representation includes \(f\) itself and the envelope is \(f\).
If \(f=\delta_C\), the representation reduces to the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Two functions have the same affine minorants exactly when their closed convex envelopes coincide.
The conjugate depends only on \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\).
boundary_notes: If no finite affine minorant exists, the envelope is identically \(-\infty\).
Closedness means lower semicontinuity in the Euclidean topology.

notation.meaning: Family of all finite affine minorants of \(f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph half-space correspondence induced by conjugacy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and let \(F=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometric encoding of conjugacy through epigraphs and upper half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((y,\beta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\), define the upper half-space \[H_{y,\beta}:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:r\ge\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\}.\] The support-epigraph correspondence is \[(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\subset H_{y,\beta}.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\) is precisely the set of parameters of all nonvertical upper closed half-spaces containing \(F\). If \(f\) is closed and convex, then \[F=\bigcap_{(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}H_{y,\beta}.\] Equivalently, the lower boundary of this intersection is the affine-minorant envelope \(f^{**}=f\). Vertical supporting half-spaces are redundant in this intersection because their exclusion can be replicated by suitable upper half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope and offset belong to the epigraph of the conjugate exactly when the upper half-space above the corresponding affine graph contains the epigraph of the original function. Thus the conjugate epigraph parametrizes all upper half-spaces supporting or containing the primal epigraph. For a closed convex function, intersecting all these half-spaces recovers the primal epigraph exactly.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^*(y)=\inf\{\beta:\operatorname{epi}f\subset H_{y,\beta}\}.\]
\[f(x)=\sup_{(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}(\langle x,y\rangle-\beta)\] for closed convex \(f\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), the construction encodes the closed half-spaces containing \(C\) through the support values \(\sigma_C(y)\).
For finite affine \(f(x)=\langle x,y_0\rangle-\beta_0\), \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{y_0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex functions are uniquely determined by their conjugate epigraphs.
Epigraph inclusion reverses under conjugacy through the order reversal of functions.
boundary_notes: The asserted exact intersection requires closed convexity; otherwise it recovers the epigraph of the biconjugate.
This record concerns upper half-spaces, not arbitrary support functions of unbounded epigraphs.

notation.meaning: Upper closed half-space whose lower boundary is an affine graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is convex, and lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed; every epigraph is vertically upward closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). It is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed. Consequently, \(f\) is closed convex precisely when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a closed convex set. Vertical upward closure also holds: if \((x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(s\ge r\), then \((x,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity and lower semicontinuity of \(f\) are equivalent to convexity and closedness, respectively, of its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph characterization of convexity and lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of an extended-real function from its epigraph and the induced order relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \[f(x)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb R:(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\] where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Hence the epigraph uniquely determines \(f\). For any such functions \(f,g\), \[f\le g\iff\operatorname{epi}f\supseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is recovered as the lower boundary of its epigraph, and pointwise function order corresponds to reverse epigraph inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraph determines the function, and \(f\le g\iff\operatorname{epi}f\supseteq\operatorname{epi}g\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Recovery and Reversed Inclusion
Vertical Supporting Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical epigraph supports encode supporting normals of the effective domain, not finite subgradients; only supports with a negative vertical normal component yield finite affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and define
\[
N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)=\{a:\langle a,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }y\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.
\]
For every nonzero \(a\in N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\), the vertical hyperplane
\[
\{(y,r):\langle a,y-x\rangle=0\}
\]
supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Its normal \((a,0)\) cannot be normalized to \((u,-1)\), so this support records a supporting normal of the effective domain rather than a finite affine minorant or a subgradient through the usual epigraph formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal \((a,0)\) defines a vertical support of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) but cannot represent a finite subgradient affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes domain supports from the nonvertical epigraph supports representing finite subgradients.

notation.meaning: normal cone to the effective domain at x

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a subgradient precisely when its affine subgradient inequality defines a hyperplane supporting the function's epigraph at the corresponding graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following are equivalent: \(u\in\partial f(x)\); the epigraph satisfies
\[
\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\{(y,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:r\ge f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\};
\]
and \(H_{x,u}\) supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\). The supporting half-space has normal \((u,-1)\), and its boundary is the graph of the affine minorant \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is a subgradient at \(x\) exactly when the corresponding nonvertical hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradients as nonvertical supporting hyperplanes of an epigraph.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary distinction between arbitrary epigraph support and support arising from a finite affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A supporting hyperplane to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) with normal \((v,0)\) is vertical and constrains only \(\operatorname{dom}f\); it does not correspond to a finite subgradient. For example, \[f(t)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt t,&t\ge0,\\+\infty,&t<0,\end{cases}\] is proper, closed, and convex, but \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), while the vertical line \(t=0\) supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain boundary, epigraph support may be purely vertical and need not yield a subgradient; minus square root at zero is an explicit example.
assumptions_latex: Supporting hyperplanes are considered at finite graph points of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of some epigraph support does not imply \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\); nonvertical support is essential.

notation.meaning: normal of a vertical epigraph-supporting hyperplane

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical-Support Boundary and Empty Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonvertical Epigraph Support on the Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of subgradient-defined supporting hyperplanes at relative-interior graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. For every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), \[\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing.\] Consequently, at every graph point \((x,f(x))\) over \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the epigraph admits a nonvertical supporting hyperplane with normal proportional to \((u,-1)\) for some \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relative-interior domain point has a subgradient and therefore a nonvertical supporting hyperplane to the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), yielding a nonvertical epigraph support at \((x,f(x))\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of the effective domain

knowledge_statements.title: Nonvertical Epigraph Support on the Relative Interior
All Epigraph Support Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every epigraph support direction is classified by its vertical component: negative directions rescale conjugate values, zero directions support the domain, and positive directions have infinite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and set \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\). For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\sigma_E(u,\beta)=
\begin{cases}
(-\beta)f^*\!\left(u/(-\beta)\right),&\beta<0,\\
\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u),&\beta=0,\\
+\infty,&\beta>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus negative vertical coefficients are homogeneous rescalings of conjugate values, zero vertical coefficient records only effective-domain support, and positive vertical coefficient gives infinite support because epigraphs are upward closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous extension of the normalized support identity to every vertical coefficient.

notation.meaning: vertical component of the support direction

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Epigraph Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each conjugate value is an epigraph support value in direction (u,-1), and for every real alpha its upper bounds correspond exactly to affine minorants of the original function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}=\sup_{(x,r)\in E}\{\langle u,x\rangle-r\}=\sigma_E(u,-1).
\]
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the inequality \(f^*(u)\le\alpha\) holds exactly when \(E\subseteq\{(x,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\langle u,x\rangle-r\le\alpha\}\), or equivalently when \(x\mapsto\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\) is an affine minorant of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is the support function of the epigraph restricted to covectors whose last coordinate is \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy represented through support values of the epigraph.

notation.meaning: Support function of a set C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Directional Support Formula for an Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the seed's normalized direction to every vertical component without importing contact-point geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\). Then
\[
\sigma_E(u,s)=\begin{cases}
(-s)f^*\!\left(u/(-s)\right),&s<0,\\
\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u),&s=0,\\
+\infty,&s>0.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-vertical epigraph supports are scaled conjugate values, horizontal supports are domain supports, and positive-vertical supports are infinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Full Directional Support Formula for an Epigraph
Conjugation as an Order Anti-Isomorphism
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On proper closed convex functions, conjugation is an involutive order anti-isomorphism: primal order is exactly reversed in the dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) denote the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. For \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\),
\[
f\le g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g^*\le f^*.
\]
Moreover, \(f^*\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) and \(f^{**}=f\). Hence Fenchel conjugation is an order-reversing bijection of \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) onto itself, with conjugation as its inverse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\le g\iff g^*\le f^*\), and conjugation is an involutive order-reversing bijection on \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

notation.meaning: proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Reversing Dual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing a function decreases its conjugate. Conjugation reverses pointwise inequalities, while biconjugation preserves them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the pointwise inequality \(f\le g\) gives
\[
g^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-g(x)\}\le\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}=f^*(u).
\]
Thus conjugation is antitone. Applying it twice restores the original order, so \(f^{**}\le g^{**}\). In particular, equality \(f=g\) implies equality of their conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fenchel conjugation reverses pointwise order: \(g^*\le f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antitonicity of Fenchel conjugation under pointwise order.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\overline{\mathbb R}^{\mathbb R^n}\) be the pointwise-ordered collection of extended-real functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise order, with the involutive part restricted to closed proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal F(f)=f^*\) by Fenchel conjugation. This map is antitone: for all functions \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), \[f\le g\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*\ge g^*.\] Moreover, \[f^{**}\le f,\qquad f^{***}=f^*.\] On the class \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) of proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, \(\mathcal F\) is an order-reversing involution: \[f\in\Gamma_0\Longrightarrow f^*\in\Gamma_0,\qquad f^{**}=f.\] Hence, for \(f,g\in\Gamma_0\), \[f\le g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^*\ge g^*.\] This is the canonical order-reversing dual correspondence of Fenchel conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation reverses pointwise inequalities: a smaller primal function has a larger conjugate. Every function dominates its biconjugate, and taking three conjugates returns the first conjugate. On proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, conjugation is an order-reversing involution, so the primal inequality and the reversed dual inequality are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\le g\Rightarrow f^*\ge g^*\); restricted to \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), \(f\le g\iff f^*\ge g^*\) and \(f^{**}=f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f\supseteq\operatorname{epi}g\Longrightarrow\operatorname{epi}f^*\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g^*.\]
For arbitrary \(f\), conjugacy identifies the same dual object for \(f\) and \(f^{**}\): \((f^{**})^*=f^*\).
special_cases_latex: For sets \(C_1\subseteq C_2\), \(\delta_{C_1}\ge\delta_{C_2}\) and \(\sigma_{C_1}\le\sigma_{C_2}\).
For closed convex sets containing the origin, \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_1^\circ\supseteq C_2^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Conjugation exchanges pointwise suprema with dual lower-envelope operations only after the relevant closure conventions are imposed.
The involutive correspondence is one-to-one on \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\).
boundary_notes: The reverse implication from \(f^*\ge g^*\) to \(f\le g\) can fail outside the closed convex regime; it yields only \(f^{**}\le g^{**}\).
Order is pointwise extended-real order.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\overline{\mathbb R}=[-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Define \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional taxonomy separating proper, nonclosed or nonconvex, and improper inputs under the same conjugate formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real Fenchel transform is \[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)).\] The input is called proper when \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\); otherwise it is improper. Three regimes are distinguished: \[(i)\ f\in\Gamma_0:\ f\text{ is proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous};\] \[(ii)\ f\text{ is proper but is nonconvex or not lower semicontinuous};\] \[(iii)\ f\text{ is improper}.\] In regime \((i)\), \(f^*\in\Gamma_0\) and \(f^{**}=f\). In regime \((ii)\), \(f^*=(f^{**})^*\), while \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\) whenever a proper lower-semicontinuous convex minorant exists. Regime \((iii)\) includes constant and pointwise degeneracies and need not produce a proper conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same supremum formula defines conjugacy for every extended-real function. Inputs are separated into proper closed convex functions, proper functions lacking convexity or lower semicontinuity, and improper functions. Conjugacy is involutive in the first regime. In the second, it discards precisely the information lost upon passage to the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope. In the third, the transform can collapse to an infinite constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended-real conjugate is defined in all three regimes, with exact involution on \(\Gamma_0\) and envelope recovery through \(f^{**}\) for proper nonclosed or nonconvex inputs.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Properness is \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\) together with \(f^{-1}(-\infty)=\varnothing\).
For a proper convex function, lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: The constants \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) are conjugate to one another.
A finite-valued function is automatically proper but need not be convex or closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper conjugate is lower semicontinuous and convex.
Nonconvex features above the closed convex envelope cannot be recovered from \(f^*\).
boundary_notes: The notation \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\) denotes the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant, not pointwise closure of values.
Extended-real arithmetic must avoid indeterminate sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Closed Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, the conjugate remains proper closed convex and the biconjugate equals the original function everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate \(f^*:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}=f(x).
\]
Thus Fenchel conjugation maps the proper closed convex class into itself, and biconjugation is the identity on that class.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is proper lower semicontinuous convex, and biconjugation recovers \(f\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau theorem in the proper closed convex regime.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean topology and dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, including extended-real domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proper closed convex regime is the class \[\Gamma_0(X):=\{f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]:\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing,\ f\text{ is convex, and }\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}\}.\] Equivalently, its members are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Fenchel conjugation maps this class onto itself and is involutive: \[f\in\Gamma_0(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*\in\Gamma_0(X^*),\qquad f^{**}=f.\] Consequently, \(f\mapsto f^*\) is a symmetric one-to-one correspondence between \(\Gamma_0(X)\) and \(\Gamma_0(X^*)\), and every member satisfies \[f(x)=\sup_{y\in X^*}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proper closed convex regime consists of extended-real convex functions with nonempty effective domain, no value minus infinity, and closed epigraph. These are exactly the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Their conjugates remain in the same class, and conjugating twice returns the original function. Thus Fenchel conjugacy is a bijective, symmetric, order-reversing correspondence on this class.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\in\Gamma_0(X)\iff f=f^{**}\text{ and }f\not\equiv\pm\infty.\]
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{y\in X^*}\{(x,r):r\ge\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: Indicators of nonempty closed convex sets belong to \(\Gamma_0\).
Finite continuous convex functions, norms, and positive-semidefinite finite quadratics belong to \(\Gamma_0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(f\in\Gamma_0\) is the supremum of its finite affine minorants.
For \(f,g\in\Gamma_0\), \(f\le g\iff f^*\ge g^*\).
boundary_notes: A proper convex function with a nonclosed epigraph is outside this regime even though its conjugate is still closed convex.
The function may take \(+\infty\), so membership does not mean finite-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation Bifunction and Adjoint for Linear-Map Fenchel Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-map Fenchel primal–dual architecture and its primal- and dual-side strong-consistency criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be proper convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g\) be proper concave on \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear. Define
\[
(Fu)(x)=f(x)-g(Ax+u).
\]
Then \(F\) is a proper convex bifunction from \(\mathbb{R}^m\) to \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and it is closed when \(f\) and \(g\) are closed. Its primal value at zero is
\[
\inf F0=\inf_x\{f(x)-g(Ax)\},
\]
and the primal problem is strongly consistent iff there exists \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) with \(Ax\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\). The adjoint is
\[
(F^*x^*)(u^*)=g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*+x^*),
\]
so
\[
\sup F^*0=\sup_{u^*}\{g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*)\}.
\]
The dual problem is strongly consistent iff there exists \(u^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g^*)\) with \(A^*u^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard perturbation of a linear-map Fenchel problem is a proper convex bifunction, closed when the component functions are closed. Its value at zero is the primal value, its adjoint produces the Fenchel dual objective, and primal and dual strong consistency are respectively equivalent to relative-interior feasibility in the original and conjugate domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (Fu)(x)=f(x)-g(Ax+u),\quad(F^*x^*)(u^*)=g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*+x^*),\quad\text{with the stated primal and dual consistency equivalences}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Interior Subgradient and Lipschitz Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional bounded-set result for a closed proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed, proper, and convex, and let \varnothing\ne S\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f) be closed and bounded. Then \partial f(S):=\bigcup_{x\in S}\partial f(x) is nonempty, closed, and bounded. With \alpha:=\sup\{\|x^*\|:x^*\in\partial f(S)\}<\infty, one has f'(x;z)\le\alpha\|z\| for every x\in S and z\in\mathbb{R}^n, and |f(y)-f(x)|\le\alpha\|y-x\| for every x,y\in S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On any nonempty closed bounded subset of the interior of the domain of a closed proper convex function, the union of all subdifferentials is nonempty, closed, and bounded. Its maximal norm uniformly bounds directional derivatives and gives a Lipschitz bound for the function on that subset.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Map Fenchel Strong Duality and One-Sided Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional Fenchel duality for a convex function and a linearly composed concave function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be closed proper convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g\) be closed proper concave on \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear. Then
\[
\inf_x\{f(x)-g(Ax)\}=\sup_{u^*}\{g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*)\}
\]
if either (a) there exists \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) such that \(Ax\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\), or (b) there exists \(u^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g^*)\) such that \(A^*u^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\). Under (a) the dual supremum is attained, whereas under (b) the primal infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed proper convex f, closed proper concave g, and a linear map A, the primal and Fenchel dual values coincide under either the original-domain or conjugate-domain relative-interior condition. The original-domain condition guarantees dual attainment, while the conjugate-domain condition guarantees primal attainment.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is closed proper convex on }\mathbb{R}^n
g\text{ is closed proper concave on }\mathbb{R}^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_x\{f(x)-g(Ax)\}=\sup_{u^*}\{g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*)\},\quad\text{with dual attainment under (a) and primal attainment under (b)}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed, proper, and convex. Assume that every z_1,\ldots,z_m satisfying \sum_{i=1}^m f_i^{0+}(z_i)\leq0 and \sum_{i=1}^m f_i^{0+}(-z_i)>0 also satisfies \sum_{i=1}^m z_i\neq0. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Gauges and Hölder Inequality from a \(p\)-Homogeneous Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a polar pair of gauges and sublevel sets from a positively homogeneous convex function and its conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, convex, and positively homogeneous of degree \(p\), where \(1<p<+\infty\). Let \(q\in(1,+\infty)\) satisfy \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\). Then \(k=(pf)^{1/p}\) is a closed gauge and \(k^\circ=(qf^*)^{1/q}\). Consequently, \(\langle x,x^*\rangle\le [pf(x)]^{1/p}[qf^*(x^*)]^{1/q}\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\). Moreover, the closed convex sets \(C=\{x\mid [pf(x)]^{1/p}\le1\}=\{x\mid f(x)\le1/p\}\) and \(C^*=\{x^*\mid[qf^*(x^*)]^{1/q}\le1\}=\{x^*\mid f^*(x^*)\le1/q\}\) are polar to each other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the pth root of p times a closed proper convex p-homogeneous function produces a closed gauge; the corresponding construction from its conjugate produces the polar gauge. These gauges give a Hölder-type pairing inequality, and their unit sublevel sets are mutually polar closed convex sets.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, convex, and positively homogeneous of degree }p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (pf)^{1/p}\text{ is a closed gauge with polar }(qf^*)^{1/q},\quad \langle x,x^*\rangle\le[pf(x)]^{1/p}[qf^*(x^*)]^{1/q},\quad C^*\text{ is polar to }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kuhn–Tucker Characterization of Fenchel Primal–Dual Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient subdifferential certificate for a zero-gap optimal pair in the closed linear-map Fenchel problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be closed proper convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g\) be closed proper concave on \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear. For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(u^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
f(x)-g(Ax)=\inf_z\{f(z)-g(Az)\}=\sup_v\{g^*(v)-f^*(A^*v)\}=g^*(u^*)-f^*(A^*u^*)

\[
A^*u^*\in\partial f(x),\qquad Ax\in\partial g^*(u^*).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential graph is homeomorphic to Euclidean space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global graph parametrization for the subdifferential of a closed proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex. The map
\[
S:\operatorname{gph}\partial f\to\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad S(x,x^*)=x+x^*,

is bijective, continuous, and has a continuous inverse. Consequently, \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy of proper nonclosed or nonconvex inputs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, without assuming convexity or lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact description of what conjugacy retains from a proper arbitrary input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonclosed/nonconvex input regime consists of proper functions \(f\notin\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\). Their conjugates are still defined by \[f^*(y)=\sup_x\{\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\}\] and are pointwise suprema of affine functions of \(y\), hence closed and convex whenever proper. Define the closed convex envelope by \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f:=\sup\{h:h\le f,\ h\text{ is lower-semicontinuous and convex}\}.\] When this envelope is proper, \[f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f,\qquad f^*=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)^*.\] Thus two proper inputs have the same conjugate whenever they have the same closed convex envelope; exact recovery of the original input occurs only if it already belongs to \(\Gamma_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function may be conjugated even if it is nonconvex or lacks lower semicontinuity. Its conjugate is a supremum of affine functions and therefore has closed convex structure. Conjugating twice returns the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function below the input, provided that envelope is proper. Consequently, conjugacy retains the closed convex envelope and discards nonconvex elevations and nonclosed boundary values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a proper input with proper closed convex envelope, \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\) and \(f^*=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\] under the proper-envelope convention.
\[f^*(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For convex but nonclosed \(f\), \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\).
For finite nonconvex \(f\), \(f^{**}\) is its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing \(f\) without changing its affine minorants does not change \(f^*\).
The strict inequality \(f^{**}<f\) somewhere certifies failure of closed convexity.
boundary_notes: The envelope may be identically \(-\infty\) if no proper closed convex minorant exists.
The biconjugate is a minorant, not a convex majorant.

notation.meaning: Greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex but nonclosed function, biconjugation returns its lower-semicontinuous closure, not the original function, while conjugation already ignores the missing closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The biconjugate is the lower-semicontinuous hull of \(f\):
\[
f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f,
\qquad
\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}.
\]
Hence \(f^{**}\le f\) everywhere, and because \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous, equality fails at at least one point. Nevertheless, conjugation cannot distinguish \(f\) from its closure: \(f^*=(\operatorname{cl}f)^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Biconjugation closes \(f\): \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\), with strict inequality wherever closure lowers its value.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper nonconvex input with an affine lower bound, biconjugation returns the greatest closed convex minorant and therefore cannot reproduce the input everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The biconjugate satisfies
\[
f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f
=\sup\{a:a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\le f\}.
\]
It is lower semicontinuous and convex, obeys \(f^{**}\le f\), and dominates every lower-semicontinuous convex function lying below \(f\). Since \(f\) is not convex, \(f^{**}\) cannot equal \(f\) everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Biconjugation convexifies and closes \(f\), producing its greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of missing convexity for a proper extended-real input.

Then \[ f^*=(f^{**})^*=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)^*. \] Thus conjugation cannot distinguish \(f\) from its closed convex envelope.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Closed Convexification
Nonclosed Nonconvex Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an input is both nonclosed and nonconvex, its conjugate retains only its closed convex hull, which is exactly what biconjugation returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\), the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of \(f\). Then
\[
f^{**}=g,
\qquad
f^*=g^*.
\]
Thus conjugation discards both nonconvex features and nonclosed boundary behavior. The inequality \(g\le f\) holds everywhere, and equality everywhere is impossible because such equality would make \(f\) lower semicontinuous and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, neither lower semicontinuous nor convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate depends only on the closed convex hull, and biconjugation returns that hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined loss of closedness and convexity under Fenchel biconjugation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous Nonclosedness and Nonconvexity in an Indicator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional example in which biconjugation both fills a nonconvex gap and adds missing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)\) and \(f=\delta_C\). Then \(f\) is proper, nonconvex, and not lower semicontinuous, while
\[
f^*(u)=\sigma_C(u)=|u|,\qquad f^{**}=\delta_{[-1,1]}.
\]
Thus \(f^{**}(x)=0<f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\in\{-1,0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of two punctured adjacent intervals is nonconvex and nonclosed; its conjugate is absolute value and its biconjugate is the indicator of the entire closed interval.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and call \(f\) improper when \(\operatorname{dom}f=\varnothing\) or \(f(x)=-\infty\) for some \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real degeneracies under the standard Fenchel supremum convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The improper-degenerate regimes are characterized as follows. If \(f\equiv+\infty\), then \[f^*\equiv-\infty.\] If \(f(x_0)=-\infty\) for at least one \(x_0\), then \[f^*\equiv+\infty,\] because every dual objective contains the value \(+\infty\) at \(x_0\). In particular, \[(+\infty)^*=-\infty,\qquad(-\infty)^*=+\infty,\] so the two constant improper closed convex functions form a conjugate pair. By contrast, every other closed convex function participating in a mutually conjugate pair is proper. These cases are excluded from \(\Gamma_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An input identically equal to positive infinity has conjugate identically equal to negative infinity. Any input attaining negative infinity has conjugate identically equal to positive infinity. Thus the two constant infinite functions are conjugates of one another and constitute the improper closed-convex degeneracy. All nonconstant members of the closed-convex conjugacy correspondence are proper.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}f=\varnothing\iff f\equiv+\infty.\]
For convex closed \(f\), impropriety is equivalent to \(f\equiv+\infty\) or \(f\equiv-\infty\).
special_cases_latex: The biconjugate of either constant infinite function is itself.
A function that is finite at one point and never equals \(-\infty\) is proper, even if it is nonconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A conjugate taking the value \(-\infty\) must be identically \(-\infty\) in the constant-positive-infinity case.
Improper inputs cannot be handled by proper-function duality statements without explicit exceptions.
boundary_notes: Some authors restrict the word conjugate to functions never taking \(-\infty\); this record uses the fully extended-real formula.
Indeterminate extended-real expressions are not introduced.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant positive- and negative-infinity inputs conjugate to the opposite infinite constants, so no finite support or affine-minorant information survives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the usual extended-real conventions, the constant extreme inputs satisfy
\[
(+\infty)^*\equiv-\infty,
\qquad
(-\infty)^*\equiv+\infty.
\]
Consequently, their conjugates contain no finite support values, and a second conjugation merely exchanges the two extremes again. These cases are degenerate because conjugation no longer produces a proper closed convex function or meaningful finite affine-minorant data.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real input to Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme constant inputs yield constant infinite conjugates and destroy informative dual geometry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy interpreted as the two constant infinite-valued extreme inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Improperness–Degeneracy Overlap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two constant infinite-valued degeneracies are both improper, and Fenchel conjugation swaps positive infinity with negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both constant extreme functions are improper: \(+\infty\) has empty effective domain, while \(-\infty\) assumes the forbidden negative-infinite value everywhere. Fenchel conjugation interchanges them:
\[
f\equiv+\infty\Longleftrightarrow f^*\equiv-\infty,
\qquad
f\equiv-\infty\Longleftrightarrow f^*\equiv+\infty.
\]
Thus the constant degenerate regime lies inside the improper regime and forms a two-element cycle under conjugation.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is one of the constant functions \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These degenerate inputs are improper, and conjugation swaps them.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of improperness with constant infinite-valued degeneracy.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Conjugation does swap the two constant infinite functions, but the displayed reverse implication from an identically positive-infinite conjugate to an identically negative-infinite primal is false without the record's restrictive two-function assumption; other functions can have conjugate identically positive infinity. More importantly, the cited source has not been shown to define the degenerate regime as exactly these constants. A source fixing that scope and convention is needed before a mathematically reliable revision can be chosen.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedding convex sets into functional conjugacy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Define its indicator \(\delta_C\), support function \(\sigma_C\), polar \(C^\circ\), and gauge \(\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional correspondences for nonempty convex sets; closure and origin assumptions are stated where required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set–function embedding is \[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle.\] Fenchel conjugacy gives \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}.\] If \(C\) is closed and convex, indicator and support functions are mutually conjugate. If additionally \(0\in C\), define \[C^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\},\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}.\] Then \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.\] These identities embed indicator-support, gauge-polar, and norm-dual-norm correspondences into conjugate geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is represented analytically by its extended-real indicator, whose conjugate is the set's support function. Conjugating the support function returns the indicator of the closed convex hull, and returns the original indicator for a closed convex set. When a closed convex set contains the origin, its gauge equals the support function of its polar, and polarity is involutive. Norm duality is the symmetric bounded-body specialization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\iff \langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y.\]
\[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), its polar is also a closed convex cone and \(\delta_K^*=\delta_{K^\circ}\) under the cone-polar sign convention of the source.
For a centrally symmetric convex body, its gauge is a norm and the polar gauge is the dual norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex sets are uniquely determined by their support functions.
Set inclusion becomes pointwise support-function order and reverses under polarity.
boundary_notes: For nonclosed or nonconvex \(C\), the support function cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closed convex hull.
The polar-set inequality uses level \(1\); cone polarity may use level \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator and support functions as a conjugate pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact conjugate pair for a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle.\] The indicator-support conjugacy pair is \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\] Equivalently, \(\sigma_C\) is the unique closed proper positively homogeneous convex function whose conjugate is \(\delta_C\). The support function encodes every containing half-space through \[C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le\beta\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sigma_C(y)\le\beta.\] Accordingly, \[C=\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-real indicator of a nonempty closed convex set and its support function are Fenchel conjugates of one another. The support value in each direction is the least offset of a closed half-space with that normal containing the set. Collecting these inequalities reconstructs the set exactly. Support functions are precisely the closed proper positively homogeneous convex functions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sigma_C(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:x\in C\}.\]
\[x\in C\iff\langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\quad\forall y.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{a\}\), then \(\sigma_C(y)=\langle a,y\rangle\).
If \(C\) is a linear subspace \(L\), then \(\sigma_L=\delta_{L^\perp}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sigma_C\) is closed, convex, proper, and positively homogeneous.
If \(C_1,C_2\) are closed convex, then \(C_1\subseteq C_2\iff\sigma_{C_1}\le\sigma_{C_2}\).
boundary_notes: For arbitrary nonempty \(C\), \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\), so exact recovery requires closed convexity.
The support function may take \(+\infty\) when \(C\) is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Calculus for Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding indicators imposes both set constraints, and positive scaling leaves an indicator unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary sets \(C,D\subseteq X\),
\[
\delta_C+\delta_D=\delta_{C\cap D}.
\]
The common function is proper exactly when \(C\cap D\neq\varnothing\). For every scalar \(\lambda>0\), \(\lambda\delta_C=\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary extended-real calculus intrinsic to set indicators.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator is zero on the set and positive infinity outside it; its convexity and lower semicontinuity correspond respectively to convexity and closedness of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The indicator function of \(C\) is the extended-real-valued function \(\delta_C:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by
\[
\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
It is proper because \(C\neq\varnothing\). It is convex exactly when \(C\) is convex, and it is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex-analysis indicator, not a Boolean-valued characteristic function.

knowledge_statements.title: Finiteness and Lipschitz Boundaries for Support Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function is finite and globally Lipschitz exactly when its generating set is bounded; the least Lipschitz constant is the set's maximal radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\). The support function \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is bounded. In that case
\[
|\sigma_C(u)-\sigma_C(v)|\leq R\|u-v\|,
\]
and \(R\) is the least global Lipschitz constant. Hence \(\sigma_C\) is globally Lipschitz exactly when \(C\) is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ bounded}\iff\sigma_C\text{ finite everywhere}\iff\sigma_C\text{ globally Lipschitz}\), and the least Lipschitz constant is \(\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundedness characterization intrinsic to support functions.

notation.meaning: supremal norm of points in C

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Support-Function Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions turn Minkowski addition into addition, scaling into scaling, translation into an affine term, and linear images into adjoint composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty sets \(C,D\subseteq X\), \(\lambda\geq0\), \(a\in X\), and a linear map \(A:X\to Y\),
\[
\sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D,\quad \sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C,\quad \sigma_{C+a}(u)=\sigma_C(u)+\langle u,a\rangle,
\]
and
\[
\sigma_{AC}(v)=\sigma_C(A^*v).
\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary transformations within the support-function representation family.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D

\]
It is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively homogeneous. Moreover, it depends only on the closed convex hull: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness criterion and exact continuity modulus for Hilbert-space support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and set \(R=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\). Then \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is bounded. When \(R<+\infty\),
\[
|\sigma_C(u)-\sigma_C(v)|\le R\|u-v\|\qquad(u,v\in X),
\]
and the least global Lipschitz constant of \(\sigma_C\) is \(R=\sup_{x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\|x\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert-space support function is finite everywhere exactly when its set is bounded, and its least global Lipschitz constant is the set's radius about the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C\text{ is finite everywhere}\iff C\text{ is bounded}\), and, when bounded, \(\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma_C)=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugates of Convex Hulls and Suprema of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the closure-sensitive arbitrary-family identities and the attained infimal representation available for a finite family with common closed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be an arbitrary index set and let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex for every \(i\in I\). Then
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{conv}\{f_i:i\in I\}\bigr)^*=\sup_{i\in I}f_i^*,
\qquad
\bigl(\sup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}f_i\bigr)^*=\operatorname{cl}\!\bigl(\operatorname{conv}\{f_i^*:i\in I\}\bigr).
\]
If \(I\) is finite and \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)=C\) for every \(i\in I\), the outer closure in the second identity is unnecessary. Moreover, for every \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\bigl(\sup_{i\in I}f_i\bigr)^*(x^*)=
\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i f_i^*(x_i^*):
\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1,\ \sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i x_i^*=x^*\right\},
\]
so the infimum over such convex-combination representations is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any family of proper convex functions on Euclidean space, conjugation exchanges the convex hull of the functions with their pointwise supremum of conjugates, and exchanges the supremum of their closed hulls with the closed convex hull of their conjugates. For a finite family whose closed domains coincide, the outer closure is unnecessary, and the conjugate of the pointwise supremum has an attained minimum over all convex-combination representations of the dual argument.
assumptions_latex: I\text{ is an arbitrary index set}
f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex for every }i\in I
\text{For the closure-free and attainment conclusions, }I\text{ is finite and }\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)=C\text{ for all }i\in I
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\operatorname{conv}\{f_i\})^*=\sup_i f_i^*,\quad (\sup_i\operatorname{cl}f_i)^*=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}\{f_i^*\}),\quad\text{with the stated closure omission and attained finite-family minimum under the additional hypotheses.}

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator–Support Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a set indicator is its support function; conjugating again yields the indicator of the closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in X\), Fenchel conjugation gives
\[
\delta_C^*(u)=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle u,x\rangle-\delta_C(x)\bigr)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u).
\]
Consequently, the biconjugate of the indicator is \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\), and equivalently
\[
\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}.
\]
If \(C\) is closed and convex, this reduces to \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets containing the origin; gauges may be infinite or vanish away from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Minkowski gauge and polar set by \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad C^\circ:=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] The gauge-polar correspondence is \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.\] In particular, \(\gamma_C\) is a closed nonnegative positively homogeneous convex function with \(\gamma_C(0)=0\), and its Fenchel conjugate is \[(\gamma_C)^*=\delta_{C^\circ}.\] The polar gauge may equivalently be written \[\gamma_C^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=\gamma_{C^\circ}(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex set containing the origin measures the least nonnegative dilation needed to contain a point. The polar set consists of dual vectors pairing to at most one with every point of the set. The gauge equals the support function of the polar, and the gauge of the polar equals the original support function. Taking the polar twice returns the set. The Fenchel conjugate of the gauge is the indicator of the polar.

special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, its gauge reduces to its indicator and set polarity reduces to cone polarity.

immediate_consequences_latex: The generalized Hölder inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\) holds whenever the gauge values are finite.
Polarity reverses inclusion: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow C_1^\circ\supseteq C_2^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauges, Minkowski representations, and polar gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines extended-valued gauges, their generating-set representation, the closed-generator uniqueness boundary, and functional polarity, including the finite positive and cone-indicator specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(k:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge if it is convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(k(0)=0\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}k\) is a convex cone containing the origin and no \((x,\mu)\) with \(\mu<0\). Gauges are precisely the functions representable as \(k(x)=\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\mu\geq0:x\in\mu C\}\) for a nonempty convex set \(C\). The unit sublevel set \(C_k=\{x:k(x)\leq1\}\) always satisfies \(\gamma_{C_k}=k\). If \(k\) is closed, \(C_k\) is the unique closed convex set containing \(0\) that generates \(k\). The polar gauge is \(k^\circ(x^*)=\inf\{\mu^*\geq0:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\mu^*k(x)\ \forall x\}\). If \(k\) is finite everywhere and positive away from \(0\), then \(k^\circ(x^*)=\sup_{x\neq0}\langle x,x^*\rangle/k(x)\). If \(k=\delta_K\) for a convex cone \(K\), then \(k^\circ=k^*=\delta_{K^\circ}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is a nonnegative convex positively homogeneous, possibly extended-valued function that vanishes at zero. Every gauge is a Minkowski functional, and its unit sublevel set is a generator; for a closed gauge, that set is the unique closed convex generator containing zero. The polar gauge is defined by domination of all dual pairings. It has a supremum-ratio formula when the gauge is finite and positive away from zero, while the polar of a convex-cone indicator is the indicator of the polar cone and equals its convex conjugate.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty and convex when }k=\gamma_C
k\text{ is closed for uniqueness of the closed convex generator}
k\text{ is finite everywhere and }k(x)>0\text{ for }x\neq0\text{ for the ratio formula}
k=\delta_K\text{ with }K\text{ a convex cone for the indicator specialization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=\gamma_{C_k},\quad C_k=\{x:k(x)\leq1\},\quad k^\circ(x^*)=\inf\{\mu^*\geq0:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\mu^*k(x)\ \forall x\},\quad k^\circ(x^*)=\sup_{x\neq0}\frac{\langle x,x^*\rangle}{k(x)}\text{ in the finite positive case}.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge–Polar Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's polar gauge equals its support function and the gauge of its polar set; applying polarity twice recovers the original gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the polar set by \(C^\circ=\{y\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). Then
\[
(\gamma_C)^\circ=\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}.
\]
Since \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), the bipolar identity \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\) implies
\[
(\gamma_C)^{\circ\circ}=\gamma_C.
\]
Hence passage from a gauge to its polar reverses the corresponding unit balls and is involutive on this class.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a proper gauge, then \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}\) is its lower-semicontinuous hull. Equivalently, if \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\), then \[ B_{\kappa^{\circ\circ}}=B_\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\overline{B_\kappa}. \] Hence \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\kappa\) exactly for lower-semicontinuous gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double polarity closes a proper gauge; exact recovery holds precisely when the gauge is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa\), with equality to \(\kappa\) iff \(\kappa\) is lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp set-side boundary for involutive gauge polarity when the generating set lacks closedness, convexity, or the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arbitrary nonempty set \(A\subseteq X\), polarity ignores precisely the defects repaired by the bipolar hull: \[A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(A\cup\{0\}),\qquad A^\circ=\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(A\cup\{0\})\bigr)^\circ.\] Therefore exact recovery of the generating set by two polarizations holds exactly when \(A\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without closedness, convexity, and inclusion of zero, double polarity recovers the closed convex hull with zero adjoined rather than the original set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual norm as polar gauge and Fenchel conjugate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\), with closed unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm duality under the canonical Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual norm is \[\|y\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_B(y).\] Its unit ball is the polar body \[B^\circ=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}.\] Since \(\|\cdot\|=\gamma_B=\sigma_{B^\circ}\), norm polarity is involutive: \[(\|\cdot\|_*)_* =\|\cdot\|.\] The associated Fenchel conjugacy identities are \[(\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{B^\circ},\qquad \left(\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2\right)^*=\tfrac12\|\cdot\|_*^2.\] Equivalently, \[\langle x,y\rangle\le\|x\|\,\|y\|_*\qquad\forall x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\] with the dual norm being the least function of \(y\) making this inequality valid for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm is the support function of the primal unit ball. Its unit ball is the polar of the primal unit ball, while the primal norm is the support function of that polar ball. Hence dualizing twice returns the original norm. As Fenchel identities, the conjugate of a norm is the indicator of the dual unit ball, and the conjugate of one half the squared norm is one half the squared dual norm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\le1}\langle x,y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: The Euclidean norm is self-dual.
The \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms are dual to one another; for \(1<p<\infty\), \(\ell_p\) is dual to \(\ell_q\) where \(1/p+1/q=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The dual norm is a finite continuous norm.
The primal and dual unit balls determine one another by polarity.
boundary_notes: Central symmetry and boundedness distinguish norms from general gauges.
The pairing used to define the dual norm must be fixed; changing the pairing changes the coordinate formula.

notation.meaning: Polar of the primal unit ball.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive; it is the gauge of its compact, convex, symmetric unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal norm is a function \(\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfying, for all \(x,z\in X\) and scalars \(\alpha\),
\[
\|x\|=0\iff x=0,\qquad \|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\|x\|,\qquad \|x+z\|\leq\|x\|+\|z\|.
\]
Its unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contains \(0\) in its interior, while \(\|\cdot\|=\gamma_B\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm viewed as the gauge of its unit ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-Dimensional Norms Need Not Be Equivalent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of universal norm equivalence outside finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(X=C([0,1])\), both
\[
\|f\|_\infty=\max_{t\in[0,1]}|f(t)|,
\qquad
\|f\|_1=\int_0^1|f(t)|\,dt
\]
are norms, but they are not equivalent. For example, the triangular functions
\[
f_n(t)=\max\{1-n|t-\tfrac12|,0\}
\]
satisfy \(\|f_n\|_\infty=1\) and \(\|f_n\|_1=1/n\) for \(n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sup norm and integral norm on continuous functions are inequivalent, demonstrating the necessity of finite dimensionality in the equivalence theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) and \(\|\cdot\|_1\) are not equivalent norms on \(C([0,1])\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Norms Need Not Be Equivalent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological equivalence of arbitrary norms on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\|\cdot\|_a\) and \(\|\cdot\|_b\) are norms on a finite-dimensional real vector space \(X\), then there exist \(m,M>0\) such that
\[
m\|x\|_a\le \|x\|_b\le M\|x\|_a
\qquad(x\in X).
\]
Consequently all norms on \(X\) induce the same topology, and each norm is continuous and coercive relative to every other norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two norms on a finite-dimensional space bound each other by positive constants and therefore induce the same topology.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Equivalence of Norms

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm is the largest absolute value attained by a linear functional on the primal unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual norm of \(y\in X^*\) is
\[
\|y\|_* = \sup_{\|x\|\leq1}|\langle y,x\rangle|.
\]
Because the primal unit ball is centrally symmetric, the absolute value may equivalently be omitted. The supremum is finite and attained in finite dimensions, and \(\|\cdot\|_*\) is a norm on \(X^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
\(X^*\) is its algebraic dual with pairing \(\langle y,x\rangle\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Norm Supremum Need Not Be Attained in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the seed's finite-dimensional attainment assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=c_0\) with \(\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|\), and let \(y=(2^{-n})_{n\ge1}\in X^*=\ell_1\). Then
\[
\|y\|_*=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}=1,
\]
but no \(x\in c_0\) with \(\|x\|_\infty\le1\) satisfies \(\langle y,x\rangle=1\). Hence the defining supremum of a continuous dual norm need not be attained outside finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On c-zero, a positive ell-one functional has dual norm one but does not attain it on the sup-norm unit ball, showing why finite dimensionality matters for attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\|x\|_\infty\le1}\langle y,x\rangle=1\) but the supremum is not attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of a weighted block ℓ2 norm on a product space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the dual of a weighted block $\ell_2$ norm on a finite product of inner-product spaces, using component dual norms and reciprocal weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $m\in\mathbb N$, let $\mathbb E=\mathbb E_1\times\cdots\times\mathbb E_m$, and equip the product with the componentwise pairing. For each $i$, let $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_i}$ be the norm on $\mathbb E_i$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_i^*}$ its dual norm. Given weights $\omega_i>0$, define $\|(u_i)_{i=1}^m\|:=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i\|u_i\|_{\mathbb E_i}^2}$. Then, for $(v_i)_{i=1}^m\in\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb E_i^*$, $\|(v_i)_{i=1}^m\|_* =\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\omega_i^{-1}\|v_i\|_{\mathbb E_i^*}^2}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a weighted block ℓ2 norm on a finite product space is the block ℓ2 norm of the component dual norms with reciprocal weights.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear growth bounds the conjugate domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A global upper growth bound from the origin confines every finite point of the convex conjugate to a closed dual-norm ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mathbb{E} be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let f:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R} be convex. If, for some L\ge 0,
\[
f(x)\le f(0)+L\|x\|\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{E},
\]
and
\[
f_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\},
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{dom}f_*\subseteq\{s\in\mathbb{E}^*:\|s\|^*\le L\},
\qquad \|s\|^*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle s,x\rangle.
\]
Consequently, \operatorname{dom}f_* is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a finite convex function grows above its value at the origin by at most L times the primal norm, then every dual vector where its conjugate is finite has dual norm at most L; hence the conjugate domain is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb{E}\text{ is a finite-dimensional real normed space}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of a positive-definite quadratic norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the dual norm, under the standard Euclidean pairing, of a norm induced by a symmetric positive-definite matrix, including its diagonal weighted specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^n$ and define $\|x\|_Q:=\sqrt{x^TQx}$ on $\mathbb R^n$, with duality induced by the standard pairing $\langle y,x\rangle=y^Tx$. Then the dual norm is $\|y\|_{Q,*}=\|y\|_{Q^{-1}}=\sqrt{y^TQ^{-1}y}$. In particular, if $Q=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_n)$ with $w_i>0$, then $\|x\|_Q=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i^2}$ and $\|y\|_{Q,*}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2/w_i}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard Euclidean pairing, the dual of the norm weighted by a symmetric positive-definite matrix Q is the norm weighted by its inverse. For positive diagonal weights, the dual norm uses the reciprocal weights.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality of the Induced Norms of an Operator and Its Adjoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint and induced-norm identities for a linear map between finite-dimensional normed inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2^*\) be linear and let \(A^*:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb E_1^*\) satisfy \(\langle Ax,u\rangle=\langle x,A^*u\rangle\) for all \(x\in\mathbb E_1\) and \(u\in\mathbb E_2\). Then
\[
\|A\|_{1,2}=\|A^*\|_{2,1}
=\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}\|Ax\|_{\mathbb E_2}^*
=\max_{\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}=1}\|A^*u\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*.
\]
Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathbb E_1\) and \(u\in\mathbb E_2\),
\[
\|Ax\|_{\mathbb E_2}^*\leq \|A\|_{1,2}\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1},\qquad
\|A^*u\|_{\mathbb E_1}^*\leq \|A\|_{1,2}\|u\|_{\mathbb E_2}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear operator and its adjoint have the same induced norm. This common norm bounds the dual norm of Ax and of A*u by the corresponding input norm for every input.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2\text{ are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces equipped with norms}
\langle Ax,u\rangle=\langle x,A^*u\rangle\quad\forall x\in\mathbb E_1,\ \forall u\in\mathbb E_2
