knowledge_statements.title: Norming-Functional and Subgradient Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector is a norm subgradient exactly when it saturates the primal-dual norm inequality; at zero the subdifferential is the dual unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\),
\[
\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\{y\in X^*:\|y\|_*\leq1,\ \langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\}.
\]
If \(x\neq0\), this is equivalent to \(\|y\|_*=1\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\); at \(x=0\), \(\partial\|\cdot\|(0)=B_*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality certificate linking primal and dual norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Norm Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a positively scaled norm is the indicator of the correspondingly scaled dual ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
(\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*(y)=\delta_{\lambda B_*}(y).
\]
Equivalently, \(\delta_{\lambda B_*}^*(x)=\lambda\|x\|\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scaling variant of norm-indicator conjugacy.

notation.meaning: dual norm ball of radius lambda

knowledge_statements.title: Norm–Dual-Norm Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual norms satisfy Hölder's inequality, determine each other by support over their unit balls, and form a norm-indicator conjugate pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in X^*\),
\[
|\langle y,x\rangle|\leq\|x\|\,\|y\|_*.
\]
Moreover, polarity is exact:
\[
\|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle,
\]
so the bidual norm equals the primal norm under the canonical identification of \(X\) with \(X^{**}\). In Fenchel-conjugate form,
\[
(\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{B_*},\qquad \delta_{B_*}^*=\|\cdot\|.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm polarity and Fenchel conjugacy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\), \(B_*=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}\), and let \(\lambda,\mu>0\). Then
\[
(\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\lambda B_*},
\qquad
(\mu\|\cdot\|_*)^*=\delta_{\mu B},

where the second conjugate uses the pairing between \(X^*\) and \(X\). Equivalently, \(\lambda\|x\|=\sigma_{\lambda B_*}(x)\) and \(\mu\|y\|_*=\sigma_{\mu B}(y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy-stable classes of closed convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), on which \(f\mapsto f^*\) is an involution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional named structural classes preserved by Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subclass \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) is called conjugacy-stable when \[f\in\mathcal C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^*\in\mathcal C.\] Canonical conjugacy-stable classes include: \[(a)\ \text{partial affine functions }f(x)=\delta_{L+a}(x)+\langle x,a^*\rangle+\alpha;\] \[(b)\ \text{partial quadratic convex functions }f(x)=q(x)+\delta_M(x),\] where \(L\) is a linear subspace, \(M\) is affine, and \(q\) is a finite convex quadratic; and \[(c)\ \text{polyhedral convex functions, equivalently functions with polyhedral epigraphs}.\] The full class \(\Gamma_0\) is itself conjugacy-stable. Each member belongs to a conjugacy orbit \([f]_*:=\{f,f^*\}\), which is a singleton exactly when \(f=f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical conjugate class is a structural family of proper closed convex functions preserved in both directions by Fenchel conjugation. Important examples are partial affine functions, partial quadratic convex functions, polyhedral convex functions, and the entire Fenchel–Moreau class. Each function and its conjugate form a two-element orbit unless the function is self-conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A class is conjugacy-stable when \(f\in\mathcal C\iff f^*\in\mathcal C\); partial affine, partial quadratic convex, polyhedral convex, and all proper closed convex functions have this property.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(f^{**}=f\) on \(\Gamma_0\), one-sided closure \(f\in\mathcal C\Rightarrow f^*\in\mathcal C\) already implies conjugacy stability.
\([f]_*\) has cardinality one or two.
special_cases_latex: The function \(x\mapsto\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is a singleton self-conjugate orbit.
Indicators and support functions of closed convex sets form conjugate pairs but do not individually remain within the indicator subclass.
immediate_consequences_latex: Structural formulas for one class member can be transferred to its conjugate within the same class.
Polyhedral and partial-quadratic subclasses permit finite-dimensional representations on both sides.
boundary_notes: A collection of familiar examples is not conjugacy-stable unless membership is preserved in both directions.
Finite-valued affine functions alone are not stable because their conjugates are generally partial affine.

notation.meaning: A subclass of proper closed convex functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of affine and polyhedral convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex piecewise-affine and polyhedral functions; extended values encode polyhedral domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite affine function has the form \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\). A finite convex piecewise-linear-affine function has a representation \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i).\] A polyhedral convex function is one whose epigraph is a polyhedral convex set. Equivalently, every proper polyhedral convex function can be written \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P(x),\] where \(P=\{x:Ax\le c\}\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set. Thus finite affine functions form a subclass of finite convex piecewise-linear-affine functions, which form the full-domain subclass of proper polyhedral convex functions. Partial affine functions arise when the domain \(P\) is affine and the maximum has one term. Fenchel conjugation preserves the polyhedral class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite affine functions have one affine formula. Finite convex piecewise-linear-affine functions are finite maxima of affine formulas. Proper polyhedral convex functions allow the same maximum together with an extended-real indicator imposing a polyhedral domain. This yields a strict hierarchy from affine to finite piecewise linear to general polyhedral functions, with partial affine functions occupying the affine-domain branch. Conjugacy preserves polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proper polyhedral convex functions are exactly the functions \(\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\) with polyhedral \(P\), and their conjugates are polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is an intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces.
A convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated in the epigraph sense.
special_cases_latex: The absolute value and \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms are finite polyhedral convex functions.
Indicators of nonempty polyhedral convex sets are polyhedral convex functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper polyhedral convex function is closed.
A finite convex piecewise-linear-affine function has a polyhedral epigraph and full effective domain.
boundary_notes: Some terminology uses “piecewise linear” for affine pieces; constants \(b_i\) are included here.
A nonconvex piecewise-affine function is not part of this hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Subdifferential and Optimization Dichotomy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function has its slope as its unique subgradient everywhere and is bounded below exactly when that slope is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\{a\}\qquad(x\in X).
\]
If \(a=0\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=X\) and \(\inf f=b\). If \(a\ne0\), then \(\inf f=-\infty\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\{a\}\), with the stated minimization dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order and minimization structure of an everywhere-finite affine function.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function is a linear functional plus a constant; its conjugate is finite only at its slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine function is an everywhere-finite function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) of the form
\[
f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b
\]
for fixed \(a\in X^*\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\). It is both convex and concave. Its Fenchel conjugate is concentrated at its slope:
\[
f^*(y)=\delta_{\{a\}}(y)-b.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\) for some \(a\in X^*\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite affine functions and their Fenchel conjugates.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral First-Order Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a polyhedral convex function exactly when a convex combination of active slopes is canceled by a domain normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in P\),
\[
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x).
\]
Equivalently, there are \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I(x)\), with \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\), and \(n\in N_P(x)\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i+n=0.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimizer test obtained from the local subdifferential representation.

notation.meaning: normal vector to P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential of a Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral function's subdifferential is the active-slope convex hull plus the normal cone to its polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_P(x),
\]
and for \(x\in P\) let
\[
I(x):=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)
\qquad(x\in P),
\]
while \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin P\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order representation for the accepted polyhedral-function normal form.

notation.meaning: normal cone of P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron, equivalently when it is a finite affine maximum over a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is polyhedral when its epigraph
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq t\}
\]
is a nonempty polyhedron. Equivalently, there are a polyhedron \(P\subseteq X\), finitely many \(a_i\in X^*\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_i\bigl(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\bigr)\quad\text{for }x\in P,
\]
and \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin P\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-valued convex polyhedral functions in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession and Attainment for Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic representation and bounded-minimization dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=\max_i(\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P\),
\[
f^\infty(d)=
\begin{cases}
\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle,&d\in\operatorname{rec}P,\\
+\infty,&d\notin\operatorname{rec}P.
\end{cases}
\]
Furthermore, \(\inf f>-infty\) exactly when \(f^\infty(d)\ge0\) for every \(d\), and every finite infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function is the maximum of recession slopes on the domain recession cone, and a polyhedral objective has no finite unattained infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper polyhedral convex function with the displayed representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf f> -\infty\iff f^\infty\ge0\), and finite infimum implies \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: recession cone of the effective domain

Active-Slope Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite max-affine function is the convex hull of its active slopes, giving its differentiability test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
I(x):=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.
\]
Consequently, \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) exactly when the active slopes have singleton convex hull; its gradient is then that unique slope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted finite max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\), with differentiability exactly when this set is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometry of a finite max-affine representation.

notation.meaning: indices of affine pieces active at x

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex piecewise-linear function is the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine functions and is affine on each cell of a polyhedral subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex piecewise-linear when there exist \(m\geq1\), slopes \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in X^*\), and offsets \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\bigl(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\bigr)
\]
for every \(x\in X\). Such a function is continuous and polyhedral, with a polyhedral subdivision of \(X\) on each cell of which \(f\) agrees with an affine function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is convex and finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)\) for finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite convex piecewise-linear functions, also called finite polyhedral convex functions.

notation.meaning: slopes and offsets of the affine pieces

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Class Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation preserves polyhedral convexity, transforms a finite maximum of affine functions through a simplex linear program, and sends an affine function to a shifted singleton indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Polyhedrality is preserved by Fenchel conjugation: \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if \(f^*\) is polyhedral. In particular, if \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\), then
\[
f^*(y)=\min\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i b_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i=y\right\},
\]
where an infeasible minimum equals \(+\infty\). Thus a finite piecewise-affine convex function transforms into a polyhedral function whose effective domain is \(\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\). An affine function \(x\mapsto\langle a,x\rangle+b\) is the limiting case, with conjugate \(\delta_{\{a\}}-b\).
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is polyhedral; for finite piecewise-affine \(f\), its conjugate is given by the displayed finite-dimensional linear program with objective \(-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i b_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional transitions among affine, piecewise-affine, and polyhedral convex functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Cx\le d\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(f(x)=\max_i(a_i^Tx+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\). Then
\[
f^*(y)=\min_{\substack{\lambda\ge0,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1,\ \mu\ge0\\C^T\mu=y-\sum_i\lambda_i a_i}}
\left(d^T\mu-\sum_i\lambda_i b_i\right),
\]
with value \(+\infty\) when infeasible. Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}+C^T\mathbb R_+^p.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a domain-restricted max-affine function is an LP over piece weights and domain multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the displayed finite affine maximum on \(P\), extended by positive infinity outside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) has the displayed multiplier-LP representation and \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}+C^T\mathbb R_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subclass correspondence within proper closed polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed polyhedral convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\),
\[
\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{dom}f^*\text{ is a nonempty bounded polyhedron}.
\]
Consequently, conjugation exchanges finite convex piecewise-linear functions with proper closed polyhedral convex functions having bounded effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full primal domain is equivalent to bounded dual domain within the polyhedral class.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Domain–Bounded-Domain Conjugacy Transition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite, singular, and partial convex quadratic classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work on \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(Q\) be symmetric, \(M\) an affine set, and \(\delta_M\) its indicator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex quadratic taxonomy, including singular Hessians and affine domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite quadratic convex function is \[q(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha,\qquad Q\succeq0.\] It is strictly convex when \(Q\succ0\), and degenerate when \(Q\succeq0\) is singular. A partial quadratic convex function is any proper function \[f(x)=q(x)+\delta_M(x),\] with \(q\) finite convex quadratic and \(M\) affine. After an invertible affine change of coordinates and addition of an affine function, every such function has an elementary diagonal form \[h(z)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i z_i^2,\qquad 0\le\lambda_i\le+\infty,\] where \(\lambda_i=+\infty\) imposes \(z_i=0\). Its conjugate has the same form with \(\lambda_i^*=1/\lambda_i\), using \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\). Hence partial quadratic convex functions form a conjugacy-stable class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex quadratic has a symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix; positive definiteness gives the nondegenerate strictly convex subclass, while a singular matrix gives flat directions. A partial quadratic adds an indicator of an affine set, allowing restricted domains. Up to invertible affine coordinates and affine terms, these functions are diagonal with coefficients ranging from zero to positive infinity. Conjugation reciprocates the coefficients, exchanging zero curvature with a domain constraint, and preserves the partial-quadratic class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial quadratic convex functions are exactly affine-coordinate transforms of elementary diagonal quadratics with \(0\le\lambda_i\le+\infty\), and conjugacy replaces each \(\lambda_i\) by \(1/\lambda_i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle\) with \(Q\succeq0\), \[h^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y,Q^\dagger y\rangle+\delta_{\operatorname{range}Q}(y).\]
When \(Q\succ0\), \[h^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y,Q^{-1}y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is self-conjugate.
For \(Q=0\), the conjugate of the zero function is \(\delta_{\{0\}}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Singular primal curvature becomes a restricted dual effective domain.
Adding affine shifts preserves the partial-quadratic class and transforms the conjugate by the corresponding adjoint inverse and affine correction.
boundary_notes: Indefinite quadratic forms are not convex and are excluded.
The reciprocal-coefficient convention encodes both flat and constrained directions; it is not ordinary finite scalar arithmetic.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose inverse of the positive-semidefinite matrix \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite convex quadratic conjugates to another quadratic: the curvature matrix is inverted, the dual variable is shifted by the linear coefficient, and the constant changes sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), let
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c.
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, closed, and strictly convex, and its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
f^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y-b,Q^{-1}(y-b)\rangle-c.
\]
Consequently, conjugation maps the positive-definite quadratic class onto itself, reverses the linear translation through \(y-b\), negates the additive constant, and replaces the curvature operator \(Q\) by \(Q^{-1}\).
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is a quadratic with Hessian \(Q^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite strictly convex quadratic functions in Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite quadratic, the primal and conjugate gradients are mutually inverse affine maps, and corresponding points satisfy Fenchel equality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal Curvature Bounds Under Quadratic Conjugation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp spectral smoothness and strong-convexity constants for positive-definite quadratic conjugate pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\) and \(L=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\). Then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, while \(f^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient. These constants are sharp because \[\nabla^2f=Q,\qquad \nabla^2f^*=Q^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic conjugation reciprocates the extreme curvature eigenvalues, exchanging the sharp smoothness and strong-convexity constants.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharp curvature interval \([\mu,L]\) becomes \([1/L,1/\mu]\) under conjugation.

notation.meaning: smallest and largest eigenvalues of Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate of a Strictly Convex Quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy for an affine-quadratic function with positive-definite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c\), where \(A\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\). For every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the maximum defining \(f^*(y)\) is attained at \(x=A^{-1}(y-b)\), and \[f^*(y)=\tfrac12(y-b)^TA^{-1}(y-b)-c.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic with positive-definite curvature, the Fenchel-conjugate maximum is attained at A inverse times y minus b, and the conjugate is the corresponding inverse-curvature quadratic minus c.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Shifted Partially Quadratic Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centering and affinely shifting a partially quadratic function shifts both conjugate blocks; its subgradient relation separates into the general block and a linear quadratic-block equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^n=U\oplus V\) orthogonally, let \(g\in\Gamma_0(U)\), let \(Q:V\to V\) be self-adjoint positive definite, and write \(b=b_U+b_V\). If
\[
f(x)=g(P_Ux)+\frac12\langle P_Vx-v_0,Q(P_Vx-v_0)\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c,
\]
then
\[
f^*(y)=g^*(P_Uy-b_U)+\langle P_Vy-b_V,v_0\rangle+ rac12\langle P_Vy-b_V,Q^{-1}(P_Vy-b_V)\rangle-c.
\]
Moreover,
\[
y\in\partial f(x)
\iff
P_Uy-b_U\in\partial g(P_Ux),\quad P_Vy-b_V=Q(P_Vx-v_0).
\]
assumptions_latex: Q:V\to V\text{ is self-adjoint and positive definite}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally separable partially quadratic functions with a quadratic center, affine term, and constant.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projections onto U and V
orthogonal components of the affine slope

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Quadratic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially quadratic function separates across orthogonal subspaces into a general convex term and a positive-definite quadratic. Its conjugate separates similarly and inverts only the quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex function belongs to the orthogonally separable partially quadratic class when it has the form
\[
f(x)=g(P_Ux)+\tfrac12\langle P_Vx,Q P_Vx\rangle.
\]
For \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), its conjugate separates as
\[
f^*(y)=g^*(P_Uy)+\tfrac12\langle P_Vy,Q^{-1}P_Vy\rangle.
\]
Thus conjugation preserves this class: the unrestricted convex component is conjugated within \(U\), while the quadratic curvature on \(V\) is inverted.
assumptions_latex: There is an orthogonal decomposition \(\mathbb{R}^n=U\oplus V\).
The function \(g:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
The operator \(Q:V\to V\) is self-adjoint and positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate separates into \(g^*\) on \(U\) and an inverse quadratic on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally separable functions having one general convex block and one quadratic block.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projections onto U and V
positive-definite operator on the quadratic block
Fenchel conjugate of g on U

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular convex quadratic conjugates to a pseudoinverse quadratic restricted to the affine range of its Hessian; dual components along null directions make the conjugate infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate of the possibly degenerate quadratic is
\[
f^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y-b,Q^{\dagger}(y-b)\rangle-c+\delta_{b+\operatorname{ran}Q}(y).
\]
Hence loss of positive definiteness changes the conjugate from an everywhere-finite quadratic to an extended-valued quadratic supported on the affine subspace \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\). Equivalently, if \(y-b\) has a nonzero component in \(\ker Q\), the supremum defining \(f^*(y)\) is \(+\infty\). The positive-definite regime is recovered precisely when \(\operatorname{ran}Q=\mathbb{R}^n\).
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is finite exactly on \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\) and uses the Moore–Penrose inverse there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular positive-semidefinite quadratics and the domain restriction created by null directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric with a negative eigenvalue and let \[f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c.\] Then \[f^*(y)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^n.\] Thus singular positive-semidefinite curvature restricts the conjugate domain, whereas indefinite curvature destroys it entirely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature direction makes the Fenchel supremum unbounded for every dual vector.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is symmetric and has at least one negative eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of primal maximizers created by null directions of a positive-semidefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be symmetric and \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c\). If \(y-b\in\operatorname{ran}Q\), then \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}=Q^\dagger(y-b)+\ker Q.\] Equivalently, \(\partial f^*(y)=Q^\dagger(y-b)+\ker Q\) on \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\), while \(\partial f^*(y)=\varnothing\) outside that affine domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite dual point, the singular-quadratic conjugate maximizers form the pseudoinverse solution plus the null space.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate maximizer set is \(Q^\dagger(y-b)+\ker Q\) on \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar entropy, exponential, and logarithmic conjugate pairs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work on \(\mathbb R\) with pairing \(\langle x,u\rangle=xu\). For an extended-real function \(f\), set \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}(ux-f(x))\), and use \(0\log 0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records canonical scalar closed convex pairs. Finite-dimensional separable versions are obtained by summing the scalar functions coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the negative Boltzmann–Shannon entropy \(h:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(h(x)=x\log x-x\) for \(x>0\), \(h(0)=0\), and \(h(x)=+\infty\) for \(x<0\). Then \(h^*(u)=e^u\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\), equivalently \((\exp)^*=h\). Define the negative Burg entropy \(b(x)=-\log x\) for \(x>0\) and \(b(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Its conjugate is \(b^*(u)=-\log(-u)-1\) for \(u<0\) and \(b^*(u)=+\infty\) for \(u\geq0\). These functions and identities constitute the scalar entropy–exponential–logarithmic conjugacy family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family consists of two standard scalar conjugate pairs. The extended negative Boltzmann–Shannon entropy, equal to x log x minus x on the positive half-line and zero at the origin, is conjugate to the exponential function. The negative logarithm on the positive half-line is conjugate to the function minus log of minus u minus one on the negative half-line, extended by positive infinity elsewhere.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[e^u=\sup_{x\geq0}\{ux-x\log x+x\}.\]
\[h(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{xu-e^u\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N h(x_i)\) on \(\mathbb R^N\), separability gives \(H^*(u)=\sum_{i=1}^N e^{u_i}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domains are \(\operatorname{dom}h=[0,+\infty)\), \(\operatorname{dom}h^*=\mathbb R\), \(\operatorname{dom}b=(0,+\infty)\), and \(\operatorname{dom}b^*=(-\infty,0)\).
boundary_notes: Changing the normalization from \(x\log x-x\) to \(x\log x\) translates the exponential conjugate by a constant in its argument.
The logarithmic pair here is the negative Burg entropy, not the concave logarithm regarded without a sign change.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Boundary Subgradient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized entropy has logarithmic derivative in the positive interior but no finite subgradient at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(h_a(x)=a(x\log x-x)+\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(x)\) with \(a>0\),
\[
\partial h_a(x)=\{a\log x\}\quad(x>0),
\qquad
\partial h_a(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus \(h_a\) is strictly convex and differentiable on \((0,+\infty)\), but it has no finite supporting slope at its finite boundary point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential behavior of scalar normalized entropy at the boundary of its nonnegative domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled normalized entropy on the nonnegative half-line conjugates to a scaled exponential that is finite and smooth on the entire dual line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the scaled normalized entropy by
\[
h_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
a(x\log x-x),&x\geq0,\\
+\infty,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(h_a\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and strictly convex on its effective domain, and
\[
h_a^*(y)=a\exp(y/a),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Thus the entropy class is an extended-valued class enforcing nonnegativity, while its conjugate is finite and smooth on the entire dual line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized entropy function has conjugate \(h_a^*(y)=a\exp(y/a)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar normalized entropy extended to the nonnegative half-line.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy and the maximizing softmax representation for negative entropy restricted to the unit simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\), and define \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\) for \(x\in\Delta_n\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, with \(0\log0=0\). For every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the maximizer in \(f^*(y)=\max_{x\in\Delta_n}\{y^Tx-\sum_i x_i\log x_i\}\) is \[x_i^*=\frac{e^{y_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^n e^{y_j}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\] and \[f^*(y)=\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^n e^{y_j}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of negative entropy restricted to the probability simplex is log-sum-exp, and its maximizing simplex point is the softmax of y.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Conjugate Boundary Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential conjugate is finite at zero, but its defining supremum is attained only for positive dual arguments, not at the boundary zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) with \(a>0\), the conjugate value at \(x=0\) is
\[
e_a^*(0)=0,
\]
but the supremum \(\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}\{-e_a(y)\}\) is not attained at any finite \(y\). For \(x>0\), the unique maximizer is \(y=a\log x\); for \(x<0\), the conjugate is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary for the conjugate of a scaled scalar exponential.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled exponential conjugates to normalized entropy with a nonnegative-domain constraint; their interior gradients are inverse through the exponential and logarithm maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) for \(y\in\mathbb{R}\). Its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
e_a^*(x)=
\begin{cases}
a(x\log x-x),&x\geq0,\\
+\infty,&x<0,
\end{cases}
\]
with \(0\log0=0\). Hence every member of this scaled exponential class is proper, closed, strictly convex, and everywhere finite, whereas its conjugate imposes the nonnegative-domain constraint. The gradient relation \(x=\exp(y/a)\) identifies the mutually inverse interior gradient coordinates \(y=a\log x\) for \(x>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled exponential \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) has conjugate equal to normalized entropy on \([0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled scalar exponentials and their extended-valued conjugates.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled negative logarithm on the positive half-line conjugates to a shifted negative logarithm on the negative half-line, with primal and dual variables related reciprocally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\ell_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
-a\log x,&x>0,\\
+\infty,&x\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
\ell_a^*(y)=
\begin{cases}
a\bigl(\log a-1-\log(-y)\bigr),&y<0,\\
+\infty,&y\geq0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus conjugation maps the positive-domain negative-logarithm class to a logarithmic class on the negative dual half-line. On the interiors of their domains, the primal and dual variables satisfy \(y=-a/x\), expressing the reciprocal gradient correspondence characteristic of logarithmic barriers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The negative-logarithm barrier conjugates to a shifted negative logarithm supported on the negative dual half-line.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar negative-logarithm barriers on the positive half-line.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy–Exponential Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized entropy and scaled exponential are mutual Fenchel conjugates. Their gradient maps, logarithm and exponential, are inverse and characterize equality in the Fenchel–Young inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
h_a(x)=a(x\log x-x)+\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a),
\]
one has the reciprocal conjugacy relations
\[
h_a^*=e_a\qquad\text{and}\qquad e_a^*=h_a.
\]
For \(x>0\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), Fenchel–Young equality is equivalent to
\[
y=a\log x\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x=\exp(y/a),
\]
and then \(h_a(x)+e_a(y)=xy\). Coordinatewise summation gives the corresponding separable entropy–exponential duality on finite-dimensional product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The entropy and exponential functions form a Fenchel-conjugate pair, and their interior gradients are inverse.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Fenchel duality between normalized entropy and scaled exponential.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space with norm \(\|\cdot\|\), let \(q(x)=\|x\|^2/2\), and define \(d_C(u)=\inf_{x\in C}\|u-x\|\) for each nonempty \(C\subset\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The radial formula uses Hilbert self-duality and an even scalar profile. The distance formula permits a nonconvex set \(C\), since the conjugate is defined for arbitrary proper extended-real functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance–radial conjugacy family consists of the following templates. First, for an even proper function \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the radial lifting \(R_\phi(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) has conjugate \(R_\phi^*(u)=\phi^*(\|u\|)\). Second, for a nonempty set \(C\subset\mathcal H\), define \(F_C=\iota_C+q\), where \(\iota_C\) is zero on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) off \(C\). Its conjugate is the distance-generated function \(F_C^*(u)=(\|u\|^2-d_C(u)^2)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even scalar profile can be lifted to a radial function by composing it with the Hilbert norm, and conjugation acts by conjugating the scalar profile. A second canonical class starts from the squared norm restricted to a nonempty set; its conjugate is one half of the squared norm minus the squared distance to that set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\phi^*(\|u\|)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\rho\|u\|-\phi(\rho)\}\quad\text{when \(\phi\) is even}.\]
\[F_C^*(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\left\{\langle x,u\rangle-\frac12\|x\|^2\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathcal H\), then \(d_C=0\) and \(q^*=q\).
If \(\phi(t)=|t|\), then \(R_\phi(x)=\|x\|\) and \(R_\phi^*=\iota_{B(0,1)}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(u\mapsto\|u\|^2-d_C(u)^2\) is convex even when \(C\) is not convex.
boundary_notes: For a general Banach norm, the radial conjugate is naturally expressed using the dual norm rather than the same norm.
The distance-generated identity concerns \(\iota_C+q\), not the conjugate of \(d_C\) itself.

knowledge_statements.title: Hölder-Power Distance Conjugates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder power of distance conjugates to the support function of the set plus the corresponding dual Hölder power.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(1<p<\infty\), and set \(q=p/(p-1)\). For \(F_p(x)=d_C(x)^p/p\),
\[
F_p=\delta_C\square \frac1p\|\cdot\|^p,
\qquad
F_p^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\frac1q\|y\|^q.
\]
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive powers greater than one of Euclidean distance to a nonempty closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a closed convex set conjugates to its support function with a unit-ball constraint; half squared distance replaces that constraint by a quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d_C(x)=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\), the conjugacy formulas are
\[
d_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\delta_B(y)
\]
and
\[
\left(\tfrac12 d_C^2\right)^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\tfrac12\|y\|^2.
\]
Thus the unsquared distance class produces a hard dual-norm constraint, while the half squared-distance class produces a quadratic dual penalty. Both formulas retain the geometry of \(C\) solely through its support function. In particular, translations of \(C\) contribute the corresponding linear term to each conjugate.
assumptions_latex: The set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Distance and support are computed using the Euclidean norm and pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distance and squared-distance conjugates equal the support function plus, respectively, a unit-ball indicator or a dual quadratic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean distance and half squared distance to a closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection and Differential Structure of Convex Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and differential properties for distance to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Each \(x\) has a unique projection \(P_Cx\), characterized by
\[
\langle x-P_Cx,z-P_Cx\rangle\le0\quad(z\in C).
\]
The function \(d_C\) is convex and \(1\)-Lipschitz, with
\[
\partial d_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
\{(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\},&x\notin C,\\
N_C(x)\cap B,&x\in C.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, \(\tfrac12d_C^2\) is continuously differentiable and
\[
\nabla(\tfrac12d_C^2)(x)=x-P_Cx,
\]
with a \(1\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is unique; distance is convex and Lipschitz, while half squared distance is smooth with projection-residual gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection characterization, distance-subdifferential formulas, and \(\nabla(\tfrac12d_C^2)=I-P_C\) hold.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of x onto C

Convex Radial Profile Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean radial function is closed proper convex exactly when its unique radius profile is closed proper convex and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge1\), a radial function \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex if and only if \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing. Its profile is unique and satisfies \(\phi(r)=f(re)\) for every unit vector \(e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of proper lower-semicontinuous convex Euclidean radial functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation preserves Euclidean radial convexity: conjugating a function of the norm reduces exactly to taking the one-sided scalar conjugate of its radial profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) and the one-sided scalar conjugate
\[
\phi_+^*(s)=\sup_{r\geq0}\{rs-\phi(r)\},\qquad s\geq0.
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and radial, and its Fenchel conjugate satisfies
\[
f^*(y)=\phi_+^*(\|y\|).
\]
Hence Euclidean Fenchel conjugation preserves the radial class and reduces the multidimensional transform to a scalar transform of the radius profile. The formula includes extended-valued profiles and therefore covers norm constraints, norm powers, and radial barriers whenever their profiles satisfy the stated hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its Euclidean norm.
The profile \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean radial convex functions generated by nondecreasing convex profiles.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal explicit conjugate pairs within the Euclidean radial class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\). For \(\alpha>0\), \(1<p<\infty\), and \(q=p/(p-1)\),
\[
\left(\frac{\alpha}{p}\|\cdot\|^p\right)^*(y)=\frac{\alpha^{1-q}}{q}\|y\|^q.
\]
The endpoint pairs are
\[
(\alpha\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\alpha B},
\qquad
(\delta_{RB})^*(y)=R\|y\|\quad(R\ge0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm powers conjugate through Hölder exponents, while scaled norms and ball indicators form endpoint pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed power, norm, and ball conjugacy formulas hold.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alignment of subgradients with the radius and behavior at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\), with \(\phi\) proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing. If \(x\ne0\), then
\[
\partial f(x)=\left\{\alpha\frac{x}{\|x\|}:\alpha\in\partial\phi(\|x\|)\right\}.
\]
At the origin,
\[
\partial f(0)=\{y:\|y\|\le\phi'_+(0)\},
\]
where radius \(+\infty\) means all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial subgradients align with the radius, and at the origin they form a centered ball.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) with \(\phi\) proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed nonzero-point and origin subdifferential formulas hold.

Powered Radial Ball-Distance Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder power of distance to a centered ball conjugates to the ball-radius norm term plus the dual Hölder power.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\ge0\), \(1<p<\infty\), and \(q=p/(p-1)\). For
\[
F_{p,R}(x)=\frac1p(\|x\|-R)_+^p=\frac1p d_{RB}(x)^p,
\]
one has
\[
F_{p,R}^*(y)=R\|y\|+\frac1q\|y\|^q.
\]
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is the closed Euclidean unit ball}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder powers of distance to a centered Euclidean ball.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Distance Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a centered ball is a radial hinge profile. In the conjugate, the ball radius becomes a norm coefficient and squaring replaces the dual ball constraint by a quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Distance to the centered ball has the radial profile
\[
d_{RB}(x)=(\|x\|-R)_+.
\]
Because \(\sigma_{RB}(y)=R\|y\|\), its conjugate and the conjugate of its half square are
\[
d_{RB}^*(y)=R\|y\|+\delta_B(y),
\qquad
\left(\tfrac12d_{RB}^2\right)^*(y)=R\|y\|+\tfrac12\|y\|^2.
\]
These formulas exhibit the radial distance transition explicitly: the primal threshold radius becomes a dual norm coefficient, while the unsquared or squared outer profile becomes, respectively, a unit-ball constraint or a quadratic penalty.
assumptions_latex: The set \(B\) is the closed Euclidean unit ball in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For distance to \(RB\), the conjugates are \(R\|y\|+\delta_B(y)\) and \(R\|y\|+\tfrac12\|y\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial profiles arising from distance to a centered Euclidean ball.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and bounded below by an affine function. Define \(f^*(u)=\sup_x(\langle u,x\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_u(\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional extended-real correspondence under the affine-minorant condition, which prevents the closed convex envelope from taking the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugation–convexification correspondence identifies \(f^{**}\) with the closed lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\): \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}f\). Equivalently, \(f^{**}\) is the pointwise greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function \(g\) satisfying \(g\leq f\), and its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph, \(\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper finite-dimensional function admitting an affine lower bound, taking two Fenchel conjugates is exactly closed convexification. The biconjugate is the largest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of the original function, and its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ is lower-semicontinuous and convex}\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle-\beta:\langle u,y\rangle-\beta\leq f(y)\ \forall y\}.\]
\[f=f^{**}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex but not lower-semicontinuous, then \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\).
If \(f\) is already proper, closed, and convex, biconjugation leaves it unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The universal inequality \(f^{**}\leq f\) holds pointwise.
Conjugation cannot distinguish \(f\) from its closed convex envelope because \(f^*=(f^{**})^*\).
boundary_notes: Without an affine minorant, the greatest closed convex minorant can be identically \(-\infty\), outside the usual proper-function class.
In non-Hausdorff or nonseparating dual systems, the relevant closure and convexification must be taken relative to the topology generated by the chosen dual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel conjugation, biconjugation, and fixed points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space. Extended-real functions take values in \((-\infty,+\infty]\), and proper means nowhere \(-\infty\), not identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry defines the Hilbert-space Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation operator and the class of its proper fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), its Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate are \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f^*(u))\). Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation is the operation \(f\mapsto f^{**}\). Its proper fixed-point class is exactly \(\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions: for proper \(f\), \(f=f^{**}\) if and only if \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation applies the Fenchel conjugate twice. On a real Hilbert space, the proper functions fixed by this operation are exactly the lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal H}\left\{\langle x,u\rangle-\sup_{y\in\mathcal H}(\langle y,u\rangle-f(y))\right\},\qquad f=f^{**}\iff f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper \(f\), \(f=f^{**}\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) being a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathcal H\times\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), \(\iota_C^{**}=\iota_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every proper \(f\), \(f^{**}\leq f\).
If \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), then \(f^*\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
boundary_notes: On a nonreflexive Banach space, the second conjugate naturally lives on the bidual unless it is explicitly restricted back to the canonical image of the primal space.
The fixed-point characterization requires properness; identically infinite functions require separate conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Biconjugation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a proper function equals its biconjugate exactly when it is lower-semicontinuous and convex; otherwise the proper biconjugate is its closed convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\},
\qquad
f^{**}(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)\}.
\]
The finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau theorem states that
\[
f=f^{**}
\]
if and only if \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex. More generally, whenever the closed convex envelope is proper,
\[
f^{**}=\operatorname{clconv}f,
\]
meaning that \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Thus biconjugation is precisely the finite-dimensional closed-convexification operation.
assumptions_latex: The space is finite-dimensional, identified with \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and its usual dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(f=f^{**}\) exactly when \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex; generally \(f^{**}\) is its closed convex envelope when proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation on finite-dimensional real vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp qualification for interpreting the finite-dimensional biconjugate as a proper closed convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Then \(f^{**}\) is proper if and only if \(f\) admits an affine minorant, equivalently if and only if \(f^*(y)<+\infty\) for some \(y\in\mathbb R^n\). If no affine minorant exists, then \(f^*\equiv+\infty\) and \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper finite-dimensional function has a proper biconjugate exactly when it has an affine lower bound; otherwise its biconjugate is identically minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: Conjugation uses the usual Euclidean dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}\text{ is proper}\iff(\exists y\in\mathbb R^n,\,a\in\mathbb R)\;\langle y,x\rangle+a\le f(x)\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n\); otherwise \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional regime, where ordinary Euclidean closedness, sequential lower semicontinuity, and weak closedness coincide for convex epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite-dimensional biconjugation assigns \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R^n}(\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u))\). It is equivalently the supremum at \(x\) of every affine function minorizing \(f\): \(f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle-\beta:\langle u,y\rangle-\beta\leq f(y)\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}\). Thus \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}f\), with closure taken in the standard topology of \(\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a real separating dual pair, so each nonzero element of either space is detected by an element of the other. Equip \(X\) with a Hausdorff locally convex topology \(\tau\) whose continuous dual is \(Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define the dual-pair conjugates by \(f^Y(y)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{YY}(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}(\langle x,y\rangle-f^Y(y))\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On L^p for 0<p<1, the continuous dual is trivial, so the biconjugate of the zero-singleton indicator is the zero function rather than the original closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<p<1\), let \(X=L^p([0,1])\) over Lebesgue measure with its usual quasi-norm topology. This Hausdorff non-locally-convex space has continuous dual \(X'=\{0\}\). Thus Hausdorffness alone does not provide enough continuous linear functionals for pointwise biconjugate recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Convex Space Biconjugation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Hausdorff locally convex space, a proper function equals its continuous-dual biconjugate exactly when it is convex and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x'\in X'\), define \(f^*(x')=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle x',x\rangle-f(x)\}\), and for \(x\in X\), define \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_{x'\in X'}\{\langle x',x\rangle-f^*(x')\}\). Then \(f^{**}\leq f\), and \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Consequently, \(f=f^{**}\) holds exactly when \(f\) is convex and lower semicontinuous for the given locally convex topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every pairing-based biconjugate is constant on cosets of the annihilator: for all \(x\in X\) and \(n\in N\), \[f^{**}(x+n)=f^{**}(x).\] Consequently, if \(N\ne\{0\}\), the proper convex function \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) cannot equal its biconjugate, since its values at \(0\) and a nonzero \(n\in N\) differ whereas the biconjugate cannot distinguish those points. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally convex topology is compatible with a separated dual pair exactly when it lies between the weak and Mackey topologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hausdorff locally convex topology \(\tau\) on \(X\) is compatible with the separated dual pair \((X,Y)\) precisely when its continuous dual is \(Y\). The Mackey–Arens theorem gives the equivalent characterization \[(X,\tau)'=Y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sigma(X,Y)\subseteq\tau\subseteq\tau(X,Y),\] where \(\tau(X,Y)\) is the topology of uniform convergence on absolutely convex \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-compact subsets of \(Y\). Thus \(\sigma(X,Y)\) and \(\tau(X,Y)\) are respectively the coarsest and finest compatible locally convex topologies.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every convex subset \(C\subseteq X\) has the same closure in \(\tau\) as in \(\sigma(X,Y)\): \(\overline C^{\tau}=\overline C^{\sigma(X,Y)}\). Therefore conjugation against \(Y\) recovers the \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous convex envelope, despite being defined solely by the pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach dual and Hilbert self-dual biconjugation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\), bidual \(X^{**}\), and canonical embedding \(J:X\to X^{**}\). A Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\) is identified with its continuous dual through the Riesz map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition explicitly separates the Banach-space bidual transform from the Hilbert-space self-dual specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x))\). Its full Banach biconjugate is \(f^{**}:X^{**}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f^{**}(x^{**})=\sup_{x^*\in X^*}(\langle x^{**},x^*\rangle-f^*(x^*))\); the primal biconjugate is \(f^{**}\circ J\). In a Hilbert space, the Riesz identification turns both conjugates into functions on \(\mathcal H\), yielding \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_u(\langle x,u\rangle-f^*(u))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Banach space the first conjugate lives on the continuous dual and the full second conjugate lives on the bidual; evaluation on the canonical image returns a primal function. In a Hilbert space, Riesz self-duality lets all three functions be represented on the same space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)),\qquad f^{**}(x^{**})=\sup_{x^*\in X^*}(\langle x^{**},x^*\rangle-f^*(x^*)),\qquad f^{**}_{X}=f^{**}\circ J.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(X\) is reflexive, \(J(X)=X^{**}\), so the full and primal biconjugation regimes can be identified.
For Hilbert \(\mathcal H\), the Riesz map replaces \(X^*\) and \(X^{**}\) by copies of \(\mathcal H\).
special_cases_latex: Every finite-dimensional Banach space is reflexive, although the coordinate formula still depends on the chosen primal-dual pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: For proper norm-lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), the primal restriction satisfies \(f=f^{**}\circ J\).
boundary_notes: In a nonreflexive Banach space, values of the full biconjugate outside \(J(X)\) are not values of the original primal function.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflexive Space Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a reflexive Banach space, the bidual is canonically the primal space, so biconjugation recovers the function and triple conjugation recovers its conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical embedding \(J\) is surjective, so \(X^{**}\) may be identified with \(X\). Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation then gives \(f^{**}(Jx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Moreover, \(f^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous, and applying biconjugation on the reflexive space \(X^*\) yields \(f^{***}=f^*\). Thus conjugation alternates symmetrically between \(X\) and \(X^*\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. All comparisons are pointwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy distinguishes algebraic convexification from the additional lower-semicontinuous closure required for biconjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope of \(f\) is \(\operatorname{co}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex}\}\). Its closed convex envelope is \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{co}f)=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ closed and convex}\}\). The canonical hierarchy is \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\leq\operatorname{co}f\leq f\). Equality in the right inequality characterizes convexity; equality throughout characterizes closed convexity, subject to properness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope is the greatest convex minorant, while the closed convex envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant. The latter equals the biconjugate and can lie strictly below the convex envelope when the convex envelope is not closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{co}f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i):\lambda\in\Delta_k,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.\]
\[\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{co}f=f\) and only the possible closure step remains.
If \(f\) is proper closed convex, then all three functions coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: The two possible defects are the nonconvexity gap \(f-\operatorname{co}f\) and the nonclosedness gap \(\operatorname{co}f-\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\).
boundary_notes: The pointwise supremum definitions require a nonempty family of admissible minorants; the affine-minorant hypothesis guarantees this.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope is the greatest convex minorant of a function, equivalently the infimum of its values averaged over finite convex decompositions of each point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope of \(f\) is the pointwise greatest convex function below \(f\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic laws of the proper closed-convexification operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On proper extended-real functions admitting continuous affine minorants, define \(E(f)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f=f^{**}\). Then \[E(f)\le f,\qquad f\le g\Longrightarrow E(f)\le E(g),\qquad E(E(f))=E(f).\] Moreover, \(E(f)=f\) exactly when \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convexification is contractive, monotone, and idempotent, with the lower-semicontinuous convex functions as its fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
The proper functions considered admit continuous affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\le\operatorname{id}\), \(E\) is monotone and idempotent, and \(E(f)=f\iff f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convexification Operator Laws
Pointwise Lower-Limit Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous closure is the neighborhood lower limit; equivalently it is obtained from convergent nets, or from sequences in first-countable spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
(\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{z\in U}g(z)
=\inf_{z_\alpha\to x}\liminf_\alpha g(z_\alpha),
\]
where the second infimum ranges over all convergent nets. If \(X\) is first countable, nets may be replaced by sequences:
\[
(\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\inf_{z_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}g(z_n).
\]
assumptions_latex: The displayed lower-semicontinuous regularization is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise topological representation of the lower-semicontinuous closure of an already convex function; nets are required without first countability.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Convex Closures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, its lower-semicontinuous closure is defined by closing its epigraph; the operation fixes exactly the lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous convex closure \(\operatorname{cl}g\) is the function whose epigraph is the closure of the convex epigraph of \(g\) in \(X\times\mathbb R\): \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}g)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{cl}g\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function majorized by \(g\); it remains convex because the closure of a convex set is convex. Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}g=g\) exactly when \(g\) is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
\(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex, and its lower-semicontinuous minorant is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure operation for an already convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Does Not Imply Lower Semicontinuity at a Domain Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional boundary example showing that lower-semicontinuous closure can strictly change a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[g(0)=1,\qquad g(x)=0\ \text{for }x>0,\qquad g(x)=+\infty\ \text{for }x<0.\] Then \(g\) is proper and convex but is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\), and its closure satisfies \((\operatorname{cl}g)(0)=0<g(0)\) while agreeing with \(g\) elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function may fail lower semicontinuity at a domain boundary, where closure lowers its value.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is defined by the displayed formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Does Not Imply Lower Semicontinuity at a Domain Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order and Idempotence of Lower-Semicontinuous Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator laws for lower-semicontinuous closure on convex functions while properness is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Lower-semicontinuous closure is a monotone idempotent minorant operation: \[\operatorname{cl}g\le g,\qquad g\le h\Longrightarrow\operatorname{cl}g\le\operatorname{cl}h,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}g)=\operatorname{cl}g.\] Its fixed points are precisely the lower-semicontinuous functions in the stated convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-semicontinuous closure is monotone, lies below its input, is idempotent, and fixes exactly the lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
The convex functions and their lower-semicontinuous closures are proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}g\le g\), the closure operation is monotone and idempotent, and \(\operatorname{cl}g=g\iff g\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Order and Idempotence of Lower-Semicontinuous Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Formula for the Lower-Semicontinuous Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological pointwise representation of the closure of an already convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \[(\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{y\in U}g(y).\] Equivalently, this is the topological lower limit \(\liminf_{y\to x}g(y)\), interpreted through neighborhoods or nets rather than sequences in a non-first-countable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous closure at a point is the supremum of neighborhood infima, equivalently the topological lower limit.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
The lower-semicontinuous minorant of \(g\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Formula for the Lower-Semicontinuous Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Sublevel Transfer from Closure to Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex function evaluated on the closure and relative interior of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex, let \(C\) be convex with \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). If there exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{cl}C\) such that \(f(x_0)<\alpha\), then there exists \(x_{\mathrm{ri}}\in\operatorname{ri}C\) such that \(f(x_{\mathrm{ri}})<\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the relative interior of a convex set lies in a convex function's domain, a strict-sublevel witness in the set's closure implies one in its relative interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of an Improper Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure behavior in the improper extended-real-valued regime, including agreement on the relative interior of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be an improper convex function. Then \(\operatorname{cl}f\) is a closed improper convex function and \((\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of an improper convex function remains convex and improper, is closed, and agrees with the original function throughout the relative interior of its effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Function Closure Is Determined by Relative-Interior Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality criterion for the lower-semicontinuous closures of two convex functions on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be convex functions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) and \(f(x)=g(x)\) for every \(x\) in this common relative interior, then \(\operatorname{cl}f=\operatorname{cl}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex functions have the same closure when their effective domains have the same relative interior and the functions agree throughout that common relative interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial representation of the lower-semicontinuous convex closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial evaluation of a convex function's closure from a relative-interior point of its effective domain, including the stated improper-function boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty] be convex and proper, and let x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f). Then, for every y\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\[(\operatorname{cl}f)(y)=\lim_{\lambda\uparrow 1}f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y).\]
The same identity holds when f is improper, provided x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f) and y\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}f).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, a radial limit from any relative-interior point of its effective domain recovers the closed hull at every point. The identity also holds for an improper convex function at points in the closure of its effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Convex Lower Bound Extends to the Closure of a Finiteness Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of a lower bound from a convex set to its closure when the convex function is finite on the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex with \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(f(x)\geq\alpha\) for every \(x\in C\), then \(f(x)\geq\alpha\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function is finite and bounded below on a convex set, the same lower bound holds on the set's closure.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\). For a set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\), define its lower-bound function by \(\ell_C(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in C\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates algebraic convexification from closed epigraphical convexification and explicitly repairs the bottom of a hull when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraphical convexification of \(f\) is the lower-bound function \(\ell_{\operatorname{co}E}\); equivalently it is \(\operatorname{co}f\). Its closed epigraphical convexification is \(\ell_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}E}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f=f^{**}\), provided \(f\) is proper and admits an affine minorant. The first construction takes the convex hull of the epigraph and then closes each vertical bottom; the second takes the closed convex hull, which is already an epigraph under these hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical convexification forms a convex hull of the epigraph and reads off its lower boundary. Because the ordinary convex hull may omit boundary points, its vertical bottoms must be closed. Taking the closed convex hull of the epigraph directly yields the closed convex envelope and hence the biconjugate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\ell_C(x)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb R:(x,r)\in C\}.\]
The epigraphical hull of \(C\) is the smallest epigraph containing \(C\), namely \(\operatorname{epi}\ell_C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) already has closed vertical bottoms, it equals \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Epigraphical convexification converts a geometric hull operation in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) into a pointwise envelope operation on functions.
boundary_notes: In general \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\neq\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\); bottom closure is the missing operation.
Topological closure and vertical-bottom closure are conceptually distinct.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Attainment Criterion for Epigraph-Hull Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph hull equals the convex-envelope epigraph exactly when every finite envelope value has an attaining finite mixture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:V\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have nonempty domain. Then \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) if and only if, for every \(x\) with \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)<+\infty\), the finite-mixture infimum defining \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)\) is attained. Equivalently, every lower-boundary point \((x,(\operatorname{co}f)(x))\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) if and only if every finite convex-envelope value is attained by a finite mixture.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion distinguishing the algebraic epigraph hull from the full convex-envelope epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing Lower-Boundary Point Under Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this function, the convex-envelope value at the origin is zero but no finite mixture attains it, so the epigraph hull omits the lower-boundary point while containing every point strictly above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f(-1)=0\), \(f(x)=x\) for \(x>0\), and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), but no finite convex decomposition of \(0\) attains weighted value \(0\). Consequently \((0,0)\in\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\setminus\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), whereas \((0,r)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example witnessing strict inclusion between the algebraic epigraph hull and the convex-envelope epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hulls of Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of an epigraph consists of finite mixtures of epigraph points; it matches the convex-envelope epigraph above the boundary, while unattained boundary points may be missing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \((x,r)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) exactly when there are finitely many \(x_i\in V\), \(r_i\geq f(x_i)\), and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\), and \(r=\sum_i\lambda_i r_i\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\), while every \((x,r)\) with \(r>(\operatorname{co}f)(x)\) lies in \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). Boundary equality may fail when the defining infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) and the two sets have identical strict upper sections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic epigraph convexification, including possible nonattainment at the lower boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of equality between the algebraic convex hull of an epigraph and the epigraph of its convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be given by \(f(1/n)=f(-1/n)=1/n\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\), and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), every \((0,1/n)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), but \((0,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). Hence \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subsetneq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete symmetric function attains convex-envelope value zero at the origin only as a limiting mixture, so its epigraph hull omits the lower boundary point.
