knowledge_statements.statement_title: Function generated by the convex hull of an epigraph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and bounded below by an affine function, and let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry concerns the nonclosed convex hull \(\operatorname{co}E\) and the lower boundary it induces, rather than its topological closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex-hull-of-epigraph function is \(h(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{co}E\}\). It is convex and equals the convex envelope \(\operatorname{co}f\). Its epigraph is the epigraphical hull of \(\operatorname{co}E\), obtained by adding the omitted vertical bottom points when the infimum is not attained. Equivalently, \(h\) is the greatest convex function satisfying \(h\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take all finite convex combinations of points in the epigraph and then read the lowest attainable height over each base point. The resulting lower-bound function is the convex envelope. Its epigraph can be slightly larger than the raw convex hull because an unattained lowest height must be inserted.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[h(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i):k\geq1,\ \lambda\in\Delta_k,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If the infimum defining \(h(x)\) is attained for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), then \(\operatorname{co}E\) has its vertical bottoms and equals \(\operatorname{epi}h\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The projection of \(\operatorname{co}E\) onto \(\mathbb R^n\) is \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), which is the effective-domain hull of \(h\).
boundary_notes: The raw set \(\operatorname{co}E\) need not be closed and need not itself be an epigraph.
Replacing \(\operatorname{co}E\) by its closed convex hull produces the closed convex envelope instead.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Continuous Affine Minorant
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minus x squared, the conjugate is everywhere infinite, the biconjugate is minus infinity, and the closed convex hull of the epigraph is the whole plane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=-x^2\). Then \(f\) is proper but has no affine minorant, \(f^*(u)=+\infty\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\), and hence \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\). Moreover, \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\mathbb R^2\). Thus, without an affine minorant, the closed convex hull need not be the epigraph of a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of proper epigraphical biconjugation when the affine-minorant hypothesis is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Epigraph Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the convex hull of a function's epigraph produces the epigraph of its closed convex envelope, equivalently its continuous-dual biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Taking closure in \(X\times\mathbb R\) removes finite-mixture nonattainment and yields an epigraph: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f).\] Since the closed convex envelope equals the continuous-dual biconjugate, this is equivalently \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\operatorname{epi}(f^{**}).\] Thus closed epigraphical convexification and Fenchel biconjugation describe the same function under the stated properness and affine-minorant assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and has a continuous affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-topology closure supplies both convexification and lower-semicontinuous boundary completion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed convex epigraph hull and its lower-bound function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Set \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(K=\overline{\operatorname{co}}E\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure is Euclidean closure in the product space. The affine-minorant condition prevents vertical lines extending to \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed epigraph hull of \(f\) is \(K=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). It is an upward-closed closed convex set and therefore the epigraph of the function \(h(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in K\}\). This function is closed and convex, equals \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\), and equals \(f^{**}\). Thus \(K=\operatorname{epi}h=\operatorname{epi}f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull of an epigraph remains upward closed and has closed vertical bottoms, so it is itself an epigraph. Its lower-bound function is the closed convex envelope and the Fenchel biconjugate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{**}=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ closed and convex}\}.\]
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle-\beta:\langle u,\cdot\rangle-\beta\leq f\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is already closed and convex, then \(K=\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The hull operation is idempotent: \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}K=K\), corresponding to \((f^{**})^{**}=f^{**}\).
boundary_notes: For functions without an affine lower bound, the closed convex hull can contain downward vertical lines and may fail to encode a proper extended-real function.
The closure is taken after convexification; the result nevertheless equals the closure of the convex envelope under the stated hypotheses.

notation.meaning: closed convex hull of the original epigraph

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be bounded, and let \(\phi:S\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) have a closed convex epigraph in \(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}\). knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Let \(\Delta_k=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^k:\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Carathéodory is applied to the epigraph in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), giving the direct bound \(n+2\) on mixture size. A sharper \(n+1\) bound for the function-value formula requires an additional refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Carathéodory finite-mixture convexification of \(f\) is \(M_f(x)=\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i):1\leq k\leq n+2,\ \lambda\in\Delta_k,\ x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\}\). It equals \(\operatorname{co}f(x)\). Geometrically, every point of \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+2\) epigraph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-dimensional convexification can be computed using only finite mixtures. Applying Carathéodory’s theorem in the epigraph space shows that no more than n plus two epigraph points are needed, and the resulting infimum is the convex envelope.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For each \((x,r)\in\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), there exist \(k\leq n+2\), \((x_i,r_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f\), and \(\lambda\in\Delta_k\) such that \((x,r)=\sum_i\lambda_i(x_i,r_i)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the direct epigraph bound is three mixture points.
When the infimum is attained at an exposed lower-boundary point, redundant mixture points may often be removed.
immediate_consequences_latex: The algebraic convex envelope in finite dimensions requires no infinite probability measure or infinite convex combination.
boundary_notes: The formula defines \(+\infty\) when \(x\notin\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
Carathéodory alone yields \(n+2\) in the \((n+1)\)-dimensional epigraph; the cited source notes a refinement to \(n+1\) for the envelope formula.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example showing that the algebraic finite-mixture formula can have a finite unattained infimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support bounds sharpen to one plus the relevant affine dimension: d+1 epigraph points and q+1 locations for an attained envelope value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\), and put \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}(E)\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) has support at most \(d+1\), and every attained finite envelope value has location support at most \(q+1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Support Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of the epigraph uses at most n+2 epigraph points, while an attained finite convex-envelope value has an optimal mixture supported on at most n+1 locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), there exist an integer \(m\le n+2\), weights \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), and points \((x_i,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) such that \((x,t)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(x_i,t_i)\). Moreover, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and suppose there exist an integer \(k\ge1\), weights \(\mu_j\ge0\), and points \(z_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_j=1\), \(\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_jz_j=x\), and \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_jf(z_j)\). Then there is such an optimal representation with at most \(n+1\) positive weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) has a representation using at most \(n+2\) epigraph points, and every attained finite convex-envelope value has an optimal mixture using at most \(n+1\) locations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite conic representation of a generated positively homogeneous convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-bounded functional representation arising at the interface between convexification and conic Carathéodory theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(k\) be the positively homogeneous convex function generated by \(f\) (equivalently, by \(\operatorname{conv}f\)). For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\),
\[
k(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i)\;\middle|\;x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.
\]
The formula remains valid when the representing vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are restricted to be linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every nonzero vector, the positively homogeneous convex function generated by f is obtained by minimizing the weighted f-values over n-term nonnegative linear representations of that vector. The same infimum results when the representing vectors are required to be linearly independent.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is the positively homogeneous convex function generated by }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i)\mid x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i=x\right\},\quad\text{with the same value under linear independence of }x_1,\ldots,x_n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse finite-mixture formula for the convex hull of convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Carathéodory support bound for epigraphical convexification of an indexed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{f_i\mid i\in I\}\) be an arbitrary collection of proper convex functions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f=\operatorname{conv}\{f_i\mid i\in I\}\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i\in J}\lambda_i f_i(x_i): J\subseteq I,\ |J|\le n+1,\ \lambda_i>0,\ \sum_{i\in J}\lambda_i=1,\ \sum_{i\in J}\lambda_i x_i=x,\ \{x_i:i\in J\}\text{ affinely independent}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of any family of proper convex functions on R^n is obtained pointwise by minimizing finite weighted sums over convex decompositions of the argument. At most n+1 positive weights are needed, their associated points may be required to be affinely independent, and the active indices correspond to distinct functions from the family.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Mixture Supports
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support-minimal mixture attaining the convex envelope uses affinely independent locations, so it has no more than n+1 positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an optimal mixture
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i,\qquad (\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i),\qquad \lambda_i>0,
\]
whose number of positive weights is minimal among all optimal mixtures at \(x\). Then \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\) is affinely independent. Consequently \(m\le n+1\). Equivalently, if the active locations are affinely dependent, the mixture is not support-minimal: an optimal feasible perturbation of its weights can eliminate at least one active index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every support-minimal optimal mixture has affinely independent locations and therefore at most \(n+1\) positive weights.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support minimality among mixtures attaining one convex-envelope value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Independence Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Support Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits the affine-independence test to a necessary condition for global support minimality among all optimal mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine independence of an optimal mixture's active locations does not by itself imply support minimality. For example, let \(f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)=0\) and \(f=+\infty\) elsewhere. At \(x=0\), the mixture \(0=\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(1)\) is optimal and has affinely independent active locations, but the one-point mixture supported at \(0\) is also optimal. Hence the two-point mixture is not support-minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine independence prevents reduction within a fixed active set but does not exclude a different optimal mixture with smaller support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{-1,1\}\text{ is affinely independent, but its optimal two-point mixture is not support-minimal}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure set for exact recovery by biconjugation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant, so \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary is defined pointwise in finite dimensions and separates failure caused by nonconvexity from failure caused solely by lack of lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugation failure boundary of \(f\) is \(\mathcal B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}\), where the extended-real order is used. With \(c=\operatorname{co}f\), it decomposes into the nonconvexity boundary \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)=\{x:c(x)<f(x)\}\) and the closure boundary \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\{x:f^{**}(x)<c(x)\}\). Hence \(\mathcal B(f)=\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)\cup\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)\), and exact biconjugate recovery is equivalent to \(\mathcal B(f)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure boundary is the set where the biconjugate lies strictly below the original function. It is the union of points lost during convexification and points lost during lower-semicontinuous closure. It is empty exactly for proper closed convex functions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathcal B(f)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is closed and convex}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)=\varnothing\).
If \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous but nonconvex, failure may remain entirely in \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A point outside \(\mathcal B(f)\) is a contact point between \(f\) and its greatest closed convex minorant.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns strict pointwise loss, not numerical instability or dual nonattainment.
If the affine-minorant condition fails, the biconjugate may be improper and the decomposition needs extended-value conventions beyond this scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Biconjugate Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function equal to zero at minus one and one, and one elsewhere, has zero biconjugate everywhere and a strict gap at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(-1)=f(1)=0\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\notin\{-1,1\}\). Every convex minorant of \(f\) that is finite on \(\mathbb{R}\) and bounded above by \(1\) is constant, and the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant is the zero function. Hence \(f^{**}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), while \(f(0)=1\). In particular, \(f^{**}(0)<f(0)\), exhibiting the loss incurred by biconjugate convexification.
assumptions_latex: Conjugacy uses the standard pairing on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper nonconvex function can satisfy \(f^{**}(x)<f(x)\), with the biconjugate equal to its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional gap caused solely by nonconvexity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The gap is defined numerically only where extended-real subtraction is unambiguous; its positivity set remains meaningful using strict extended-real order everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonconvex biconjugate gap is \(G_f:D_f\to[0,+\infty]\), \(G_f(x)=f(x)-f^{**}(x)\). Its contact set is \(\mathcal C_f=\{x:f(x)=f^{**}(x)\}\), and its strict-gap set is \(\mathcal G_f=\{x:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}\). Since \(f^{**}\) is the greatest closed convex minorant of \(f\), \(G_f\geq0\), and \(G_f\equiv0\) exactly when \(f\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate gap measures the vertical distance from a function to its greatest closed convex minorant wherever subtraction is defined. Zero-gap points are contact points, while positive-gap points are precisely those not recovered by biconjugation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G_f(x)=f(x)-\sup\{a(x):a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\leq f\}.\]
\[G_f\equiv0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}.\]
special_cases_latex: For an indicator \(f=\iota_S\), the biconjugate is \(\iota_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S}\); the gap is infinite on \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}S\setminus S\) under the extended-value convention.
If \(f\) is convex but nonclosed, the gap is purely a closure defect.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimizers of \(f\) that also minimize \(f^{**}\) must lie in the contact set whenever their optimal values agree.
boundary_notes: The gap is not a metric distance and need not be continuous.
Expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) are excluded by restricting the numerical definition to \(D_f\).

notation.meaning: contact set of f and its biconjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate of a nonclosed convex set's indicator is the indicator of its closure, producing a strict boundary gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Since \(C\) is convex, \(\delta_C\) is convex; since \(C\) is not closed, it is not lower semicontinuous. Its Fenchel biconjugate is
\[
\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}.
\]
Thus every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) satisfies \(\delta_C^{**}(x)=0<+\infty=\delta_C(x)\). Closedness, equivalently lower semicontinuity of the indicator, is therefore necessary for exact recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, convex, and not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicator satisfies \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}\), so biconjugation changes its values on \(\overline C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure of exact biconjugation without closedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugacy of indicators before and after closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\delta_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sigma_{\overline C}(y)=\delta_{\overline C}^*(y)\quad(y\in\mathbb R^n).\] Thus the first conjugate cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set and its closure have the same support function and conjugate indicator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure defect of a proper convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex. Its lower-semicontinuous hull is \((\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional convex-but-not-closed regime. Convexification is already complete, so biconjugation performs only lower-semicontinuous closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonclosed convex input is a proper convex function \(f\) for which \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is not closed, equivalently \(f\neq\operatorname{cl}f\). Its biconjugate satisfies \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\), and \(\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\). The closure-defect set is \(D_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\{x:(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)<f(x)\}\); it is nonempty exactly when the convex input is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex input is convex but fails lower semicontinuity. Biconjugation does not further convexify it; it replaces the function by its lower-semicontinuous hull, whose epigraph is the closure of the original epigraph. The closure-defect set records where values drop.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}.\]
\[(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is finite on an open set, convexity implies continuity there, so closure defects can occur only at the boundary of its effective domain.
For an indicator of a nonclosed convex set \(C\), \(\iota_C^{**}=\iota_{\overline C}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The conjugates agree: \(f^*=(\operatorname{cl}f)^*\).
boundary_notes: Nonclosedness refers to the epigraph in the ambient topology, not merely to whether the effective domain is closed.
A convex function can have a nonclosed domain while still being lower-semicontinuous; domain nonclosedness alone is not the defining defect.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Annihilator boundary for nonseparating conjugate duality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces with a bilinear pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\), not assumed to separate points. Define \(N_X=\{n\in X:\langle n,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in Y\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates failure caused by an insufficient dual space, independently of nonconvexity or lower-semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The topological dual-separation failure boundary is the regime \(N_X\neq\{0\}\). For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f^Y(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{YY}(x)=\sup_y(\langle x,y\rangle-f^Y(y))\). Every such biconjugate is invariant along annihilator cosets: \(f^{YY}(x+n)=f^{YY}(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(n\in N_X\). Consequently, exact recovery \(f=f^{YY}\) is possible only if \(f(x+n)=f(x)\) for all annihilator directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the chosen dual space does not distinguish all primal points, its common annihilator is nonzero. Every biconjugate is then constant on the corresponding affine cosets. Therefore, a function that varies along an invisible direction cannot be recovered by that conjugacy, even if it is convex and closed in some stronger topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_X\neq\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^{YY}(x+n)=f^{YY}(x)\ \ \forall x\in X,\ \forall n\in N_X,\] \[f=f^{YY}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x+n)=f(x)\ \ \forall x\in X,\ \forall n\in N_X.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The pairing separates points of \(X\) exactly when \(N_X=\{0\}\).
The weak topology \(\sigma(X,Y)\) is Hausdorff exactly when \(Y\) separates points of \(X\).
special_cases_latex: If \(Y=\{0\}\), then \(N_X=X\), and every biconjugate is constant on \(X\).
For the canonical pairing \((X,X^*)\) of a normed space, Hahn–Banach separation gives \(N_X=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Dual separation is a structural prerequisite for a pointwise Fenchel–Moreau recovery theorem on the original primal space.
boundary_notes: This failure is distinct from a topology being too weak to make a particular epigraph closed; here the topology is non-Hausdorff because the dual does not separate points.
No supplied or inspected source gives this exact annihilator-boundary formulation, so independent sourcing is required.

notation.meaning: primal annihilator of the chosen paired dual space
biconjugate formed using the pairing with Y

review_flags: Needs an authoritative dual-pair source for the equivalence between separation, Hausdorff weak topology, and annihilator-coset invariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Annihilator boundary for nonseparating conjugate duality
Sequentially Closed Dense Convex Subspace
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an uncountable product space, the countable-support subspace is sequentially closed but dense, so its indicator is sequentially lower semicontinuous yet continuous-dual biconjugation fills the entire space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be uncountable, let \(X=\mathbb R^I\) have the product topology, and set
\[
\Sigma(I)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{supp}x\text{ is countable}\}.
\]
The linear subspace \(\Sigma(I)\) is sequentially closed: the support of the limit of any convergent sequence in \(\Sigma(I)\) is contained in a countable union of countable sets. It is nevertheless dense and proper in \(X\). Hence \(\delta_{\Sigma(I)}\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous. The continuous dual of \(X\) consists of finitely supported coordinate functionals, and
\[
\delta_{\Sigma(I)}^{**}=\delta_X\equiv0\ne\delta_{\Sigma(I)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma(I)\) is sequentially closed but not closed, and \(\delta_{\Sigma(I)}^{**}\equiv0\ne\delta_{\Sigma(I)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonmetrizable example where sequential lower semicontinuity does not imply topological lower semicontinuity or exact continuous-dual biconjugation.

notation.meaning: subspace of vectors having countable support

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonmetrizable example separating sequential lower semicontinuity from topological lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be uncountable, let \(X=\mathbb R^I\) have the product topology, and let \[C=\{x\in X:\operatorname{supp}x\text{ is countable}\}.\] The linear subspace \(C\) is sequentially closed because the support of the limit of a sequence in \(C\) is contained in a countable union of countable sets. It is dense and not closed because the finitely supported vectors lie in \(C\) and are dense in \(X\). Every continuous linear functional on \(X\) depends on finitely many coordinates; hence every nonzero such functional is unbounded above on \(C\). Therefore \[\delta_C^{**}=0=\delta_X\ne\delta_C.\] Thus \(\delta_C\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous but is not recovered by continuous-dual biconjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an uncountable product space, the countable-support subspace is sequentially closed but dense, so its sequentially lower-semicontinuous indicator has zero biconjugate everywhere.
assumptions_latex: Conjugation uses the continuous dual of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is sequentially closed but not closed, and \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_X\ne\delta_C\).

notation.meaning: set of coordinates at which x is nonzero

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Closedness Does Not Suffice
Topological Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biconjugation closes epigraphs in the weak topology induced by the chosen continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological vector space with continuous dual \(X'\), and define conjugates using the pairing \(\langle X',X\rangle\). For any proper extended-real function \(f\), the biconjugate \(f^{**}\) is lower semicontinuous for \(\sigma(X,X')\). Therefore biconjugation can recover a proper convex \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous function only if its epigraph is also closed in \(\sigma(X,X')\). If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is \(\tau\)-closed but not \(\sigma(X,X')\)-closed, then \(f^{**}\ne f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation uses weak closure generated by the continuous dual; closure in another topology alone does not guarantee recovery.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced by the continuous dual

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial-Dual Separation Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only the zero functional available, biconjugation cannot distinguish any exterior point from the singleton set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(X=\mathbb R\), \(Y=\{0\}\), and \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(H_Y(C)=\mathbb R\), so
\[
\delta_C^{**}\equiv0,
\]
even though \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal algebraic example showing that an inadequate functional family can make every point indistinguishable under biconjugation.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairing-Invisible Exterior Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator biconjugate is the indicator of the intersection of all halfspaces detected by the selected functional family; an exterior point is incorrectly recovered precisely when that family cannot separate it from the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces in duality through a bilinear pairing, and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty. Define
\[
H_Y(C)=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq \sigma_C(y)\text{ for every }y\in Y\}.
\]
Then
\[
\delta_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y),\qquad \delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}.
\]
Consequently, for \(x_0\notin C\), one has \(\delta_C^{**}(x_0)=0<+\infty=\delta_C(x_0)\) exactly when every pairing-defined affine inequality valid on \(C\) is also valid at \(x_0\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are paired real vector spaces; separation of points is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}\), and \(x_0\in H_Y(C)\setminus C\) is exactly a pairing-invisible exterior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact indicator-recovery boundary for a chosen linear-functional family, without assuming that the pairing separates points.

notation.meaning: intersection of all pairing-defined closed affine halfspaces containing C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical example in which the chosen functional family detects no nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonzero real vector space, let \(Y=\{0\}\), and let \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(H_Y(C)=X\), so \[\delta_C^{**}=0=\delta_X,\] although \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only the zero functional available, biconjugation cannot distinguish the origin from any other point.
knowledge_statements.title: Trivial-Dual Nonseparation Example
Dual-Separation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A trivial continuous dual makes biconjugation unable to distinguish points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\ne\{0\}\) be a topological vector space whose continuous dual is \(X'=\{0\}\), and let \(f:X\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfy \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)>0\) for \(x\ne0\). Conjugacy with respect to \(X'\) gives \(f^*(0)=0\), hence \(f^{**}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus \(f^{**}(x)<f(x)\) at every nonzero point: a dual that does not separate points cannot recover such a function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the continuous dual contains only zero, every biconjugate is blind to point distinctions; a positive function with minimum zero collapses to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hull Generated by the Selected Dual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator biconjugation for an arbitrary bilinear pairing, including a nonseparating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces in bilinear pairing and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty. Define \[H_Y(C)=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\le \sigma_C(y)\text{ for every }y\in Y\}.\] Then \[\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}.\] Consequently, \(x_0\notin C\) is incorrectly admitted by biconjugation exactly when no \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(\langle x_0,y\rangle>\sigma_C(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate of an indicator is the indicator of the intersection of all halfspaces generated by the selected dual family.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces with a bilinear pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}\), and \(x_0\in H_Y(C)\) exactly when the family \(Y\) supplies no strict separating inequality.

notation.meaning: support function of C relative to the pairing
intersection of all Y-generated closed affine halfspaces containing C

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Generated by the Selected Dual Family
Ambient–Pairing Closure Agreement Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation using a selected separating dual subspace performs weak closure for that pairing; it agrees with ambient closed convexification exactly when the two topologies close every convex set identically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,\tau)\) be a Hausdorff locally convex space and let \(Y\subset X'\) separate points. For every nonempty convex set \(C\subset X\), conjugation with the pairing \((X,Y)\) gives
\[
\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C}.
\]
The pairing-induced and \(\tau\)-closed convexifications agree for every function having a proper pairing-closed convex minorant if and only if
\[
\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C
\]
for every convex \(C\subset X\). Thus one convex set with unequal closures is an exact mismatch witness.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
For the function-level formulation, the relevant closed convex minorant is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairing and ambient convexification agree exactly when \(\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\) for every convex \(C\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set-level criterion for agreement between ambient closed convexification and biconjugation using a selected separating subspace of the ambient continuous dual.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced by the selected functional space Y
continuous dual of the ambient topology τ

knowledge_statements.title: Norm–Coordinatewise Closure Mismatch
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-sum hyperplane in ℓ¹ is norm closed but dense for the coordinatewise topology induced by c₀₀, so c₀₀-biconjugation loses the norm-closed constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\ell^1\) with its norm topology and pair it only with \(Y=c_{00}\subset\ell^\infty=X'\). The space \(Y\) separates points and \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})\) is coordinatewise convergence. For
\[
C=\left\{x\in\ell^1:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=0\right\},
\]
\(C\) is a norm-closed hyperplane, but it is \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})\)-dense in \(\ell^1\): any finite collection of prescribed coordinates can be matched while one unused coordinate corrects the total sum. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|_1}C=C,
\qquad
\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})}C=\ell^1,
\qquad
\delta_C^{**}\equiv0
\]
for conjugation against \(c_{00}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit mismatch between norm closure and closure induced by a separating proper subspace of the norm-continuous dual.
Exact criterion for equality of pairing-induced and ambient closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a separated dual pair and let \(\tau\) be a Hausdorff locally convex topology on \(X\). Pairing biconjugation agrees with \(\tau\)-closed convexification for all functions admitting a proper closed convex minorant if and only if \[\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\] for every convex set \(C\subset X\). A strict inequality for one convex set yields different convexifications of its indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairing biconjugation matches ambient closed convexification exactly when the weak pairing topology and ambient topology give every convex set the same closure.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\) is a Hausdorff locally convex topology on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairing and \(\tau\)-closed convexifications agree exactly when all convex \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closures and \(\tau\)-closures agree.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced on X by Y

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Compatibility Criterion
Topology–Separation Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery criterion when ambient and dual-induced topologies need not agree on convex epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological vector space, let \(Y\subseteq X^\#\) be a separating linear subspace of the algebraic dual, and define conjugates using the pairing \(\langle Y,X\rangle\). For a proper convex function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), equality \(f=f^{**}\) holds if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous for \(\sigma(X,Y)\), equivalently if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(\sigma(X,Y)\times\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, \(\tau\)-lower semicontinuity of a particular \(f\) yields recovery only when its epigraph is also \(\sigma(X,Y)\times\mathbb{R}\)-closed; a uniform implication for all proper convex functions requires the corresponding closure property for all such convex epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugate recovery of a proper convex function is equivalent to closure of its epigraph in the topology induced by the selected separating dual. Lower semicontinuity in the ambient topology alone is insufficient unless that epigraph also has the required weak closure.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq X^\#\) is a separating linear subspace

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing, and let \(\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). For every proper function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), its Fenchel conjugate is \(f^*(s)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the calculus records how standard primal constructions are transformed by Fenchel conjugation, including any closure or qualification required for an exact identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conjugate calculus on a class \(\mathcal F\) of proper functions is the transformation system \(\mathfrak C=\{\mathfrak C_{\mathcal O}\}_{\mathcal O}\) indexed by admissible primal operations \(\mathcal O\), where \(\mathfrak C_{\mathcal O}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*)=(\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m))^*\). Its canonical operations include affine changes of variables, linear images, sums, infimal convolutions, pointwise extrema, marginals, and monotone convex postcomposition. A rule is exact when it gives pointwise equality without an additional lower-semicontinuous closure and, when an infimum occurs in the dual representation, that infimum is attained. Thus each rule comprises its primal construction, the dual expression, and the domain or relative-interior qualification under which closure and nonattainment disappear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel-conjugate calculus is the indexed family of rules that assigns to each admissible construction \(\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m)\) an expression for its conjugate \((\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m))^*\) in terms of \(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*\). The family covers affine transformations, linear images, sums, infimal convolutions, extrema, marginalization, and increasing convex postcomposition. A calculus rule is called exact only when its displayed equality needs no lower-semicontinuous closure and every dual infimum appearing in it is attained; consequently, qualifications are part of the rule rather than optional annotations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The calculus may equivalently be viewed as a collection of dual pairs of operations: addition versus infimal convolution, linear image versus linear precomposition, and supremum versus closed convexification of an infimum.
special_cases_latex: For the identity operation, \(\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{Id}}(f^*)=f^*\).
For an invertible linear map \(A\), the corresponding elementary rule is \((f\circ A)^*=f^*\circ(A^{-1})^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every rule specifies whether closure, exactness, or a relative-interior qualification is necessary.
The system reduces computation of a structured function's conjugate to conjugates of its constituent functions.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that every formal dual expression is closed or proper.
Infinite-dimensional variants may require topological duals and weak or weak-star lower-semicontinuous closures.

notation.meaning: Conjugate-calculus rule associated with the primal operation \(\mathcal O\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate under an Invertible Affine Change of Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation rule combining invertible affine precomposition, addition of a linear functional, and an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\), let \(\mathcal A:\mathbb V\to\mathbb E\) be an invertible linear transformation, and let \(a\in\mathbb V\), \(b\in\mathbb V^*\), and \(c\in\mathbb R\). If \(g(x)=f(\mathcal A(x-a))+\langle b,x\rangle+c\), then for every \(y\in\mathbb V^*\), \[g^*(y)=f^*((\mathcal A^T)^{-1}(y-b))+\langle a,y\rangle-c-\langle a,b\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an invertible affine change of variables followed by addition of a linear functional and a constant, the conjugate uses the inverse-transpose dual change of variables together with the corresponding translation and constant corrections.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A:\mathbb V\to\mathbb E\text{ is an invertible linear transformation}
a\in\mathbb V,\quad b\in\mathbb V^*,\quad c\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y\in\mathbb V^*,\quad g^*(y)=f^*((\mathcal A^T)^{-1}(y-b))+\langle a,y\rangle-c-\langle a,b\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary Scalar, Translation, and Tilt Conjugate Rules
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, let \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(\alpha>0\), \(x_0,s_0\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be invertible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional elementary transformations that require no constraint qualification beyond properness and the displayed positivity or invertibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The elementary transformation calculus of \(f\) is the family of transformed functions \(g\) and conjugate identities
\[g=f+a\Rightarrow g^*=f^*-a,\qquad g=\alpha f\Rightarrow g^*(s)=\alpha f^*(s/\alpha),\]
\[g=f\circ A\Rightarrow g^*=f^*\circ(A^{-1})^*,\qquad g(x)=f(x-x_0)\Rightarrow g^*(s)=f^*(s)+\langle s,x_0\rangle,\]
\[g(x)=f(x)+\langle s_0,x\rangle\Rightarrow g^*(s)=f^*(s-s_0).\]
For a product decomposition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) with product pairing and \(g(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j(x_j)\), the elementary separability rule is \(g^*(s_1,\ldots,s_m)=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j^*(s_j)\). These identities collectively define the elementary calculus family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elementary conjugate calculus consists of the exact rules for vertical shifts, positive value scaling, invertible changes of variables, translations of the argument, addition of a linear functional, and separable product sums. Vertical shifts reverse sign in the conjugate; positive value scaling also rescales the dual argument; translation adds the corresponding dual linear form; a primal linear tilt translates the dual argument; and an invertible coordinate change acts through the adjoint of the inverse. Under a product pairing, conjugation preserves a separable sum component by component.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The tilt rule can be written \((f+\langle s_0,\cdot\rangle)^*=f^*(\cdot-s_0)\).
The translation and tilt operations are dual translations in graph coordinates.
special_cases_latex: If \(A=\beta I\) with \(\beta\ne0\), then \((f(\beta\cdot))^*(s)=f^*(s/\beta)\).
If \(a=0\), \(x_0=0\), or \(s_0=0\), the corresponding rule reduces to the identity.
immediate_consequences_latex: The order reversal property \(f_1\le f_2\Rightarrow f_1^*\ge f_2^*\) is compatible with all displayed transformations.
Known scalar or coordinatewise conjugates can be assembled without solving a new supremum.
boundary_notes: The invertible-map formula does not cover rank-deficient precomposition; that case is an infimal image formula and may require closure.
Negative value scaling is excluded because it does not preserve convexity and has no analogous Fenchel rule.

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the inverse linear map.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to X\), and let \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear-map transformations; this child-level calculus isolates the dual pair formed by precomposition and infimal postcomposition, rather than scalar shifts and tilts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the infimal image of \(g\) under \(A^*\) by
\[(A^*\triangleright g^*)(s):=\inf\{g^*(p):p\in Y,\ A^*p=s\},\]
with value \(+\infty\) when the fiber is empty. Define linear precomposition by \(P_Ag=g\circ A\). The linear-map elementary calculus is the correspondence
\[(P_Ag)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*\triangleright g^*).\]
Dually, for a proper \(h:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its infimal image under \(A\) by \((A\triangleright h)(y)=\inf\{h(x):Ax=y\}\); whenever it has an affine minorant, its conjugate satisfies \((A\triangleright h)^*=h^*\circ A^*\). Thus precomposition and infimal linear image form the elementary linear transformation pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the linear-map level, elementary transformation calculus has two paired operations. Precomposition sends \(g\) to \(g\circ A\), while infimal image sends \(h\) to the function whose value at \(y\) is the infimum of \(h(x)\) over the fiber \(Ax=y\). The conjugate of precomposition is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the infimal image of \(g^*\) under \(A^*\). Conversely, the conjugate of a well-defined infimal image is \(h^*\circ A^*\). Exactness requires the relevant relative-interior qualification.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Pointwise, \((g\circ A)^*(s)=\operatorname{cl}_s\inf_{A^*p=s}g^*(p)\).
The operation \(A\triangleright h\) is the marginal of \(h(x)+\iota_{\{y=Ax\}}(x,y)\) over \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \(A^*\triangleright g^*=g^*\circ(A^{-1})^*\), so no closure is needed.
If \(A\) is a coordinate projection, the infimal image is an ordinary marginal value function.
immediate_consequences_latex: A rank-deficient linear map generally converts a direct substitution rule into a constrained dual minimization.
Relative-interior regularity can simultaneously remove closure and guarantee attainment on each finite dual fiber.
boundary_notes: The infimal image may take \(-\infty\) unless a compatible affine minorant exists.
The notation \(A\triangleright h\) denotes infimal postcomposition, not ordinary function composition.

notation.meaning: Infimal image or infimal postcomposition of \(h\) by \(A\).
Lower-semicontinuous closure of a convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essential Smoothness under a Qualified Surjective Linear Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here the convex linear-image function is \((Af)(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, convex, and essentially smooth, and let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear and surjective. Define \((Af)(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\}\). If there exists \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(A^*y^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\), then \(Af\) is essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex linear image of an essentially smooth closed proper convex function remains essentially smooth when the linear map is surjective and the range of its adjoint meets the relative interior of the conjugate domain.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, convex, and essentially smooth}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Af\text{ is essentially smooth as a convex function on }\mathbb{R}^m

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating the argument adds a linear term to the conjugate, while adding a linear term shifts the conjugate's dual argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(x)=f(x-a)+c\). Then, for every \(u\in X^*\),
\[
g^*(u)=f^*(u)+\langle u,a\rangle-c.
\]
More generally, if \(h(x)=f(x-a)+\langle b,x\rangle+c\), then
\[
h^*(u)=f^*(u-b)+\langle u-b,a\rangle-c.
\]
These identities hold as extended-real equalities directly from the definition of the Fenchel conjugate; no convexity or lower-semicontinuity assumption on \(f\) is required.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Translations and affine perturbations become explicit affine changes of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Argument translations, vertical shifts, and linear perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying function values by a positive scalar rescales conjugate values and arguments; invertible scalar precomposition inversely rescales the dual argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(g(x)=\alpha f(x)\), then for every \(u\in X^*\),
\[
g^*(u)=\alpha f^*(u/\alpha).
\]
If \(h(x)=f(sx)\), then
\[
h^*(u)=f^*(u/s).
\]
Combining both transformations, \(k(x)=\alpha f(sx)\) satisfies
\[
k^*(u)=\alpha f^*\!\left(\frac{u}{\alpha s}\right).
\]
All formulas are extended-real identities and require only \(\alpha>0\) and \(s\ne0\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive value scaling and nonzero scalar argument scaling have explicit conjugate formulas.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive value scaling and invertible scalar argument scaling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate regimes excluded by the seed's positive-value and nonzero-argument hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(0)\in\mathbb R\). For zero argument scaling, \(h(x)=f(0)\) and
\[
h^*(u)=\delta_{\{0\}}(u)-f(0).
\]
Hence the seed's nonzero argument-scaling formula cannot be extended by substituting \(s=0\). For an extended-real function, value scaling by zero has no convention-independent meaning because \(0(+\infty)\) is undefined; under the convention \(0f\equiv0\), its conjugate is \(\delta_{\{0\}}\). Negative value scaling has no corresponding formula in terms of \(f^*\): for \(f(x)=x^2/2\) and \(\alpha=-1\),
\[
(\alpha f)^*(u)=+\infty\quad\text{for every }u,
\]
whereas \(\alpha f^*(u/\alpha)=-u^2/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero argument scaling produces a constant-function conjugate, zero value scaling is convention-dependent for extended-real functions, and negative value scaling invalidates the positive-scaling formula.
assumptions_latex: For the zero argument-scale identity, \(f(0)\) is finite.
The negative-value-scale counterexample is on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At zero argument scale, \((x\mapsto f(0))^*=\delta_{\{0\}}-f(0)\); zero or negative value scaling does not satisfy the seed's positive-scaling rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero and Negative Scaling Boundaries
Reflection Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reflecting a function through the primal origin reflects its Fenchel conjugate through the dual origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(g(x)=f(-x)\). Then, for every \(u\in X^*\),
\[
g^*(u)=f^*(-u).
\]
Thus reflection commutes with Fenchel conjugacy after applying the corresponding reflection in the dual space. The identity is valid for arbitrary extended-real \(f\); convexity and lower semicontinuity are unnecessary.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reflection of the primal argument reflects the dual argument of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflection through the origin in primal and dual variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Elementary Transformations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single formula describes how conjugacy transforms any composition of translations, linear perturbations, positive scaling, dilation, and reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
g(x)=\alpha f\bigl(s(x-a)\bigr)+\langle b,x\rangle+c.
\]
Then, for every \(u\in X^*\),
\[
g^*(u)=\alpha f^*\!\left(\frac{u-b}{\alpha s}\right)+\langle u-b,a\rangle-c.
\]
This extended-real identity simultaneously covers argument translation, vertical translation, linear perturbation, positive value scaling, and either scalar dilation or reflection according to the sign of \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate of the composite elementary transformation is given by one affine-rescaling formula.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed formula combining translation, scaling, reflection, and affine perturbation.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a relative-interior qualification, affine precomposition conjugates to minimizing the shifted conjugate over dual vectors mapped to the requested argument by the transpose.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
g^*(u)=\min\left\{f^*(y)-\langle y,a\rangle:y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=u\right\},
\]
with the convention that the minimum is \(+\infty\) when the constraint set is empty. The relative-interior qualification ensures exactness and attainment whenever the value is finite. Without such a qualification, the right-hand infimum can require lower-semicontinuous closure and need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate of \(x\mapsto f(Ax+a)\) is an attained constrained infimum of \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact formula under a relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unqualified Closure Formula for Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine-precomposition formula without an exactness or attainment qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(a\in\mathbb R^m\). Suppose \(g(x)=f(Ax+a)\) is proper, and define
\[
h(u)=\inf\{f^*(y)-\langle y,a\rangle:A^{\mathsf T}y=u\}.
\]
Then
\[
g^*=h^{**}=\operatorname{cl}h.
\]
Thus the unclosed fiber infimum is exact at every point where it agrees with its lower-semicontinuous hull. The relative-interior qualification in the seed ensures global exactness and attainment at finite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a range qualification, the conjugate of an affine precomposition is the lower-semicontinuous convex closure of the corresponding adjoint-fiber infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^m\).
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(f\circ(A\cdot+a)\) is proper.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(y_0\in\mathbb R^m\), set \(A(x)=A_0x+y_0\), and let \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^m)\) with \(A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proper convex functions in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces; both the always-valid closure formula and its relative-interior exact form are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine precomposition of \(g\) by \(A\) is \(P_Ag:=g\circ A\). Its affine-precomposition conjugate transform is the function
\[Q_Ag^*(s):=\inf\{g^*(p)-\langle y_0,p\rangle:p\in\mathbb R^m,\ A_0^*p=s\}.\]
The canonical correspondence is
\[(g\circ A)^*=\operatorname{cl}Q_Ag^*.\]
If \(A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\), then \(Q_Ag^*\) is already closed on its effective domain, and for every \(s\in\operatorname{dom}(g\circ A)^*\) the defining infimum is attained and equals \((g\circ A)^*(s)\). The translation \(y_0\) therefore contributes the dual affine term \(-\langle y_0,p\rangle\), while the linear part contributes the fiber constraint \(A_0^*p=s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition forms the function \(g(A_0x+y_0)\). Its conjugate is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the function obtained by minimizing \(g^*(p)-\langle y_0,p\rangle\) over all dual vectors satisfying \(A_0^*p=s\). When the affine range meets the relative interior of \(\operatorname{dom}g\), the closure is unnecessary and the constrained minimum is attained for every dual argument where the conjugate is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(g\circ A)^*(s)=\operatorname{cl}_s\inf_{A_0^*p=s}\bigl(g^*(p)-\langle y_0,p\rangle\bigr),\] with an attained minimum under \(A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(y_0=0\), \((g\circ A_0)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A_0^*\triangleright g^*)\).
The qualification is equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g-A(\mathbb R^n))\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A_0\) is invertible, \((g\circ A)^*(s)=g^*((A_0^{-1})^*s)-\langle y_0,(A_0^{-1})^*s\rangle\).
If \(y_0=0\), the dual correction term vanishes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine translation changes dual values but not the fiber equation.
The relative-interior condition supplies both equality without closure and dual attainment.
boundary_notes: Mere feasibility \(A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\) does not in general ensure attainment.
In infinite dimensions, algebraic relative interior is generally insufficient for this formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal Linear Image and Its Conjugate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper. The empty-fiber infimum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional infimal postcomposition; a compatible affine minorant excludes the value \(-\infty\) and makes the displayed conjugate a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear-image infimal postcomposition of \(g\) by \(A\) is
\[(A\triangleright g)(x):=\inf\{g(y):y\in\mathbb R^m,\ Ay=x\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
Assume \(\operatorname{Im}A^*\cap\operatorname{dom}g^*\ne\varnothing\); equivalently, \(g\) has an affine minorant whose slope belongs to \(\operatorname{Im}A^*\). Then \(A\triangleright g\) is proper in the sense of never taking \(-\infty\), and its conjugate is exactly
\[(A\triangleright g)^*(s)=g^*(A^*s),\qquad s\in\mathbb R^n.\]
This identity defines the linear-image infimal-postcomposition correspondence: the primal fiberwise infimum becomes ordinary precomposition of the conjugate by the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal postcomposition of \(g\) by a linear map \(A\) assigns to \(x\) the infimum of \(g\) over the fiber \(Ay=x\). If \(g^*\) is finite at some point in the range of \(A^*\), the image function has a compatible affine lower bound and does not take the value \(-\infty\). Its Fenchel conjugate is then exactly \(g^*\circ A^*\). Thus a fiberwise primal minimization is transformed into a simple adjoint precomposition in dual space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The domain condition is \(\exists s_0\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(g^*(A^*s_0)<+\infty\).
The epigraph of \(A\triangleright g\) is the vertical closure-sensitive image of \(\operatorname{epi}g\) under \(A\times\operatorname{Id}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((A\triangleright g)(x)=g(A^{-1}x)\).
If \(A(x,z)=x\) is a product-space projection, \(A\triangleright g\) is the marginal \(x\mapsto\inf_z g(x,z)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No closure appears in the conjugate identity, even though the primal image function itself need not be lower semicontinuous.
The effective domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}(A\triangleright g)=A(\operatorname{dom}g)\).
boundary_notes: Without a compatible affine minorant, a fiber infimum can equal \(-\infty\).
Attainment of the primal fiber infimum is not part of this definition.

notation.meaning: Infimal postcomposition or infimal image of \(g\) under \(A\).

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Scope of Linear-Image Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward linear-image conjugacy is an algebraic identity and does not require finite dimensionality, convexity, closedness, or fiber attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real vector spaces in separating duality with \(X^*,Y^*\), let \(A:X\to Y\) admit an adjoint \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Defining \((A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)(y)=\inf_{Ax=y}f(x)\) with extended infimum conventions, one has \[(A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)^*(y^*)=f^*(A^*y^*)\qquad(y^*\in Y^*).\] Finite dimensionality, convexity, lower semicontinuity, properness of the infimal image, and attainment of fiber infima are not needed for this forward algebraic identity.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear and admits the adjoint \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp assumption variant of the forward conjugacy identity on a dual pair.

notation.meaning: linear infimal image of f under A
adjoint of A relative to the stated pairings

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the infimal image of a function under a linear map equals its conjugate postcomposed with the adjoint map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the linear infimal image by \((A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ Ax=y\}\), with the infimum of the empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\), \[(A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)^*(y^*)=f^*(A^*y^*).\] Thus conjugation converts a linear image into postcomposition of the conjugate by the adjoint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugacy of a linear infimal image.

notation.meaning: Infimal image of f under A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-linear locally convex variant of the finite-dimensional seed identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real locally convex spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be continuous linear, and define \(h(y)=\inf_{Ax=y}f(x)\). Then, with extended-real Fenchel conjugates, \[h^*(y^*)=f^*(A^*y^*)\qquad(y^*\in Y^*).\] Convexity, lower semicontinuity, and attainment of the fiber infima are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint-composition identity extends algebraically to continuous linear maps between locally convex spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Pair Linear-Image Conjugacy
Identity and Associativity of Infimal Postcomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal postcomposition by the identity changes nothing, and successive linear infimal postcompositions equal postcomposition by the composite map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) and \(B:Y\to Z\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions. Define \((f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)(x)=\inf_{x_1+\cdots+x_m=x}\sum_i f_i(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper convex functions; the family distinguishes the unconditional conjugate of infimal convolution from the closure-sensitive conjugate of a sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The additive-infimal conjugate calculus is the dual operation pair
\[(f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)^*=f_1^*+\cdots+f_m^*,\]
\[(\operatorname{cl}f_1+\cdots+\operatorname{cl}f_m)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f_1^*\square\cdots\square f_m^*).\]
When \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\ne\varnothing\), the second rule becomes exact:
\[(f_1+\cdots+f_m)^*(s)=\min_{s_1+\cdots+s_m=s}\sum_i f_i^*(s_i).\]
The minimum notation records attainment. This collection of the primal addition operation, the primal infimal-convolution operation, their dual identities, and the exactness qualification is the additive-infimal calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Addition and infimal convolution form a dual pair under Fenchel conjugation. The conjugate of an infimal convolution is always the sum of the conjugates. In the reverse direction, the conjugate of a sum is generally the lower-semicontinuous closure of the infimal convolution of the conjugates. If the relative interiors of the primal domains have a common point, closure is unnecessary and the dual decomposition infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\square_i f_i)^*=\sum_i f_i^*,\qquad (\sum_i f_i)^*=\operatorname{cl}(\square_i f_i^*),\] with exact attained infimal convolution under the common-relative-interior condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact sum rule is \((\sum_i f_i)^*(s)=\min\{\sum_i f_i^*(s_i):\sum_i s_i=s\}\).
Epigraphically, infimal convolution corresponds to addition of epigraphs when the defining infimum is exact.
special_cases_latex: For indicator functions, infimal convolution encodes Minkowski addition of the underlying sets.
immediate_consequences_latex: Primal regularization by infimal convolution becomes additive penalization in dual space.
Failure of exactness is represented by a closure correction, not by changing the algebraic dual operation.
boundary_notes: Infimal convolution of proper functions can take \(-\infty\) without a common affine minorant.
A finite value of the infimum does not by itself imply that a minimizing decomposition exists.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions, and define \((f\square g)(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\{f(u)+g(v)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary finite-dimensional correspondence, with the exact qualification stated separately from the universal closure formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sum–infimal-convolution correspondence is the pair of identities
\[(f\square g)^*=f^*+g^*,\qquad (f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*).\]
Here
\[(f^*\square g^*)(s)=\inf_{p+q=s}\{f^*(p)+g^*(q)\}.\]
If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\), then the second correspondence is exact and decomposable:
\[(f+g)^*(s)=\min_{p+q=s}\{f^*(p)+g^*(q)\}\quad\text{for every }s,\]
where the minimum is attained whenever the value is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two proper convex functions, the infimal convolution is the fiberwise infimum over decompositions \(x=u+v\). Its conjugate is the ordinary sum \(f^*+g^*\). Conversely, the conjugate of the pointwise sum \(f+g\) is the lower-semicontinuous closure of \(f^*\square g^*\). A common relative-interior point of the primal domains removes the closure and guarantees an attaining dual split \(s=p+q\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first identity is equivalent after biconjugation to \(\operatorname{cl}(f\square g)=(f^*+g^*)^*\).
Under qualification, the dual variable \(s\) admits an optimal decomposition \(s=p+q\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=\iota_{\{0\}}\), then \(f\square g=f\).
If \(f=\iota_C\) and \(g=\iota_D\), then \(f\square g=\iota_{C+D}\) when the infimum is exact.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain of \(f\square g\) is \(\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
Infimal convolution is commutative and, under compatible minorants, associative.
boundary_notes: Even for \(f,g\in\Gamma_0\), \(f\square g\) need not be lower semicontinuous or exact.
The common-relative-interior condition is sufficient, not necessary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugation of a Separable Product-Space Sum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) be a finite product of Euclidean spaces with product pairing \(\langle s,x\rangle=\sum_i\langle s_i,x_i\rangle\), and let \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products with a pairing compatible with the product decomposition; no convexity or closure qualification is needed for the basic identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(F:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is separable across the stated product when
\[F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\]
Its product-space conjugate calculus is the componentwise identity
\[F^*(s_1,\ldots,s_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(s_i).\]
Thus the conjugate of a separable sum on independent blocks is itself separable on the dual product. The definition includes compatibility of the pairing: each \(s_i\) pairs only with \(x_i\). Without that compatibility, the displayed componentwise formula is not the conjugate associated with the chosen bilinear form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-space function is separable when it is the sum of functions acting on independent coordinate blocks. With the product inner product, its Fenchel conjugate equals the sum of the individual conjugates evaluated at the corresponding dual blocks. The requirement on the pairing is part of the definition because cross-block terms would destroy the componentwise factorization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraphical supremum defining \(F^*\) separates into \(m\) independent one-block suprema.
For identical one-dimensional blocks, separability means \(F(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)\) and \(F^*(s)=\sum_i f_i^*(s_i)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f_i=\iota_{C_i}\), then \(F=\iota_{C_1\times\cdots\times C_m}\) and \(F^*=\sum_i\sigma_{C_i}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective dual domain factors as \(\operatorname{dom}F^*=\prod_i\operatorname{dom}f_i^*\).
Coordinatewise conjugate tables extend directly to block-separable models.
boundary_notes: This rule differs from the conjugate of a sum of functions sharing the same primal variable, which produces infimal convolution.
Infinite products require additional summability and dual-pair specifications.

notation.meaning: Separable direct sum of functions on independent product blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Dual Decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate maximization of a finite separable function splits into independent component problems, and, when all component optima are attained, its maximizers form their Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conjugate maximization decomposes componentwise: \[F^*(x^*)=\sup_{(x_i)\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\langle x_i^*,x_i\rangle-f_i(x_i)\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(x_i^*).\] If every component supremum is attained, then \[\operatorname{Argmax}_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x^*,x\rangle-F(x)\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Argmax}_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(\langle x_i^*,x_i\rangle-f_i(x_i)\bigr).\]
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 1\) is an integer and \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space for each \(1\le i\le m\).
\(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper for each \(1\le i\le m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*(x^*)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(x_i^*)\), with a Cartesian-product decomposition of the maximizers when every component supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value and optimizer decomposition of a finite separable conjugate problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and Exactness Corrections for Dual Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) be proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), and set \(H=f_1^*\square\cdots\square f_m^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sum conjugacy; the record formalizes the two distinct defects that may occur: lack of lower semicontinuity and lack of attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closure-exactness correction system attached to the sum \(F=\sum_i f_i\) consists of:
(1) the closure-corrected identity \(F^*=\operatorname{cl}H\);
(2) pointwise exactness at \(s\), meaning that there exist \(s_1,
\ldots,s_m\) with \(\sum_i s_i=s\) and \(H(s)=\sum_i f_i^*(s_i)\);
(3) global exactness, meaning pointwise exactness for every \(s\in\operatorname{dom}H\); and
(4) closure exactness, meaning \(H=\operatorname{cl}H\).
Under \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\ne\varnothing\), both corrections vanish: \(H\) is closed and every finite defining infimum is attained, hence \(F^*=H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sum, the raw dual candidate is the infimal convolution \(H\) of the conjugates. The closure correction replaces \(H\) by its lower-semicontinuous closure. Exactness is a separate property: it says that the infimum defining \(H(s)\) is achieved by a decomposition of \(s\). The correction system records these defects independently. A common relative-interior point of the primal domains guarantees both closedness of \(H\) and attainment of its finite values.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Closure exactness is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of \(H\).
Pointwise exactness at \(s\) is equivalent to existence of an optimal dual decomposition \(s=\sum_i s_i\).
special_cases_latex: For two functions, exactness means \((f^*\square g^*)(s)=f^*(p)+g^*(s-p)\) for some \(p\).
If one conjugate is supercoercive and the other is bounded below, standard coercivity conditions can also yield exact closed infimal convolution.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equality \(F^*=H\) alone identifies the value function; explicit exactness additionally supplies an optimizer.
Closure and nonattainment must not be conflated, since either defect can be considered separately.
boundary_notes: The relative-interior condition is sufficient but not necessary.
Exactness at one dual argument does not imply global exactness or closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Corrections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When infimal convolution is not closed, its lower-semicontinuous convex closure gives the conjugate of the primal sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The raw infimal convolution \(f^*\square g^*\) is convex but need not be lower semicontinuous. The universally valid repaired formula is \[(f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*)=(f^*\square g^*)^{**}.\] Thus biconjugation removes precisely the lower-semicontinuity defect in the unqualified sum–infimal-convolution rule.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure repair for nonclosed infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Exactness Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When one summand is polyhedral, intersection of its domain with the relative interior of the other domain suffices for the exact attained conjugate-sum formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\) is polyhedral and \[\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing.\] Then for every \(x^*\) for which the common value is finite, \[(f+g)^*(x^*)=\min_{u^*+v^*=x^*}\bigl(f^*(u^*)+g^*(v^*)\bigr).\] This condition may hold even when \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)=\varnothing\). The symmetric assertion holds when \(g\) is the polyhedral summand.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral}.
g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed polyhedral relaxation of the ordinary relative-interior qualification for exact conjugate addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Corrections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior intersection condition removes the closure and ensures attainment in the conjugate sum formula whenever the value is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative-interior qualification \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\] removes the closure correction. For every \(x^*\in X^*\), \[(f+g)^*(x^*)=\min_{u^*+v^*=x^*}\bigl(f^*(u^*)+g^*(v^*)\bigr)\] whenever the common value is finite. Hence the infimal convolution is lower semicontinuous and exact at such points.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)^*=f^*\square g^*\), and the defining infimum is attained whenever finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior qualification for exact conjugate addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Exactness Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonclosed sums of orthogonal complements in Hilbert space show that raw infimal convolution can differ from the conjugate of a sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(f+g=\delta_{U\cap V}\), one has \[(f+g)^*=\delta_{(U\cap V)^\perp}=\delta_{\overline{U^\perp+V^\perp}}.\] However, \[f^*\square g^*=\delta_{U^\perp}\square\delta_{V^\perp}=\delta_{U^\perp+V^\perp}.\] If \(U^\perp+V^\perp\) is not closed, the raw infimal convolution differs from the conjugate sum, and closure is indispensable.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(U,V\subset H\) are closed subspaces with \(U^\perp+V^\perp\) nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional nonclosed-subspace-sum failure mechanism.
