knowledge_statements.title: Neutral Element for Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of the origin is the neutral element of binary infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) be zero at \(0\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere. For every extended-real function \(f\), \[f\square\delta_{\{0\}}=\delta_{\{0\}}\square f=f.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity law for the binary operation.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain, Convexity, and Commutativity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary infimal convolution is commutative, has the Minkowski sum of the operand domains as its domain, and preserves convexity and properness once minus-infinite values are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=f\square g\) avoid \(-\infty\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}h=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g,\qquad f\square g=g\square f.\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex, then \(h\) is convex. Consequently, if both operands are proper and \(h\) avoids \(-\infty\), then \(h\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g,\quad f\square g=g\square f,\quad f,g\text{ convex}\Rightarrow f\square g\text{ convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural laws specific to the binary operation.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the effective domains

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary infimal convolution minimizes the sum of two functions over additive decompositions of the argument; its conjugate is the sum of their conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The binary infimal convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is the extended-real function \[(f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf\{f(u)+g(v):u+v=x\}=\inf_{u\in X}\{f(u)+g(x-u)\}.\] With the convention that the resulting function does not take \(-\infty\), its Fenchel conjugate satisfies the exact identity \[(f\mathbin{\square}g)^*(x^*)=f^*(x^*)+g^*(x^*)\] for every \(x^*\in X^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
\(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are extended-real functions and their infimal convolution never takes \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary operation and its unconditional algebraic conjugacy identity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, let \(h=f\square g\) be proper, and suppose \(u+v=x\) with \(h(x)=f(u)+g(v)\). Then \[x^*\in\partial h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\partial f(u)\cap\partial g(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a minimizing decomposition, a vector is a convolution subgradient exactly when it is a common subgradient of both operands at their decomposition points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic binary-operation laws; associativity remains with the arity-decomposition sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended-real functions whose displayed infimal convolutions avoid \(-\infty\), \[f\square g=g\square f,\qquad f\square\delta_{\{0\}}=f,\qquad \operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g.\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex, then \(f\square g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary infimal convolution is commutative, has the singleton indicator as identity, adds effective domains, and preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\square g=g\square f,\quad f\square\delta_{\{0\}}=f,\quad \operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g,\quad f,g\text{ convex}\Rightarrow f\square g\text{ convex}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic specialization of binary infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary sets \(C,D\subseteq X\), \[\delta_C\square\delta_D=\delta_{C+D},\qquad C+D=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}.\] Thus binary infimal convolution extends Minkowski addition from sets to extended-real functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal convolution of two set indicators is the indicator of their Minkowski sum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Representation and Smoothness of Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate representation of binary infimal convolution and the stated smoothness consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and \(\omega\) are proper, closed, and convex, then \[f\square\omega=(f^*+\omega^*)^*.\] Moreover, if \(\omega^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex, equivalently if \(\omega\) is \(L\)-smooth, then \(f\square\omega\) is \(L\)-smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions, their infimal convolution is the conjugate of the sum of their conjugates. If the second conjugate is 1/L-strongly convex, equivalently the second function is L-smooth, then the infimal convolution is L-smooth.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(\omega\) are proper, closed, and convex.
For the smoothness conclusion, \(\omega^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex, equivalently \(\omega\) is \(L\)-smooth.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness and Gradient Formula for Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of kernel smoothness to an everywhere-finite binary infimal convolution, with a gradient formula conditional on attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(\omega:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth, and assume \(f\square\omega\) is real-valued. Then \(f\square\omega\) is \(L\)-smooth. Moreover, for any \(x\in\mathbb{E}\), if \(u(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u}\{f(u)+\omega(x-u)\}\), then \[\nabla(f\square\omega)(x)=\nabla\omega(x-u(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper closed convex function is infimally convolved with a real-valued convex L-smooth function and the convolution is finite everywhere, the convolution is L-smooth. At a point where the defining minimization is attained, its gradient equals the kernel gradient at the corresponding residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\square\omega\text{ is }L\text{-smooth},\qquad \nabla(f\square\omega)(x)=\nabla\omega(x-u(x))\text{ whenever the stated minimizer exists}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Domain, Convexity, and Properness of Multiway Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain of a finite multiway convolution is the Minkowski sum of the operand domains; convexity and properness are preserved once minus-infinite values are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i\) avoid \(-\infty\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}h=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i.\] If every \(f_i\) is convex, then \(h\) is convex. If every \(f_i\) is proper, then, under the no-\(-\infty\) assumption, \(h\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic structural preservation for the finite-arity operation.

notation.meaning: finite Minkowski sum of the effective domains

knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiway infimal convolution minimizes a sum over all additive decompositions into the prescribed number of components, and conjugation turns it into an ordinary sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge2\), the multiway infimal convolution is \[\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i):x_i\in X,\ \sum_{i=1}^m x_i=x\right\}.\] Its conjugate separates across all components: \[\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i\right)^*(x^*)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(x^*)\] for every \(x^*\in X^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\), and \(m\ge2\).
Each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and the displayed infimum never equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-arity infimal convolution on a common vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Invariance of Finite Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite infimal convolution is invariant under reordering of its operands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge2\), let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and suppose the relevant infima avoid \(-\infty\). For every permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i=\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_{\pi(i)}.\] Thus a finite infimal convolution depends on the multiset of operands, not their enumeration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order independence of the finite decomposition problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Arity-Dependent Decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite infimal convolution can be decomposed into binary convolutions, and the result is independent of grouping or parenthesization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=x\) can be introduced one component at a time. Consequently, finite infimal convolution is associative: \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i=((f_1\mathbin{\square}f_2)\mathbin{\square}\cdots)\mathbin{\square}f_m,\] and every other parenthesization gives the same function. More generally, if \(\{1,\ldots,m\}=I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J\) is a nontrivial partition, then \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m f_i=\left(\mathop{\square}_{i\in I}f_i\right)\mathbin{\square}\left(\mathop{\square}_{j\in J}f_j\right).\]
assumptions_latex: All intermediate and multiway infimal convolutions under consideration avoid the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Associative decomposition of finite-arity infimal convolution into binary operations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted infimal convolution under linear synthesis
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X_i\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces, let \(A_i:X_i\to Y\) be linear maps, let \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(\lambda_i>0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, strictly positive weights and linear synthesis maps. Zero or negative weights require separate recession or sign conventions and are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scaled-weighted infimal convolution associated with \((\lambda_i,A_i,f_i)_{i=1}^m\) is \[\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m{}^{A_i}_{\lambda_i}f_i\right)(y):=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i=y\right\}.\] Its effective domain is \[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i(\operatorname{dom}f_i).\] Equivalently, with \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x_i)\) and \(L(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_iA_ix_i\), the family is \(L\mathbin{\triangleright}F\). When every \(X_i=Y\), every \(A_i=\operatorname{Id}\), and every \(\lambda_i=1\), it reduces to ordinary finite-arity infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled-weighted infimal convolution minimizes a positively weighted sum of component costs over decompositions synthesized by specified linear maps. Its domain is the Minkowski sum of the mapped component domains. It is equivalently the infimal postcomposition of the separable weighted cost by the synthesis map. Ordinary finite-arity convolution is recovered when all maps are identities and all weights equal one.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m{}^{A_i}_{\lambda_i}f_i=L\mathbin{\triangleright}\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\lambda_if_i\right).\]
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(A_1=A_2=\operatorname{Id}\), the value is \(\inf_x\{\lambda_1f_1(x)+\lambda_2f_2(y-x)\}\).
If one \(A_i\) is the zero map, its component contributes the constant \(\inf \lambda_i f_i\), when meaningful.
immediate_consequences_latex: If every \(f_i\) is convex, then the weighted separable cost and its infimal projection are convex.
Exactness at \(y\) means that the displayed constrained infimum has a finite minimizer.
boundary_notes: The inspected sources support infimal postcomposition and separable infimal convolution but do not name this full weighted-linear family as a standalone definition.
Weights equal to zero are excluded because \(0\cdot(+\infty)\) needs an explicit convention.

notation.meaning: Component function with positive objective weight and synthesis map.

knowledge_statements.title: Semigroup Law for Positive Perspective Scaling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive perspective scalings compose multiplicatively and have unit scale one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda,\mu>0\) and every extended-real function \(g\), \[\lambda\odot(\mu\odot g)=(\lambda\mu)\odot g.\] In particular, \(1\odot g=g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition law for the scaling convention used by this leaf.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain and Convexity of Scaled Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive perspective scaling multiplies the second effective domain by the scale; scaled infimal convolution preserves convexity and properness once minus-infinite values are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda>0\), \((\lambda\odot g)(v)=\lambda g(v/\lambda)\), and \(h=f\square(\lambda\odot g)\). If \(h\) avoids \(-\infty\), then \[\operatorname{dom}h=\operatorname{dom}f+\lambda\operatorname{dom}g.\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex, then \(h\) is convex; if they are proper, then under the no-\(-\infty\) assumption \(h\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural effect of a strictly positive perspective scale.

notation.meaning: scalar dilation of the effective domain of g

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled infimal convolution uses perspective scaling on one operand; Fenchel conjugation converts that scaling and convolution into a correspondingly scaled sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), define the perspective scaling \((\lambda\odot g)(v)=\lambda g(v/\lambda)\). The scaled infimal convolution of \(f\) with \(g\) is \[(f\mathbin{\square}(\lambda\odot g))(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\{f(u)+\lambda g(v/\lambda)\}.\] Since \((\lambda\odot g)^*(x^*)=\lambda g^*(x^*)\), its conjugate is \[(f\mathbin{\square}(\lambda\odot g))^*(x^*)=f^*(x^*)+\lambda g^*(x^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective-scaled second operand with strictly positive scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Subgradient Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained weighted decomposition is characterized by a common subgradient of all operands at their barycentric components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_i=\alpha_i y_i\) and \(\sum_i x_i=x\). A vector \(u\in X^*\) satisfying \(u\in\partial f_i(y_i)\) for every \(i\) certifies \[W(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(y_i),\qquad u\in\partial W(x),\qquad W(x)+W^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle.\] Conversely, if this decomposition attains \(W(x)\) and \(u\in\partial W(x)\), then \(u\in\partial f_i(y_i)\) for every \(i\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, \(\alpha_i>0\), and \(W\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\bigcap_i\partial f_i(y_i)\) is the primal-dual optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual certificate for an attained weighted decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Barycentric Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted infimal convolution is a barycentric minimization; normalized averaging of identical convex operands leaves the operand unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha_i>0\), substituting \(x_i=\alpha_i y_i\) gives \[W(x)=\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=x}\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i(y_i).\] If \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\) and every operand equals the same convex function \(f\), then \(W=f\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper and convex and each \(\alpha_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(x)=\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=x}\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(y_i)\), and normalized identical operands satisfy \(W=f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent primal formulation for positive weights.

notation.meaning: Weighted infimal convolution under the seed convention

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted infimal convolution combines perspective-scaled operands over additive decompositions; its conjugate is the same weighted sum of the individual conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive weights \(\alpha_i\), define \((\alpha_i\odot f_i)(x_i)=\alpha_i f_i(x_i/\alpha_i)\). Their weighted infimal convolution is \[W(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i(x_i/\alpha_i):\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=x\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(W=\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m(\alpha_i\odot f_i)\), and therefore \[W^*(x^*)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i^*(x^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\), and \(m\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite multiway convolution with positive perspective weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse rule for positive perspective copies of one convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, let \(\alpha_i>0\), and set \(A=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\). Then
\[
\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m(\alpha_i\odot f)=A\odot f.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=x}\sum_i\alpha_i f(y_i)=A f(x/A),
\]
and whenever this value is finite it is attained by \(y_i=x/A\) for every \(i\). In particular, normalized weights reproduce \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive perspective copies of one convex function combine into a single perspective copy with the total weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Identical Convex Operands

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barycentric Form of Weighted Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent positive-weight formulation obtained by rescaling decomposition variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha_i>0\), substituting \(x_i=\alpha_i y_i\) gives
\[
\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m(\alpha_i\odot f_i)\right)(x)
=
\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i(y_i):\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i y_i=x\right\}.
\]
When \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), the constraint represents \(x\) as the weighted barycenter of the component arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted infimal convolution equivalently minimizes a weighted sum over weighted decompositions of the target.
assumptions_latex: The displayed infimum does not equal \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Barycentric Form of Weighted Infimal Convolution
Negative-Weight Convexity Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative perspective weight can turn a convex operand into a concave function, so the weighted convex-conjugacy rules fail outside the nonnegative regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive perspective formula does not extend as convex calculus to negative weights. For \(f(t)=t^2\) and \(\alpha<0\), \[(\alpha\odot f)(x)=\alpha f(x/\alpha)=\frac{x^2}{\alpha},\] which is strictly concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto x^2/\alpha\) is concave and is not a convex perspective-scaled operand.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary beyond the nonnegative closed-perspective regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Weight Collapse
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all weights vanish and the resulting convolution is proper, its conjugate is the indicator of the intersection of the closed conjugate domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W_0=\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m\operatorname{rec}f_i\). If \(W_0\) is proper, then \[W_0^*=\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{dom}f_i^*}}=\delta_{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\overline{\operatorname{dom}f_i^*}}.\] Thus complete weight collapse retains precisely the common dual-domain constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and each \(f_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-zero boundary of closed perspective-weighted infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero weight, closed perspective scaling becomes the recession function. Its conjugate is the indicator of the closed domain of the original conjugate, so zero-weight operands impose dual-domain constraints rather than contributing an everywhere-zero term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), let \((\alpha\odot f)(x)=\alpha f(x/\alpha)\). Its closed convex extension to zero weight is \[(0\odot f)(x)=\operatorname{rec}f(x).\] In finite dimensions, the conjugate of this zero-weight term is \[(0\odot f)^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{dom}f^*}},\] rather than the zero function on the entire dual space. Consequently, if \(P=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}\) and \(Z=\{i:\alpha_i=0\}\), then \[\left(\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m(\alpha_i\odot f_i)\right)^*=\sum_{i\in P}\alpha_i f_i^*+\sum_{i\in Z}\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{dom}f_i^*}}.\] Thus a zero-weight operand imposes a dual-domain constraint and does not generally disappear.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space, \(m\ge 2\), and each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The weights satisfy \(\alpha_i\ge 0\), with at least one positive weight, and the resulting infimal convolution does not take the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary behavior of closed perspective weights when one or more weights vanish.

notation.meaning: Closed perspective scaling, extended to zero by the recession function
Indicator function of the closure of the effective domain of the conjugate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp obstruction to extending perspective weights to negative values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(t)=t^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and \(\alpha<0\), the algebraic formula for perspective scaling gives
\[
(\alpha\odot f)(x)=\alpha f(x/\alpha)=\frac{x^2}{\alpha},
\]
which is strictly concave. Thus negative weights fall outside the convex weighted-infimal-convolution calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative perspective weight turns the convex square into a concave quadratic.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative Weights Destroy Perspective Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint where every closed perspective weight vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a finite-dimensional space, and suppose \(R:=\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m\operatorname{rec}f_i\) never equals \(-\infty\). Then
\[
R^*=\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{dom}f_i^*}}
 =\delta_{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\overline{\operatorname{dom}f_i^*}}.
\]
Thus an all-zero weight vector retains the convolution of the recession functions and imposes the intersection of their closed dual domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With all weights zero, the result is a convolution of recession functions whose conjugate is the indicator of the intersection of the closed conjugate domains.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-real marginal functions. Convexity passes to the marginal under joint convexity, while closedness and attainment require additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fiberwise infimal elimination of the variable \(y\) from \(F\) is the marginal function \[M_F:X\to[-\infty,+\infty],\qquad M_F(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y).\] Its domain and minimizing fiber are \[\operatorname{dom}M_F=\{x\in X:(\exists y\in Y)\ F(x,y)<+\infty\},\qquad S_F(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y).\] The elimination is exact at \(x\) when \(S_F(x)\neq\varnothing\) and \(M_F(x)>-\infty\). Equivalently, if \(P:X\times Y\to X\) is the projection \(P(x,y)=x\), then \[M_F=P\mathbin{\triangleright}F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise infimal elimination removes a latent variable by taking the infimum of a joint extended-real function over each fiber above the retained variable. The marginal domain is the projection of the joint domain. The minimizing fiber records whether elimination is exact. This is precisely infimal postcomposition through the coordinate projection. Joint convexity implies convexity of the marginal, but neither attainment nor lower semicontinuity follows from the definition alone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using an indicator of the fiber, \[M_F(x)=\inf_{(u,y)\in X\times Y}\{F(u,y)+\iota_{\{x\}}(u)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(F(x,y)=f(y)+g(x-y)\), then \(M_F=f\square g\).
If \(Y\) is a singleton, then \(M_F\) is the corresponding section of \(F\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\) is jointly convex, then \(M_F\) is convex.
If \(F(x,\cdot)\) has a minimizer, then \(S_F(x)\neq\varnothing\) and the fiberwise infimum is attained at that point.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain, Convexity, and Properness of the Infimal Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal image has domain equal to the linear image of the original domain, preserves convexity, and is proper exactly when the original domain is nonempty once unbounded-below fibers are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=A\triangleright f\), where \(h(y)=\inf_{Ax=y}f(x)\), and suppose \(h\) never takes \(-\infty\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}h=A(\operatorname{dom}f).\] If \(f\) is convex, then \(h\) is convex. Moreover, under the no-\(-\infty\) assumption, \(h\) is proper if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}(A\triangleright f)=A(\operatorname{dom}f),\qquad f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow A\triangleright f\text{ convex}

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Postcomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal postcomposition minimizes a function over each linear fiber; its conjugate is the original conjugate composed with the adjoint map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal postcomposition of \(f\) by \(A\) is \[(A\triangleright f)(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ Ax=y\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when the fiber is empty. Its Fenchel conjugate is obtained by adjoint precomposition: \[(A\triangleright f)^*(y^*)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\langle y^*,y\rangle-(A\triangleright f)(y)\}=f^*(A^*y^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear between real vector spaces paired with \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise infimum along a linear mapping and its conjugate.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization preserves convexity. Once fibers unbounded below are excluded, the marginal is proper exactly when the joint function has nonempty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=\inf_{z\in Z}F(x,z)\), and assume \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\). If \(F\) is convex on \(X\times Z\), then \(g\) is convex on \(X\). Furthermore, \(g\) is proper if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}F\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Minimization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a partial minimum is the product-space conjugate restricted to dual vectors whose eliminated component is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the partial minimum of \(F\) by \[g(x)=\inf_{z\in Z}F(x,z).\] Conjugation eliminates the second dual variable by setting it to zero: \[g^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-g(x)\}=\sup_{(x,z)\in X\times Z}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-F(x,z)\}=F^*(x^*,0).\] This identity is algebraic and does not require attainment of the infimum defining \(g\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Z\) are real vector spaces paired with \(X^*\) and \(Z^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Domain and Strict-Epigraph Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise elimination exactly projects the effective domain and strict epigraph. Lack of a minimizer can remove only ordinary-epigraph boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=\inf_{z\in Z}F(x,z)\), with \(g\) never taking \(-\infty\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}g=\operatorname{proj}_X(\operatorname{dom}F)\] and \[\operatorname{epi}_{<}g:=\{(x,t):g(x)<t\}=\operatorname{proj}_{X\times\mathbb R}\{(x,z,t):F(x,z)<t\}.\] Thus domain and strict-epigraph projection are exact without fiberwise attainment; only the lower boundary of the ordinary epigraph can be lost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set projections under fiberwise elimination, independent of attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Fiberwise Elimination Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization projects an epigraph. Missing minimizers can remove boundary points, but the projected epigraph and the partial minimum's epigraph have the same closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\), epigraph projection satisfies \[\operatorname{proj}_{X\times\mathbb{R}}(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g,\qquad \overline{\operatorname{proj}_{X\times\mathbb{R}}(\operatorname{epi}F)}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}.\] The first inclusion is an equality exactly when, for every \(x\) with finite \(g(x)\), the infimum \(\inf_zF(x,z)\) is attained. Without attainment, only boundary points \((x,g(x))\) can be missing from the projection; every \((x,t)\) with \(t>g(x)\) belongs to it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Z\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph projection, attainment, and closure under fiberwise elimination.

For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[\{x:g(x)<\alpha\}=\operatorname{proj}_X\{(x,z):F(x,z)<\alpha\},\] whereas \[\operatorname{proj}_X\{(x,z):F(x,z)\le\alpha\}\subseteq\{x:g(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Equality in the latter formula holds exactly when every \(x\) with \(g(x)=\alpha\) has some \(z\) satisfying \(F(x,z)=\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict sublevels project exactly; a closed-sublevel boundary point is lost precisely when its fiber infimum equals the level but is unattained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph addition and its lower-bound function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For sets in \(X\times\mathbb R\), addition means Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic epigraph calculus for extended-real functions. Ordinary epigraph equality records attainment; strict epigraph addition records the infimal value without attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For upper sets \(E,F\subset X\times\mathbb R\), their epigraph sum is \[E+F:=\{(x_1+x_2,r_1+r_2):(x_1,r_1)\in E,\ (x_2,r_2)\in F\}.\] Applied to functions, its lower-bound function is \[\ell_{\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g}(x):=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\}=(f\square g)(x).\] Always \[\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(f\square g).\] If the infimum is attained at every point of \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)\), then equality holds. With \(\operatorname{epi}_{<}f:=\{(x,r):f(x)<r\}\), one has the attainment-free identity \[\operatorname{epi}_{<}(f\square g)=\operatorname{epi}_{<}f+\operatorname{epi}_{<}g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph algebra adds epigraphs by Minkowski addition in the product of the argument space and the real line. The lower boundary of the sum is the infimal convolution. The ordinary sum is always contained in the epigraph of that convolution and equals it when all relevant decompositions are attained. Strict epigraphs remove the boundary-attainment issue and add exactly. Thus epigraph algebra distinguishes the numerical infimum from the existence of a decomposition realizing its boundary value.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(f\square g)(x)=\inf\{r_1+r_2:(x_i,r_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f_i,\ x_1+x_2=x\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For exact infimal convolution, \(\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\).
For indicator functions, epigraph addition reduces to Minkowski addition of the underlying sets together with the nonnegative vertical ray.
immediate_consequences_latex: The horizontal projection of the epigraph sum is \(\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
boundary_notes: The sum of two closed convex epigraphs need not be closed.
Ordinary epigraph equality can fail solely because the infimum is not attained.

notation.meaning: Lower-bound function of an upper subset of the product space.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Addition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph sum contains precisely decompositions with achieved upper bounds; it equals the infimal-convolution epigraph when every finite infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(h(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}\). For every \((x,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\), one has \((x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\) exactly when some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(f(y)+g(x-y)\le r\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h\). If \(h\) is proper, equality holds precisely when, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), the infimum defining \(h(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(f\square g), \text{ with equality exactly under pointwise attainment}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real epigraph algebra for proper infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(f_1,f_2:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional algebraic definition as presented in the cited source; no closedness or attainment is presumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph addition of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) is the Minkowski sum \[\operatorname{epi}f_1+\operatorname{epi}f_2:=\{(x_1+x_2,r_1+r_2):r_i\geq f_i(x_i),\ i=1,2\}.\] Its lower-bound function is \[x\mapsto\inf\{r_1+r_2:r_i\geq f_i(x_i),\ x_1+x_2=x\}=\inf_{x_1+x_2=x}\{f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)\}.\] Hence epigraph addition induces the infimal convolution \(f_1\square f_2\). The vertical boundary point \((x,(f_1\square f_2)(x))\) belongs to the epigraph sum exactly when some decomposition \(x=x_1+x_2\) attains the infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph addition is Minkowski addition of the two epigraphs in the product space. Its lower boundary is computed by minimizing the sum of the function values over additive decompositions of the argument, which is precisely infimal convolution. A boundary point belongs to the actual epigraph sum exactly when the corresponding infimum is attained; otherwise only points strictly above the boundary are represented.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f_1+\operatorname{epi}f_2\Longleftrightarrow(\exists x_1+x_2=x)(\exists r_1+r_2=r)\ r_i\geq f_i(x_i).\]
special_cases_latex: If both functions are indicators, horizontal epigraph addition is addition of their feasible sets.
If one function is \(\iota_{\{0\}}\), epigraph addition leaves the other epigraph unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f_1+\operatorname{epi}f_2\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(f_1\square f_2).\]
boundary_notes: Minkowski addition does not generally preserve closedness.
The lower-bound function depends only on the infimum and therefore does not itself encode attainment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicators turn infimal convolution into Minkowski addition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C,D\subset\mathcal H\) be nonempty. Define \(\iota_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure set–function correspondence; convexity and closedness of the sets are not required for the identity itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski sum is \[C+D:=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}.\] The indicator–Minkowski correspondence is the exact infimal-convolution identity \[\iota_C\square\iota_D=\iota_{C+D}.\] Indeed, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \[(\iota_C\square\iota_D)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathcal H}\{\iota_C(y)+\iota_D(x-y)\}=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C+D,\\+\infty,&x\notin C+D.\end{cases}\] Whenever \(x\in C+D\), every representation \(x=c+d\) with \(c\in C\) and \(d\in D\) is an attaining decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a nonempty set takes value zero on the set and infinity outside it. Infimal convolution of two indicators asks whether the argument can be decomposed into one point from each set. Its value is zero exactly on the Minkowski sum and infinity elsewhere. Thus the result is the indicator of the Minkowski sum, and every feasible decomposition attains the infimum.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in C+D\Longleftrightarrow(\exists y\in C)\ x-y\in D\Longleftrightarrow(\iota_C\square\iota_D)(x)=0.\]
\[\operatorname{epi}\iota_C=C\times\mathbb R_+,\qquad \operatorname{epi}\iota_D=D\times\mathbb R_+,\] so their epigraph sum is \((C+D)\times\mathbb R_+\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\{0\}\), then \(C+D=C\) and \(\iota_C\square\iota_{\{0\}}=\iota_C\).
If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(C+D\) and \(\iota_{C+D}\) are convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}(\iota_C\square\iota_D)=C+D.\]
boundary_notes: Even when \(C\) and \(D\) are closed and convex, \(C+D\) need not be closed in general infinite-dimensional settings.
The correspondence uses extended-real indicators, not binary-valued characteristic functions.

notation.meaning: Exact infimal convolution notation used in the cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal convolution of two set indicators is zero exactly at points decomposable as one point from each set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\delta_C(x)=0\) when \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. The indicator infimal convolution is \[(\delta_C\square\delta_D)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\delta_C(y)+\delta_D(x-y)\}.\] It has value \(0\) exactly when there exist \(c\in C\) and \(d\in D\) with \(x=c+d\), and has value \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real indicators use value zero on the set and positive infinity outside.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Closedness Regimes for Minkowski Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-plus-closed and polyhedral-plus-polyhedral are standard regimes in which Minkowski addition preserves closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). If one summand is compact and the other is closed, then \(C+D\) is closed. If both summands are polyhedral convex sets, then \(C+D\) is polyhedral and hence closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [C\text{ compact},D\text{ closed}]\Rightarrow C+D\text{ closed};\quad [C,D\text{ polyhedral}]\Rightarrow C+D\text{ polyhedral}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient conditions ensuring that a Minkowski sum is closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Summands with a Nonclosed Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum, as shown by a reciprocal epigraph plus the vertical axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y\ge x^{-1}\},\qquad D=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\] Both \(C\) and \(D\) are closed and convex, but \[C+D=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R,\] which is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C,D\text{ closed convex},\qquad C+D=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\text{ is not closed}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional counterexample to preservation of closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Laws of Minkowski Addition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition is commutative and associative, has the singleton zero as identity, and commutes with linear maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B,C\) of a real vector space, \[A+B=B+A,\qquad (A+B)+C=A+(B+C),\qquad A+\{0\}=A.\] For every linear map \(L\), \[L(A+B)=L(A)+L(B).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic and linear-image laws for set addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Set Addition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski sum consists of all pairwise sums of points from the two sets. Convex summands yield a convex sum, but closed summands need not yield a closed sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski sum of \(C\) and \(D\) is \[C+D:=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists c\in C,\ \exists d\in D,\ x=c+d\}.\] If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex, then \(C+D\) is convex. Closedness is not guaranteed merely from closedness of both summands in general finite-dimensional settings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic set addition in a finite-dimensional vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Summands with Nonclosed Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional witness for failure of closedness under Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x>0,\ y\ge 1/x\},\qquad D=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}.\] Then \(C\) and \(D\) are nonempty closed convex sets, whereas \[C+D=(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\] is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex reciprocal epigraph plus the vertical axis is the nonclosed open right half-plane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C,D\text{ are closed and convex, but }C+D\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Summands with Nonclosed Sum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal finite-dimensional sufficient conditions ensuring a closed Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), if \(C\) is compact and \(D\) is closed, then \(C+D\) is closed; if both sets are compact, their sum is compact. If \(C\) and \(D\) are convex polyhedra, then \(C+D\) is a convex polyhedron and hence closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-plus-closed and polyhedral-plus-polyhedral Minkowski sums retain closedness in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ compact},\ D\text{ closed}\Rightarrow C+D\text{ closed};\qquad C,D\text{ convex polyhedra}\Rightarrow C+D\text{ is a convex polyhedron}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness-Preserving Regimes
Support-Function Dual of the Indicator–Minkowski Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating the indicator correspondence gives the support-function identity for a Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[(\delta_C\square\delta_D)^*=\delta_C^*+\delta_D^*=\sigma_C+\sigma_D=\sigma_{C+D}.\] Thus the primal identity \(\delta_C\square\delta_D=\delta_{C+D}\) is dual to additivity of support functions under Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual support-function identity induced by the indicator infimal-convolution representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator–Minkowski Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition corresponds exactly to infimal convolution: the indicators convolve to the indicator of the set sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[(\delta_C\square\delta_D)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\delta_C(y)+\delta_D(x-y)\}=\delta_{C+D}(x).\] The common value is \(0\) when \(x\in C+D\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Thus Minkowski addition of sets is represented exactly by infimal convolution of their indicators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between extended-real function addition and set addition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the binary functional-geometric correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\mathop{\square}_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}=\delta_{C_1+\cdots+C_m}.\] Equivalently, the left side is zero at \(x\) exactly when \(x=c_1+\cdots+c_m\) for some \(c_i\in C_i\), and is \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite infimal convolution of set indicators is the indicator of their finite Minkowski sum.

Epigraph Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the epigraph sum yields the epigraph of the lower-semicontinuous hull; missing boundaries may reflect nonattainment or nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\). Then \[E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h\subseteq\overline{E},\qquad \overline{E}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\] Thus failure to attain a finite infimum can remove boundary points from \(E\), while failure of lower semicontinuity can make \(\operatorname{epi}h\) nonclosed. Taking closure repairs both defects at the epigraph level, but it does not supply an attained decomposition for the original infimal convolution.
assumptions_latex: f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] \text{ are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure formula for a proper convex infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and attainment gaps in epigraph addition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and set \(h=f\square g\). For an extended-real function \(q\), its lower-semicontinuous hull \(\operatorname{cl}q\) has epigraph \(\overline{\operatorname{epi}q}\) whenever this closure defines a proper function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex inputs; the output may fail to be exact or lower semicontinuous. The record separates the attainment gap from the closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the epigraph-attainment gap and epigraph-closure gap by \[G_{\mathrm{att}}:=\operatorname{epi}h\setminus(\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g),\qquad G_{\mathrm{cl}}:=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}\setminus\operatorname{epi}h.\] The universal inclusions are \[\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\] Exactness of \(h\) makes \(G_{\mathrm{att}}=\varnothing\); lower semicontinuity makes \(G_{\mathrm{cl}}=\varnothing\). Thus \(h\) is both exact and lower semicontinuous precisely when \[\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g=\operatorname{epi}h\] and this common epigraph is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an infimal convolution of closed convex functions, two distinct boundary defects can occur. The attainment gap consists of epigraph points not represented by sums of epigraph points. The closure gap consists of limit epigraph points missing from the epigraph of the convolution. Exactness removes the first gap, and lower semicontinuity removes the second. Both properties hold exactly when the epigraph sum equals the convolution epigraph and that set is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G_{\mathrm{att}}=\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow f\square g\ \text{is exact on its domain}.\]
\[G_{\mathrm{cl}}=\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow f\square g\ \text{is lower semicontinuous}.\]
special_cases_latex: If coercivity conditions ensure exactness and lower semicontinuity, both gaps vanish.
There exist \(f,g\in\Gamma_0\) for which the convolution is nowhere exact, and indicator examples for which the epigraph sum is not closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closing the epigraph replaces \(h\) by its lower-semicontinuous hull without repairing the original attainment relation.
boundary_notes: The equality \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}\) needs the usual proper-hull convention.
Closedness of each input epigraph does not imply closedness of their Minkowski sum.

notation.meaning: Set-valued gap caused by failure of attaining decompositions.
Set-valued gap caused by failure of lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f,g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(h=f\square g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real pointwise regime classification. Exactness requires an attained value in \((-\infty,+\infty]\) as in the cited definition; proper finite-domain exactness is singled out separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\mathcal H\), define \[D_{f,g}(x):=\{y\in\mathcal H:h(x)=f(y)+g(x-y)>-\infty\}.\] The convolution is exact at \(x\) when \(D_{f,g}(x)\neq\varnothing\). It is globally exact when it is exact at every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\). The pointwise regime map is \[\rho_{f,g}(x):=\begin{cases}\mathrm{attained},&D_{f,g}(x)\neq\varnothing,\\\mathrm{nonattained},&h(x)\in\mathbb R\ \text{and }D_{f,g}(x)=\varnothing,\\\mathrm{improper\ below},&h(x)=-\infty,\\\mathrm{outside\ domain},&h(x)=+\infty.\end{cases}\] In the globally exact regime, the notation \(f\boxdot g\) may be used for the exact infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exactness-attainment regime system classifies every point according to whether the infimal convolution has a minimizing decomposition, has a finite but unattained value, equals minus infinity, or lies outside the effective domain. Exactness at a point means that a decomposition realizes a value above minus infinity. Global exactness means this happens throughout the effective domain. The notation for exact infimal convolution records this global attainment property, not merely equality of infimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h\ \text{is exact at }x\Longleftrightarrow D_{f,g}(x)\neq\varnothing;\qquad h\ \text{is exact}\Longleftrightarrow(\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}h)\ D_{f,g}(x)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[h(x)=\min_{y\in\mathcal H}\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}>-\infty\] is the pointwise exactness condition.
At an exact point, \((x,h(x))\in\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\).
special_cases_latex: Indicators of nonempty sets are globally exact because membership in the Minkowski sum supplies a decomposition.
Closed convex inputs can nevertheless yield a nowhere-exact convolution.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is globally exact, then \(\operatorname{epi}h=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\).
boundary_notes: Existence of minimizing sequences does not imply exactness.
A value of \(-\infty\) is classified as improper below rather than as an attained finite decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Subgradient Certificate for an Attained Decomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared subgradient certifies an optimal decomposition; under the relative-interior sum-rule qualification, every attained decomposition has this certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(x-y\in\operatorname{dom}g\) admit \(u\in\partial f(y)\cap\partial g(x-y)\), then \[f(y)+g(x-y)=(f\square g)(x).\] Conversely, if \(y\) attains the infimum and \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\bigl(x-\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\bigr)\ne\varnothing,\] then such a common subgradient \(u\) exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificate for a realizing decomposition, with the qualification needed for necessity.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Bounded Attainment Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite lower-semicontinuous decomposition problem attains its infimum whenever its decomposition objective is level-bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and define \(\phi_x(y)=f(y)+g(x-y)\). If \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, \(\inf\phi_x\in\mathbb R\), and \(\phi_x\) is level-bounded, then \(\operatorname*{argmin}\phi_x\) is nonempty and compact. Consequently, \(f\square g\) is exact at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard compactness regime guaranteeing pointwise exactness of an infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Decomposition Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution is exact at a point precisely when an input decomposition attains its defining infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution is exact at \(x\) when there exists \(y_x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[h(x)=f(y_x)+g(x-y_x).\] Equivalently, its boundary point satisfies \((x,h(x))\in\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\). It is exact on a set \(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\) when this condition holds for every \(x\in S\), and globally exact when it holds throughout \(\operatorname{dom}h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h \text{ is exact at }x \iff \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ h(x)=f(y)+g(x-y)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise exactness and its epigraph-boundary characterization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Subgradient Certificate for an Attaining Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise first-order certificate under the qualification needed for the exact subdifferential sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), fix \(x\), and suppose \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\bigl(x-\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\bigr)\ne\varnothing\). Then \[y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_u\{f(u)+g(x-u)\}\iff \partial f(y)\cap\partial g(x-y)\ne\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior sum-rule qualification, a decomposition is optimal exactly when its two components share a subgradient.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness regime sufficient for pointwise exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower-semicontinuous, let \((f\square g)(x)\in\mathbb R\), and set \(\phi_x(y)=f(y)+g(x-y)\). If \(\{y:\phi_x(y)\le\alpha\}\) is nonempty and bounded for some \(\alpha>(f\square g)(x)\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}\phi_x\) is nonempty and compact. In particular, coercivity of \(\phi_x\) suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous decomposition objective attains its finite infimum when one near-optimal sublevel set is bounded; the minimizer set is then compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attaining decomposition set and uniqueness strata
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and set \(h=\square_{i=1}^m f_i\) on a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-arity pointwise attainment. The definition distinguishes existence from uniqueness and permits multiple optimal decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), the attaining decomposition set is \[\mathcal D(x):=\left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X^m:\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=x,\ \sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)=h(x)>-\infty\right\}.\] The attained regime is \(\mathcal A:=\{x:\mathcal D(x)\neq\varnothing\}\). It separates into the unique and multiple strata \[\mathcal A_1:=\{x:|\mathcal D(x)|=1\},\qquad \mathcal A_{>1}:=\{x:|\mathcal D(x)|>1\}.\] Thus \(h\) is exact at \(x\) precisely when \(x\in\mathcal A\), while exactness does not require \(x\in\mathcal A_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-arity infimal convolution, the attaining decomposition set contains all additive decompositions whose total cost equals the infimal value and is above minus infinity. Points with a nonempty set form the attained regime. This regime splits into points with one optimal decomposition and points with several. Exactness is equivalent to membership in the attained regime and does not imply uniqueness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(m=2\), \[\mathcal D(x)=\{(y,x-y):y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z[f_1(z)+f_2(x-z)]\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For indicators, \(\mathcal D(x)=\{(c,d)\in C\times D:c+d=x\}\).
Strict convexity of the decomposition objective on the affine fiber can force the unique stratum, when a minimizer exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: At any attained point, the boundary epigraph point decomposes as \[(x,h(x))=\sum_i(x_i,f_i(x_i))\] for every element of \(\mathcal D(x)\).
boundary_notes: The cardinality strata do not describe stability of minimizers under perturbations.
An empty decomposition set may reflect nonattainment or the improper value \(-\infty\); the value of \(h\) distinguishes them.

notation.meaning: Set of all attaining additive decompositions.
Points with a unique attaining decomposition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau envelope identity and unique decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-parameter Euclidean Moreau decomposition for closed proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex, and let \(w(z)=\tfrac12\lVert z\rVert^2\). Then
\[
(f\square w)(z)+(f^*\square w)(z)=w(z)\qquad(\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
Both defining infima are finite and uniquely attained. For each \(z\), their respective unique minimizers \(x\) and \(x^*\) are exactly the unique vectors satisfying
\[
z=x+x^*,\qquad x^*\in\partial f(x),
\]
and
\[
x=\nabla(f^*\square w)(z),\qquad x^*=\nabla(f\square w)(z).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic envelopes of a closed proper convex function and its conjugate sum to one half the squared norm. Both infimal convolutions have unique minimizers, which uniquely decompose every vector into a point and one of its subgradients; the components are the gradients of the conjugate-side and primal-side envelopes, respectively.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ (f\square w)(z)+(f^*\square w)(z)=w(z);\text{ both infima are finite and uniquely attained, with }z=x+x^*,\ x^*\in\partial f(x),\ x=\nabla(f^*\square w)(z),\ x^*=\nabla(f\square w)(z).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy, closedness, and attainment for a convex-process image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two conclusions use distinct relative-interior qualifications: the first gives exact conjugacy and dual-side attainment, while the second gives primal closedness and attainment together with a closure formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be a supremum-oriented convex process and let \(f\) be a proper convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}A)\neq\varnothing\), then \[(Af)^*=A^{*-1}f^*,\] and the infimum defining \((A^{*-1}f^*)(x^*)\) is attained for every \(x^*\). Separately, if \(A\) and \(f\) are closed and \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}A^{*-1})\neq\varnothing\), then \(Af\) is closed, the infimum defining \((Af)(x)\) is attained for every \(x\), and \[(Af)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^{*-1}f^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a supremum-oriented convex process and a proper convex function, intersection of the relative interiors of their domains gives an exact conjugate formula and attainment of the inverse-adjoint infimum at every dual point. Under the separate assumptions that the process and function are closed and that the corresponding dual domains have intersecting relative interiors, the process image is closed, its defining infimum is attained at every primal point, and its conjugate is the closure of the inverse-adjoint transform of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}(Af)^*=A^{*-1}f^*\text{ and the defining infimum is attained for every }x^*,&\text{under the first regime},\\Af\text{ is closed, its defining infimum is attained for every }x,\text{ and }(Af)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^{*-1}f^*),&\text{under the second regime}.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-semicontinuous hull of an infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(h:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, typically \(h=f\square g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper convex Hilbert-space regime. Closure is epigraphical and may change boundary values without supplying attaining decompositions for the original convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous closure of \(h\) is the function \[\operatorname{cl}h(x):=\sup\{a(x):a\ \text{is continuous affine and }a\leq h\},\] equivalently characterized by \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}.\] For \(h=f\square g\), the lower-semicontinuity closure interface is the chain \[\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\] The convolution is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(h=\operatorname{cl}h\), or equivalently when \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is closed. Closure and exactness coincide only under additional conditions ensuring that the epigraph sum itself is closed and equals \(\operatorname{epi}h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous closure of a proper convex function is its largest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant and has the closure of the original epigraph as its epigraph. For an infimal convolution, the epigraph sum lies inside the convolution epigraph, which lies inside its closure. The convolution is lower semicontinuous precisely when the second inclusion is equality. This closure operation changes limiting boundary values but does not by itself create minimizers for the original decomposition problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}(f\square g))=\overline{\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)},\qquad f\square g\ \text{is lsc}\Longleftrightarrow f\square g=\operatorname{cl}(f\square g).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Sequentially, \[h\ \text{is lsc}\Longleftrightarrow h(x)\leq\liminf_n h(x_n)\quad\text{whenever }x_n\to x.\]
For proper convex \(h\), lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}h\).
special_cases_latex: Under a supercoercivity condition on one input, cited results ensure that the convolution is exact and belongs to \(\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(x\), then \((\operatorname{cl}h)(x)<h(x)\) can occur.
Biconjugation provides another representation of the closed convex hull when the standard Fenchel–Moreau hypotheses apply.
boundary_notes: The closure of the epigraph sum and the epigraph of the exact convolution should not be identified without an attainment argument.
If the closure is improper, additional conventions are needed.

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous convex closure of a proper convex function.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Continuity of Proper Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is automatically relatively continuous inside its domain, so lower-semicontinuity failures are boundary phenomena.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex, then its restriction to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) is continuous relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}h)\). Consequently, every possible failure of lower semicontinuity occurs at the relative boundary of \(\operatorname{dom}h\). If \(h\) is finite everywhere, it is continuous and lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb R^n\).
assumptions_latex: h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automatic regularity on the relative interior of the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph, equivalently every real sublevel set, is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) when \[h(x)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}h(x_k)\] for every sequence \(x_k\to x\). It is lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\). For proper convex \(h\), this is also equivalent to all sublevel sets \(\{x:h(x)\le\alpha\}\) being closed for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h \text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}h \text{ is closed}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and epigraphical lower-semicontinuity criteria in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) when \[h(x)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}h(x_k)\] for every sequence \(x_k\to x\). It is lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\). For proper convex \(h\), this is also equivalent to all sublevel sets \(\{x:h(x)\le\alpha\}\) being closed for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph, equivalently every real sublevel set, is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Lower-Semicontinuity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Biconjugate Representation of Convex Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate of a proper convex function is its lower-semicontinuous closure, provided that closure remains proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex and \(\operatorname{cl}h\) is proper, then \[h^{**}=\operatorname{cl}h.\] In particular, \(h=h^{**}\) exactly when \(h\) is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Moreau representation of the lower-semicontinuous closure of a proper convex function.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a proper convex function means closing its epigraph; the result is its greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous hull \(\operatorname{cl}h\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function majorized by \(h\). Under the stated properness condition, it is characterized epigraphically by \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{cl}h\le h\), the function \(\operatorname{cl}h\) is proper lower-semicontinuous and convex, and \(h=\operatorname{cl}h\) exactly when \(h\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical closure of a proper finite-dimensional convex function.

Strict-Epigraph Sandwich for an Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph sum always contains the strict epigraph and can omit only unattained lower-boundary points; closure fills those points and any lower-semicontinuity gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=f\square g\) and \(E=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\). Then \[\{(x,r):r>h(x)\}\subseteq E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h.\] For a finite value \(h(x)\), the boundary point \((x,h(x))\) belongs to \(E\) exactly when the defining infimum is attained at \(x\). Consequently, whenever \(h\) and \(\operatorname{cl}h\) are proper, \[\overline E=\overline{\operatorname{epi}h}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact location of an epigraph sum between the strict and ordinary epigraphs of the infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity–Closure Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph sum is closed exactly when the infimal convolution is both lower semicontinuous and globally attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g\). The closure identity is \(\overline{E}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h)\), whereas exactness gives \(E=\operatorname{epi}h\). Hence \[E\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h=\operatorname{cl}h\text{ and }h\text{ is exact at every }x\in\operatorname{dom}h.\] Thus lower semicontinuity controls whether \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is closed, while attainment controls whether its finite boundary points already belong to the epigraph sum.
assumptions_latex: f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] \text{ are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g \text{ is closed}\iff h \text{ is lower semicontinuous and globally exact}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates lower-semicontinuity from exactness in epigraph-sum closedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure sets for finite nonattainment and improper values
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f,g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and set \(h=f\square g\) and \(D(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise classification of failures of infimal convolution. It separates finite nonattainment from descent to \(-\infty\) and infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[N_{f,g}:=\{x\in\mathcal H:h(x)\in\mathbb R,\ D(x)=\varnothing\},\] \[I^-_{f,g}:=\{x\in\mathcal H:h(x)=-\infty\},\qquad I^+_{f,g}:=\{x\in\mathcal H:h(x)=+\infty\}.\] The nonattainment–improperness failure boundary is the disjoint classification \[\mathcal F_{f,g}:=N_{f,g}\mathbin{\dot\cup}I^-_{f,g}\mathbin{\dot\cup}I^+_{f,g}.\] Points outside \(\mathcal F_{f,g}\) have a finite attained decomposition. Here \(N_{f,g}\) represents a meaningful finite infimum with no optimizer, \(I^-_{f,g}\) represents unbounded descent or other improper behavior, and \(I^+_{f,g}=\mathcal H\setminus(\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g)\) represents infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure boundary partitions unsuccessful points of an infimal convolution into three types. At finite nonattainment points, the value is real but no minimizing decomposition exists. At improper-below points, the value is minus infinity. At outside-domain points, no finite decomposition exists and the value is plus infinity. Every point not in these sets has a finite attained decomposition. This classification prevents nonattainment from being conflated with infeasibility or unbounded descent.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\notin\mathcal F_{f,g}\Longleftrightarrow h(x)\in\mathbb R\ \text{and}\ (\exists y)\ h(x)=f(y)+g(x-y).\]
special_cases_latex: There are closed convex inputs whose convolution is finite everywhere but nowhere exact, so \(N_{f,g}=\mathcal H\).
Real-valued linear functions with opposite slopes can yield \(h\equiv-\infty\), so \(I^-_{f,g}=\mathcal H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A common continuous affine minorant excludes \(I^-_{f,g}\).
Exactness on the domain excludes \(N_{f,g}\).
boundary_notes: This is a pointwise failure classification, not a topological boundary in the sense of set closure.
The minimizing set \(D(x)\) is used only when the infimal value is finite.

notation.meaning: Set on which the convolution equals minus infinity.
Union of the three failure regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Escape of Every Minimizing Sequence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite nonattainment occurs exactly when all minimizing decompositions escape every compact set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and let \(\phi_x(y)=f(y)+g(x-y)\), where \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(\inf\phi_x\in\mathbb R\). The infimum is not attained if and only if every minimizing sequence \((y_k)\) for \(\phi_x\) is unbounded. Equivalently, for every nonempty compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\inf_{y\in K}\phi_x(y)>\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\phi_x(y).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness characterization of finite nonattainment for a lower-semicontinuous decomposition problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous convex inputs can have a finite, lower-semicontinuous infimal convolution whose infimum is nowhere attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(y)=e^y\) and \(g(z)=0\) for \(y,z\in\mathbb{R}\). Both functions are proper continuous convex functions. For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \[(f\square g)(x)=0,\] but no \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) attains this value. Therefore \(f\square g\) is proper, finite, convex, and lower semicontinuous, while its defining decomposition is nowhere attained and its epigraph sum omits every boundary point \((x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f\square g)(x)=0 \text{ for every }x, \text{ but the infimum is never attained}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional continuous convex example of finite nonattainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Domain Properness Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infimal convolution is proper exactly when a feasible primal decomposition exists and the two conjugates have a common finite point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions. Then \(f\square g\) is proper if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{dom}f^*\cap\operatorname{dom}g^*\ne\varnothing.\] Any \(u\) in the dual-domain intersection supplies the common affine lower bound \[(f\square g)(x)\ge \langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)-g^*(u),\] excluding the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient finite-dimensional certificate preventing an infimal convolution from taking minus infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Descent Certificate for Improperness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative paired recession direction makes the decomposition objective unbounded below without changing the represented point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\). If there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[f^{\infty}(d)+g^{\infty}(-d)<0,\] then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\), \[(f\square g)(x)=-\infty.\] The direction \((d,-d)\) preserves the represented sum while driving the decomposition cost to \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for an infimal convolution to equal minus infinity on its feasible sum domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Improperness Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even proper continuous convex inputs can have an infimal convolution identically minus infinity when a decomposition direction permits unbounded descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(y)=-y\) and \(g(z)=0\) for \(y,z\in\mathbb{R}\). Both functions are proper continuous convex functions, but for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \[(f\square g)(x)=-\infty.\] Hence their infimal convolution is improper: the decomposition objective is unbounded below while the represented point \(x=y+(x-y)\) remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional recession mismatch producing an improper infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properness Criterion via a Common Conjugate-Domain Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional dual criterion excluding minus-infinity values for the infimal convolution of proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions and set \(h=f\square g\). Since \(\operatorname{dom}h=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\), \(h\) is proper if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f^*\cap\operatorname{dom}g^*\ne\varnothing.\] Indeed, every \(p\) in this intersection supplies the global bound \[h(x)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)-g^*(p)>-\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal convolution of two proper finite-dimensional convex functions is proper exactly when their conjugates have a common finite point, equivalently when the convolution has a global affine lower bound.
assumptions_latex: f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.title: Properness Criterion via a Common Conjugate-Domain Point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural certificate for an unbounded-below decomposition objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), suppose \(f(y_0)+g(x-y_0)<+\infty\), and assume that some \(d\) satisfies \[f^\infty(d)+g^\infty(-d)<0.\] Then \(f(y_0+td)+g(x-y_0-td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to+\infty\), so \((f\square g)(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair of opposed recession directions with negative total recession cost makes the fixed-point decomposition objective unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.title: Opposed Recession Direction Certificate
Nonattainment–Improperness Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In one affine-tilt family, positive parameters give attainment, zero gives finite nonattainment, and negative parameters make the convolution improper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \[h_a(x)=ax+\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\{e^y-ay\}.\] If \(a>0\), the unique minimizer is \(y=\log a\), and \(h_a(x)=ax+a-a\log a\). If \(a=0\), then \(h_0(x)=0\), but no minimizer exists. If \(a<0\), then \(h_a(x)=-\infty\). Thus \(a=0\) is the finite-nonattainment boundary separating exact proper convolution from improperness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a>0 \Rightarrow h_a \text{ attained};\quad a=0 \Rightarrow h_a \text{ finite but unattained};\quad a<0 \Rightarrow h_a\equiv-\infty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized one-dimensional boundary between attainment, nonattainment, and improperness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General affine-tilt classification into attained, finite-unattained, and improper regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, let \(g_a(z)=az\), and let \(h_a=f\square g_a\). Then \[h_a(x)=ax-f^*(a).\] If \(f^*(a)<+\infty\), then \(h_a\) is finite everywhere; its defining infimum is attained exactly when \(a\in\partial f(y)\) for some \(y\). If \(f^*(a)=+\infty\), then \(h_a\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine second operand, the conjugate domain determines properness, while attainment of the conjugate supremum distinguishes attained from finite-unattained convolution.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_a(x)=ax-f^*(a),\quad f^*(a)<+\infty\text{ determines finiteness, and }a\in\bigcup_y\partial f(y)\text{ determines attainment}

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at y
