knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \((k_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) be extended-real kernels on \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-invariant additive kernels. The cited norm-power family includes Pasch–Hausdorff and Moreau envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal regularization family generated by \((k_\theta)\) is \[R_\theta f:=f\square k_\theta,\qquad (R_\theta f)(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathcal H}\{f(y)+k_\theta(x-y)\}.\] For \(p\geq1\) and \(\gamma>0\), the norm-power family is \[R_{\gamma,p}f:=f\square\left(\frac{1}{\gamma p}\|\cdot\|^p\right).\] Its principal named members are the Pasch–Hausdorff envelope \[P_\beta f:=f\square(\beta\|\cdot\|),\qquad \beta\geq0,\] and the Moreau envelope \[{}^\gamma f:=f\square\left(\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|\cdot\|^2\right),\qquad \gamma>0.\] Each member is an infimal convolution; exactness, finiteness, smoothness, and lower semicontinuity depend on \(f\) and the selected kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infimal regularization family is obtained by convolving one function with a parameterized collection of penalty kernels. Norm-power kernels penalize displacement from the latent point. The degree-one kernel produces the Pasch–Hausdorff envelope, and the squared-norm kernel produces the Moreau envelope. These names specify the kernels and parameters only; whether a member is proper, exact, finite, continuous, or smooth requires additional hypotheses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(R_{\gamma,p}f)(x)=\inf_y\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{\gamma p}\|x-y\|^p\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(p=1\) and \(\beta=1/\gamma\), the norm-power family is the Pasch–Hausdorff envelope.
For \(p=2\), it is the Moreau envelope of parameter \(\gamma\).
For an indicator \(f=\iota_C\), \({}^\gamma f=d_C^2/(2\gamma)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Choosing \(y=x\) yields \(R_{\gamma,p}f(x)\leq f(x)\).
For proper \(f\), the norm-power regularizations have full formal domain, although they can equal \(-\infty\) without further assumptions.
For suitable proper closed convex \(f\) and \(p>1\), the norm-power regularization is exact and continuous.
boundary_notes: The parameter convention changes across the literature; this record uses the cited factor \((\gamma p)^{-1}\).
The case \(\gamma=0\) is excluded from the norm-power and Moreau definitions.
Infinite-dimensional discontinuous linear functions show that a norm-power regularization may be identically \(-\infty\).

notation.meaning: Regularized member corresponding to kernel parameter \(\theta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Steep-Affine Improperness Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function whose slope exceeds the requested Lipschitz modulus has an envelope identically minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=\mathbb R\), \(f(y)=ay\), and \(|a|>r\), \[(P_rf)(x)=\inf_y\{ay+r|x-y|\}=-\infty\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when no minorant of the prescribed Lipschitz modulus exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Pasch–Hausdorff Envelope and Greatest Lipschitz Minorant
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Pasch–Hausdorff envelope infimally convolves a function with a scaled norm and, when finite, is its greatest Lipschitz minorant of that modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r>0\), define \[(P_r f)(x)=\inf_{y\in X}\{f(y)+r\|x-y\|\}=f\mathbin{\square}(r\|\cdot\|)(x).\] One has \(P_r f\le f\). If \(P_r f\) is real-valued, it is \(r\)-Lipschitz and is the greatest real-valued \(r\)-Lipschitz function majorized by \(f\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_r f=f\square(r\|\cdot\|)\), and when real-valued it is the greatest \(r\)-Lipschitz minorant of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-kernel infimal regularization and its extremal characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ball Truncation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a Pasch–Hausdorff envelope restricts the original conjugate to a dual ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_*:=\{u\in X^*:\|u\|_*\le1\}\). Whenever \(P_r f\) is proper, \[(P_r f)^*=f^*+\delta_{rB_*}.\] Thus Pasch–Hausdorff regularization restricts the effective conjugate domain to the radius-\(r\) dual ball.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space, \(f\) is proper, \(r>0\), and \(P_r f\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate representation of norm-kernel regularization.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the dual norm

knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Regularization and Fixed-Point Laws
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition retains the smaller Lipschitz modulus, and fixed points are exactly functions already satisfying that modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r,s>0\), whenever the displayed envelopes avoid \(-\infty\), \[P_r(P_s f)=P_{\min\{r,s\}}f.\] Hence \(P_r\) is idempotent. For real-valued \(f\), \(P_r f=f\) exactly when \(f\) is \(r\)-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space, \(f\) is proper, and the displayed envelopes avoid \(-\infty\).
For the fixed-point equivalence, \(f\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition, idempotence, and fixed points of Pasch–Hausdorff envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pasch–Hausdorff Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric infimal regularization by a norm penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\rho>0\). The Pasch–Hausdorff envelope of index \(\rho\) is \[f_\rho(x)=\inf_{y\in X}\bigl(f(y)+\rho\|x-y\|\bigr).\] It satisfies \(f_\rho\leq f\). If \(f_\rho(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), then \(f_\rho\) is real-valued, \(\rho\)-Lipschitz, and is the greatest \(\rho\)-Lipschitz function majorized by \(f\). If \(f\) is convex, then \(f_\rho\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Pasch–Hausdorff envelope infimally convolves a function with a scaled norm and, when finite, is its greatest Lipschitz minorant of that modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\rho=f\mathbin{\square}(\rho\|\cdot\|)\), and finiteness makes \(f_\rho\) the greatest \(\rho\)-Lipschitz minorant of \(f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of norm-kernel infimal regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_r f=f\mathbin{\square}(r\|\cdot\|)\). Then
\[
(P_r f)^*=f^*+\delta_{rB_{X^*}},
\qquad B_{X^*}:=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*\|_*\le1\}.
\]
Thus conjugation restricts the effective dual slopes to the closed dual ball of radius \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a Pasch–Hausdorff envelope adds the indicator of the radius-r dual ball.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space with continuous dual \(X^*\).

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball for the dual norm

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of the Pasch–Hausdorff Envelope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional boundary between a finite envelope and collapse to minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f(y)=-ay\). Then
\[
(P_r f)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}\{-ay+r|x-y|\}.
\]
If \(|a|\le r\), this equals \(-ax\); if \(|a|>r\), it equals \(-\infty\) for every \(x\). Thus properness of \(f\) alone does not ensure a proper or real-valued Pasch–Hausdorff envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function has a finite envelope exactly when its slope lies in the radius-r dual ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_r f=f\) if \(|a|\le r\), while \(P_r f\equiv-\infty\) if \(|a|>r\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Affine-Slope Finiteness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition and idempotence across Lipschitz parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r,s>0\),
\[
P_r(P_s f)=P_{\min\{r,s\}}f
\]
whenever these envelopes avoid the value \(-\infty\). In particular, \(P_r(P_r f)=P_r f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive Pasch–Hausdorff regularizations retain the smaller Lipschitz parameter; equal-parameter regularization is idempotent.
assumptions_latex: The displayed envelopes do not take the value \(-\infty\).

notation.meaning: Pasch–Hausdorff regularization operator defined in the immutable deferred context

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Minimum Composition Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition and fixed points of Pasch–Hausdorff envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r,s>0\), \[P_r(P_s f)=P_{\min\{r,s\}}f.\] Consequently \(P_r\) is idempotent. If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is lower-semicontinuous, then \(P_r f=f\) exactly when \(f\) is \(r\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing two Pasch–Hausdorff regularizations keeps the smaller Lipschitz bound, and the fixed points are precisely the lower-semicontinuous functions already satisfying that bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space, \(f\) is proper, and the displayed envelopes avoid \(-\infty\).
For the fixed-point equivalence, \(f\) is real-valued and lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Regularization Law
Minimizer Preservation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau regularization preserves the infimum and minimizer set; minimizers are exactly proximal fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), \[\inf_H e_\lambda f=\inf_H f,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}e_\lambda f=\operatorname*{argmin}f=\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}).\] Equivalently, \(x\) minimizes these functions exactly when \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of optimal values and minimizers under quadratic regularization.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Semigroup Law
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two successive Moreau regularizations equal one regularization with the summed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda,\mu>0\), \[e_\lambda(e_\mu f)=e_{\lambda+\mu}f.\] Thus infimal convolution by \(q_\lambda(x)=\|x\|^2/(2\lambda)\) forms an additive semigroup.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), and \(\lambda,\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additivity of successive quadratic regularization parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Monotonicity and Endpoint Limits
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The envelope increases to the original closed convex function as its parameter vanishes and decreases to the global infimum as the parameter diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0<\lambda<\mu\), then \[\inf f\le e_\mu f(x)\le e_\lambda f(x)\le f(x).\] For every \(x\in H\), \[e_\lambda f(x)\uparrow f(x)\quad(\lambda\downarrow0),\qquad e_\lambda f(x)\downarrow\inf_H f\quad(\lambda\to\infty),\] with the latter limit allowed to be \(-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\lambda f\uparrow f\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\) and \(e_\lambda f\downarrow\inf f\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise order and limiting behavior of the Moreau family.

knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Envelopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau envelope is quadratic infimal regularization, and its uniquely minimizing point is the proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Moreau envelope of \(f\) with parameter \(\lambda\) is
\[
e_\lambda f(x):=\inf_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\right\}.
\]
For every \(x\in H\), the objective has a unique minimizer, denoted
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x):=\underset{y\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\right\}.
\]
Consequently, \(e_\lambda f\) is finite on \(H\) and \(e_\lambda f(x)\leq f(x)\) whenever \(f(x)<+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space quadratic infimal regularization using the standard parameter convention.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 6.7 The Moreau Envelope p. 163

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact certificate for the minimizing point in the Moreau-envelope subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in H\),
\[
p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\partial f(p)+\frac{p-x}{\lambda}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial f(p).
\]
At such a point,
\[
e_\lambda f(x)=f(p)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-p\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is the proximal minimizer exactly when its scaled residual is a subgradient of the original function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and Recovery as the Parameter Vanishes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise approximation behavior of Moreau envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(0<\lambda<\mu\), then
\[
e_\lambda f(x)\ge e_\mu f(x).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}e_\lambda f(x)=f(x)
\]
for every \(x\in H\), with the extended-real interpretation when \(f(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau envelopes decrease as the parameter increases and recover the closed convex function as the parameter tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity and Recovery as the Parameter Vanishes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Semicontinuity Is Needed for Proximal Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the seed's attainment conclusion when closedness is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f=\delta_{(0,1)}\). At \(x=0\),
\[
\inf_y\left\{f(y)+\frac{|y|^2}{2\lambda}\right\}=0,
\]
but no \(y\in(0,1)\) attains the infimum. Thus convexity and properness alone do not ensure proximal attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an open interval is convex and proper but yields an unattained Moreau infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\lambda f(0)=0\), but the minimizing set is empty.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower Semicontinuity Is Needed for Proximal Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Needed for Proximal Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniqueness for a proper closed nonconvex operand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f=\delta_{\{-1,1\}}\). At \(x=0\), both \(-1\) and \(1\) minimize
\[
f(y)+\frac{|y|^2}{2\lambda}.
\]
Thus properness and lower semicontinuity without convexity do not ensure a single-valued proximal mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of two points has two proximal minimizers at their midpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Needed for Proximal Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition law for successive quadratic infimal regularizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda,\mu>0\),
\[
e_\lambda(e_\mu f)=e_{\lambda+\mu}f.
\]
Thus successive Moreau regularizations add their parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying Moreau regularization twice equals one regularization with the sum of the parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Envelope Semigroup Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal-convolution representation using a scaled squared-norm kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\mu>0\). Define
\[
\omega_\mu(x):=\frac{1}{2\mu}\|x\|^2.
\]
Then
\[
M_f^\mu=f\square\omega_\mu.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau envelope is the infimal convolution of the function with the quadratic kernel whose value at x is the squared norm of x divided by twice mu.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, closed, and convex}

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Average
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal average combines quadratically shifted conjugates with convex weights, conjugates the result, and subtracts the same quadratic; zero-weight operands are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_\mu(x)=\|x\|^2/(2\mu)\), let \(\alpha_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), and omit indices with \(\alpha_i=0\). The proximal average is \[\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\alpha)=\left(\sum_{i:\alpha_i>0}\alpha_i(f_i+q_\mu)^*\right)^*-q_\mu.\] It belongs to \(\Gamma_0(H)\) and is invariant under simultaneous permutation of operands and weights.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(\mu>0\), \(\alpha_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted proximal average under the quadratic parameter convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugation Self-Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a proximal average is the proximal average of the conjugates with reciprocal parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the adopted convention, \[\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\alpha)^*=\operatorname{pav}_{1/\mu}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*;\alpha).\]
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(\alpha_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), and \(\mu>0\).
Zero-weight indices are omitted as in the definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal-parameter conjugacy of proximal averages.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope and Proximal-Mapping Averaging
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The envelope and proximal mapping of a proximal average are the corresponding weighted averages of the component envelopes and proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the defining scale, \[e_\mu\bigl(\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)\bigr)=\sum_i\alpha_i e_\mu f_i,\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\mu\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)}=\sum_i\alpha_i\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f_i}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(\alpha_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), and \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational identities at the defining quadratic scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic–Harmonic Bounds and Limits
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average lies between the conjugate harmonic average and arithmetic average and interpolates between them as the parameter varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For normalized nonnegative weights, \[\left(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*\right)^*\le \operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)\le\sum_i\alpha_i f_i.\] In finite dimensions, as \(\mu\downarrow0\) the proximal average epi-converges to \(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\), while as \(\mu\to\infty\) it epi-converges to \((\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*)^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*)^*\le\operatorname{pav}_\mu\le\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\), with the stated endpoint epi-limits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise interpolation bounds and finite-dimensional endpoint epi-limits.
Reciprocal-parameter conjugacy for positive finite weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\bigl(\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\alpha)\bigr)^*=\operatorname{pav}_{1/\mu}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*;\alpha).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a proximal average conjugates its inputs and reciprocates the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the ith function.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Self-Duality of Proximal Averaging

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Averaging of Proximal Maps and Moreau Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identities at the proximal average's defining parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\mu\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)}(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f_i}(x),\qquad e_\mu(\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha))(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i e_\mu f_i(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the defining parameter, proximal mappings and envelopes are averaged exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Averaging of Proximal Maps and Moreau Envelopes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise bounds for positive finite weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(L(x):=\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i x_i=x}\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(x_i)\). Then \[L(x)\leq\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)(x)\leq\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average lies between the weighted barycentric infimal convolution and arithmetic mean.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution and Arithmetic-Mean Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reproduction when all positively weighted inputs coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1=\cdots=f_m=f\), then for every \(\mu>0\), \[\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f,\ldots,f;\alpha)=f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal average of identical functions is the same function, independently of the parameter and positive weights.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Idempotence of Proximal Averaging

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formula for strictly positive finite weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \[\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)(x)=\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i x_i=x}\left\{\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(x_i)+\frac1{2\mu}\sum_i\alpha_i\|x_i-x\|^2\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average is a barycentric infimum with a quadratic dispersion penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Barycentric Variational Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpolation between the arithmetic mean and the closed weighted barycentric infimal convolution for strictly positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_\mu=\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_i;\alpha)\), \(A=\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\), and \[L(x)=\inf_{\sum_i\alpha_i x_i=x}\sum_i\alpha_i f_i(x_i).\] If \(0<\mu_1\leq\mu_2\), then \(p_{\mu_2}\leq p_{\mu_1}\) pointwise. Moreover, \[p_\mu\xrightarrow[\mu\downarrow0]{\mathrm{epi}}A,\qquad p_\mu\xrightarrow[\mu\uparrow\infty]{\mathrm{epi}}L^{**}=\left(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*\right)^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the parameter grows, the proximal average decreases from the arithmetic mean toward the closed weighted infimal convolution.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and \(f_i\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\mu\) is pointwise nonincreasing in \(\mu\), with epi-limits \(A\) at zero and \(L^{**}\) at infinity.

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous convex hull of the weighted barycentric infimal convolution

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Monotonicity and Epi-Limits

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted proximal average on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_\mu(x):=\|x\|^2/(2\mu)\). The proximal average of \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) with weights \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m)\) and parameter \(\mu\) is
\[
\operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\alpha):=
\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i(f_i+q_\mu)^*\right)^*-q_\mu.
\]
The conjugates and weighted sum are taken as extended-real-valued convex functions on \(H\). This construction yields a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and is invariant under simultaneous permutation of the functions and their weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal average combines quadratically shifted conjugates using convex weights, conjugates the result, and subtracts the same quadratic.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Averages

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise interpolation bounds for the proximal average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive normalized weights, \[\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i^*\right)^*\le \operatorname{pav}_\mu(f_1,\ldots,f_m;\alpha)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i.\] Moreover, as \(\mu\downarrow0\) the proximal average increases to the arithmetic average \(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\), while as \(\mu\to\infty\) it decreases to the lower-semicontinuous convex harmonic average \((\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*)^*\), in the standard epi-limit sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal average interpolates between the conjugate harmonic average and the ordinary arithmetic average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sum_i\alpha_i f_i^*)^*\le\operatorname{pav}_\mu\le\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\), with the stated endpoint epi-limits.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), let \(\gamma>0\), and set \(q(x)=\|x\|^2/2\). Define the Moreau envelope by \(e_\gamma f=f\square(\gamma^{-1}q)\) and the proximity operator by \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)=\arg\min_y\{f(y)+\|x-y\|^2/(2\gamma)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hilbert-space correspondence for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions and quadratic Moreau regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathfrak M_\gamma(f):=\left\{\begin{aligned}(f+\gamma q)^*&=e_\gamma(f^*),\\ q/\gamma&=e_\gamma f+e_{1/\gamma}(f^*)\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}),\\ \operatorname{Id}&=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}+\gamma\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}),\\ f(p)+f^*(u)&=\langle p,u\rangle\quad\text{when }p=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x,\ u=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma).\end{aligned}\right.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled Moreau conjugacy correspondence of \(f\) at parameter \(\gamma\) is the family consisting of the quadratic conjugacy identity, the complementary-envelope identity, the complementary-proximity identity, and the associated Fenchel–Young contact identity. For every \(x\in\mathcal H\), the primal proximal point \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x\) and dual proximal point \(u=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)\) satisfy \(x=p+\gamma u\), while their function values satisfy \(f(p)+f^*(u)=\langle p,u\rangle\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak M_\gamma(f)\) is the four-identity correspondence displayed in the statement.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x\bigr).\]
\[e_\gamma f(x)+e_{1/\gamma}(f^*)(x/\gamma)=\frac{\|x\|^2}{2\gamma}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(\gamma=1\), \(e_1f+e_1f^*=q\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_f+\operatorname{prox}_{f^*}=\operatorname{Id}\).
For \(f=\iota_K\) with a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\), the proximity identity becomes Moreau’s cone decomposition.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(u\in\partial f(p)\) and \(p\in\partial f^*(u)\).
The primal and dual residuals determine one another by \(x-p=\gamma u\).
boundary_notes: The identities require exact Fenchel conjugacy and quadratic Hilbert-space regularization; nonquadratic Bregman envelopes are not included.
No differentiability of \(f\) or \(f^*\) is assumed.

knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Decomposition Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled proximal points of a convex function and its conjugate sum to the original point, with a parallel identity for their envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x):=\underset{y\in H}{\operatorname{argmin}}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\right\},
\]
the scaled Moreau decomposition is
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)+\lambda\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda)=x.
\]
The corresponding envelope decomposition is
\[
e_\lambda f(x)+e_{1/\lambda}f^*(x/\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x\|^2.
\]
Both identities hold for every \(x\in H\) and every \(\lambda>0\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(x\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaled vector and envelope decompositions in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[D_\gamma^f(x):=(p_\gamma(x),u_\gamma(x)),\qquad p_\gamma(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x,\quad u_\gamma(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma),\] \[x=p_\gamma(x)+\gamma u_\gamma(x),\qquad \frac{\|x\|^2}{2\gamma}=e_\gamma f(x)+e_{1/\gamma}(f^*)(x/\gamma).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau decomposition family associated with \(f\) is the parameterized collection \(\{D_\gamma^f(x):\gamma>0,\ x\in\mathcal H\}\). Its member at \((\gamma,x)\) is the ordered primal–dual pair \((p_\gamma(x),u_\gamma(x))\), where \(p_\gamma(x)\) minimizes \(f(y)+\|x-y\|^2/(2\gamma)\) and \(u_\gamma(x)\) minimizes \(f^*(v)/\gamma+\|x/\gamma-v\|^2/2\). The pair decomposes \(x\) as \(x=p_\gamma(x)+\gamma u_\gamma(x)\), and the corresponding primal and dual envelopes decompose the quadratic energy \(\|x\|^2/(2\gamma)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_\gamma^f(x)\) is the unique pair defined by the two proximal minimizers and satisfying the displayed vector and value decompositions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[p_\gamma(x)=x-\gamma u_\gamma(x).\]
\[u_\gamma(x)=\nabla e_\gamma f(x).\]
special_cases_latex: At \(\gamma=1\), \(x=\operatorname{prox}_f x+\operatorname{prox}_{f^*}x\).
If \(f=\iota_V\) for a closed linear subspace \(V\), then \(x=P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(x-p_\gamma(x)\) is the scaled dual component \(\gamma u_\gamma(x)\).
Both components are defined for every \(x\in\mathcal H\).
boundary_notes: The two components need not be orthogonal for a general convex function.
The parameter must be strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Proximity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal proximal point corresponds exactly to a complementary proximal point of the conjugate, related through the primal optimality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y\in H\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x),
\qquad
\frac{x-y}{\lambda}\in\partial f(y),
\qquad
\frac{x-y}{\lambda}=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda).
\]
Equivalently, the primal proximal point \(y\) and the dual proximal point \((x-y)/\lambda\) determine one another, and their scaled sum satisfies
\[
y+\lambda\frac{x-y}{\lambda}=x.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise correspondence between complementary proximal points.

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of lambda times f.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-level correspondence between the proximal mappings of a function and its Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal P_\gamma(f):\quad \operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id})=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Id}-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate proximity correspondence at scale \(\gamma\) is the operator identity that reconstructs the proximal mapping of the conjugate from the residual of the primal proximal mapping. Explicitly, for every \(x\in\mathcal H\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}(x/\gamma)=(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x)/\gamma\). Thus either proximal operator determines the other after the reciprocal scaling of the argument and function.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{Id}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}+\gamma\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}).\]
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\gamma}\circ(\gamma^{-1}\operatorname{Id}).\]
special_cases_latex: For \(\gamma=1\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{f^*}=\operatorname{Id}-\operatorname{prox}_f\).
For \(f=\iota_C\), the primal operator is the metric projection \(P_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal residual map \(\gamma^{-1}(\operatorname{Id}-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f})\) is itself a conjugate proximity operator after scaling.
For \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}x\), the reconstructed vector \((x-p)/\gamma\) belongs to \(\partial f(p)\).
boundary_notes: The identity concerns Fenchel conjugates and exact proximity operators.
It does not assert that the two proximal components are orthogonal.

knowledge_statements.title: Converse Envelope Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite closed convex function is a Moreau envelope at scale lambda exactly when its gradient has the corresponding Lipschitz bound, equivalently when its conjugate retains a closed convex remainder after subtracting the quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\Gamma_0(H)\) be finite everywhere and \(\lambda>0\). The following are equivalent: \(g=e_\lambda f\) for some \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\); \(g\) is Fréchet differentiable with \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz gradient; and \[g^*-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\in\Gamma_0(H).\] In this case one may take \[f=\left(g^*-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\right)^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(g\in\Gamma_0(H)\) is finite everywhere, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization and reconstruction of convex smooth functions representable as Moreau envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope–Smoothing Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moreau regularization adds a quadratic after conjugation and produces a differentiable envelope whose gradient is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Quadratic infimal convolution becomes quadratic addition under Fenchel conjugacy:
\[
(e_\lambda f)^*(u)=f^*(u)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|u\|^2.
\]
Consequently, \(e_\lambda f\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(H\), with
\[
\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr)
=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*/\lambda}(x/\lambda).
\]
Its gradient is \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz. Thus primal envelope regularization corresponds to adding a strongly convex quadratic to the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic infimal regularization corresponds to dual quadratic strengthening and primal smoothness.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(F\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(\beta>0\), and \(q(x)=\|x\|^2/2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Fréchet smoothness with a global Lipschitz gradient on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[F\text{ is Fréchet differentiable on }\mathcal H\text{ with }\beta\text{-Lipschitz }\nabla F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F=e_{1/\beta}G\text{ for some }G\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H),\] \[G=\left(F^*-\beta^{-1}q\right)^*,\qquad \nabla F=\beta\bigl(\operatorname{Id}-\operatorname{prox}_{G/\beta}\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The envelope–smoothing correspondence identifies globally smooth convex functions with quadratic Moreau envelopes. A function \(F\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) has an everywhere-defined Fréchet derivative whose gradient is \(\beta\)-Lipschitz exactly when \(F\) is the Moreau envelope of parameter \(1/\beta\) of a function \(G\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). The canonical underlying function is \(G=(F^*-q/\beta)^*\), and the gradient of the envelope is the scaled proximal residual.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F^*-\beta^{-1}q\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H).\]
\[F=\left(F^*-\beta^{-1}q\right)^*\square(\beta q).\]
special_cases_latex: For every \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(e_\gamma f\) has a \(1/\gamma\)-Lipschitz gradient.
When \(\gamma=1\), \(\nabla e_1f=\operatorname{Id}-\operatorname{prox}_f=\operatorname{prox}_{f^*}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\nabla F\) is continuous on all of \(\mathcal H\).
The smoothness constant is the reciprocal of the envelope parameter.
boundary_notes: The equivalence is global; local Lipschitz smoothness is not characterized here.
The underlying function \(G\) may be nonsmooth or extended-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau smoothability of globally Lipschitz convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative Moreau-envelope smoothing guarantee for an everywhere-finite globally Lipschitz convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) be convex and satisfy \[|h(x)-h(y)|\leq \ell_h\lVert x-y\rVert\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb E.\] Then, for every \(\mu>0\), its Moreau envelope \[M_h^\mu(x)=\min_{u\in\mathbb E}\left\{h(u)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\lVert x-u\rVert^2\right\}\] is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(h\) with parameters \((1,\ell_h^2/2)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_h^\mu\text{ is a }\frac{1}{\mu}\text{-smooth approximation of }h\text{ with parameters }\left(1,\frac{\ell_h^2}{2}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau envelope of the Euclidean norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit multidimensional Huber representation and smoothing parameters for the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=\lVert x\rVert_2\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(\mu>0\), its Moreau envelope is the multidimensional Huber function \[M_h^\mu(x)=H_\mu(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{2\mu}\lVert x\rVert_2^2,&\lVert x\rVert_2\leq\mu,\\[3pt]\lVert x\rVert_2-\dfrac{\mu}{2},&\lVert x\rVert_2>\mu.\end{cases}\] It is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(h\) with parameters \((1,1/2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau envelope of the Euclidean norm is the multidimensional Huber function: it is quadratic within radius μ and equals the norm minus μ/2 outside. It is a 1/μ-smooth approximation with parameters (1, 1/2).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_h^\mu(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{\lVert x\rVert_2^2}{2\mu},&\lVert x\rVert_2\leq\mu,\\ \lVert x\rVert_2-\frac{\mu}{2},&\lVert x\rVert_2>\mu,\end{cases}\quad\text{and }M_h^\mu\text{ is a }\frac{1}{\mu}\text{-smooth approximation with parameters }\left(1,\frac{1}{2}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform-error comparison of three smooth approximations to absolute value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of three explicit approximations at the common smoothness scale \(1/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=|x|\) and \(\mu>0\). Define \[h_\mu^1(x)=\sqrt{x^2+\mu^2}-\mu,\qquad h_\mu^2(x)=\mu\log\!\left(e^{x/\mu}+e^{-x/\mu}\right)-\mu\log 2,\qquad h_\mu^3(x)=H_\mu(x).\] These are \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximations with respective parameters \((1,1)\), \((1,\log 2)\), and \((1,1/2)\). Consequently, among these three approximations, \(H_\mu\) has the smallest stated uniform-approximation parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the common smoothness scale 1/μ, the square-root, centered log-sum-exp, and Huber approximations of absolute value have stated uniform-error parameters 1, log 2, and 1/2. Thus Huber has the tightest stated bound among these three constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac12<\log 2<1,\quad\text{so }h_\mu^3=H_\mu\text{ has the smallest stated uniform-approximation parameter among }h_\mu^1,h_\mu^2,h_\mu^3

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\) be a closed proper convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed proper convex analysis, combining first-order inversion, essential regularity, and quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal R(f):=\left(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1},\quad f\text{ essentially strictly convex}\Longleftrightarrow f^*\text{ essentially smooth},\quad f\text{ essentially smooth}\Longleftrightarrow f^*\text{ essentially strictly convex}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate regularity profile of \(f\) is the collection of regularity properties transported by Fenchel conjugacy. Its fundamental component is the inverse-subdifferential identity \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\). Under this inversion, single-valuedness of one subdifferential corresponds to essential strict convexity of the other function, while essential smoothness and essential strict convexity are exchanged between \(f\) and \(f^*\). Quadratic strong convexity and global Lipschitz differentiability form the quantitative specialization of this profile.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is closed, proper, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(f)\) is the stated inversion-and-regularity profile, and the same profile with \(f\) and \(f^*\) exchanged follows from \(f^{**}=f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\partial f(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial f^*(u).\]
\[f\text{ is Legendre}\Longleftrightarrow f^*\text{ is Legendre}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(f^*\) is differentiable with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient.
If \(f\) and \(f^*\) are essentially smooth, their gradients furnish the Legendre correspondence on the interiors of their domains.
immediate_consequences_latex: The domains and ranges of the two subdifferentials are exchanged.
Properties expressed through injectivity or single-valuedness of \(\partial f\) acquire dual formulations for \(f^*\).
boundary_notes: The essential-smoothness formulation uses finite-dimensional boundary behavior.
Recession and domain identities beyond those implied by the displayed profile are not included.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x,u\in\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, zero-gap Fenchel–Young correspondence; closedness is added only where full bidirectional subdifferential inversion is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[x\mathrel{\mathsf{FY}_f}u\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in\partial f(x).\] \[\text{If }f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H),\qquad x\mathrel{\mathsf{FY}_f}u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Young inversion correspondence of \(f\) is the relation \(\mathsf{FY}_f\subseteq\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\) whose related pairs are exactly the equality pairs in the Fenchel–Young inequality. Thus \(x\mathrel{\mathsf{FY}_f}u\) means that the gap \(f(x)+f^*(u)-\langle x,u\rangle\) vanishes, equivalently that \(u\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\). When \(f\) is lower semicontinuous as well as proper and convex, the relation is symmetric under conjugation: the same equality is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\Longleftrightarrow u\in\partial f(x),\] with equivalence to \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\) when \(f=f^{**}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\arg\max_v\{\langle x,v\rangle-f^*(v)\}.\]
\[x\in\arg\max_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-f(y)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), contact means \(u=\nabla f(x)\).
If \(f^*\) is differentiable at \(u\), contact means \(x=\nabla f^*(u)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The correspondence is the graph of \(\partial f\).
For closed proper convex \(f\), reversing each ordered pair gives the graph of \(\partial f^*\).
boundary_notes: If \(f\) is not closed, equality still implies \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\), but the clean inverse identity is stated here only for \(f=f^{**}\).
Pairs with infinite function values cannot be contact pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Normal Representation of Contact
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope supports a convex function at a point exactly when the corresponding downward-pointing vector is normal to the epigraph at the graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in H\),
\[
u\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (u,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)).
\]
The associated supporting hyperplane, with normal \((u,-1)\), is
\[
\{(z,t)\in H\times\mathbb R:t=f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone representation of supporting contact at a finite graph point; closedness of the epigraph is not required for the equivalence.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to the epigraph at the graph point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertical Supporting Normals at Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes finite-slope graph contact from vertical support caused solely by effective-domain geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v\in H\),
\[
(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v
e 0\text{ or }v=0,\qquad v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x).
\]
Equivalently, without the redundant case distinction,
\[
(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x).
\]
A nonzero such normal defines a vertical supporting hyperplane and cannot be normalized to a finite-slope contact normal \((u,-1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical epigraph supports encode normals to the effective domain rather than finite subgradient slopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\iff v\in N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\); nonzero such normals are not finite-slope contact normals.

notation.meaning: normal cone to the effective domain at x

For every \(u\in H\),

More generally, if \((v,\beta)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\) and \(\beta<0\), then

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Normal Representation of Nonvertical Contact
Contact Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane interpretation of Fenchel contact pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real locally convex space with continuous dual \(X^*\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous and convex. For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(u\in X^*\), define
\[
a_{x,u}(z)=f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle.
\]
The pair \((x,u)\) is a contact pair precisely when \(a_{x,u}(z)\le f(z)\) for every \(z\in X\). Geometrically, the hyperplane \(r=a_{x,u}(z)\) supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and meets it at \((x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contact pair consists of a point and slope whose affine minorant supports the epigraph and touches it at that point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real locally convex space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,u)\) is a contact pair exactly when \(f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle\le f(z)\) for every \(z\in X\).

knowledge_statements.title: The Fenchel–Young Equality Set Need Not Be Convex
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a smooth strictly convex function, the Fenchel–Young zero-gap set can be a nonconvex graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=x^4/4\),
\[
\{(x,u):f(x)+f^*(u)=xu\}=\operatorname{gra}\partial f
=\{(x,x^3):x\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
This equality set is not convex: it contains \((0,0)\) and \((2,8)\), but not their midpoint \((1,4)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp geometric boundary for the zero-gap set in primal-dual product space.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Symmetry of the Equality Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Young equality set of the conjugate is obtained by swapping the primal and dual coordinates of the original equality set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
Z_f:=\{(x,u)\in H\times H:f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\}.
\]
Since \(f^{**}=f\), conjugation reverses the coordinates of this set:
\[
Z_{f^*}=\{(u,x)\in H\times H:(x,u)\in Z_f\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(Z_f=\operatorname{gra}\partial f\) and \(Z_{f^*}=\operatorname{gra}\partial f^*\) are coordinate transposes.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate symmetry of the equality set in primal-dual product space.

notation.meaning: Fenchel–Young equality set of a function.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Young Equality Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the equality locus in primal–dual product space, expressed relative to the dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real locally convex space with continuous dual \(X^*\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex. Define the Fenchel–Young equality locus by
\[
E_f=\{(x,u)\in X\times X^*:f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle\}.
\]
Then
\[
E_f=\operatorname{gra}\partial f.
\]
Define the conjugate-side equality locus relative to the dual pair \((X^*,X)\) by
\[
E_{f^*}^{X}=\{(u,x)\in X^*\times X:f^*(u)+f(x)=\langle u,x\rangle\}.
\]
Coordinate reversal identifies the two loci: for every \(x\in X\) and \(u\in X^*\),
\[
(x,u)\in E_f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(u,x)\in E_{f^*}^{X}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Young equality locus is the graph of the convex subdifferential. Reversing the primal and dual coordinates gives the conjugate-side equality locus defined relative to the dual pair.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real locally convex space with continuous dual \(X^*\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel–Young equality locus of f in X × X*.
Conjugate-side equality locus in X* × X relative to the dual pair (X*,X).
Graph of the convex subdifferential of f.

knowledge_statements.title: Contact–Equality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal supporting contact, Fenchel–Young equality, and conjugate supporting contact are equivalent descriptions of the same primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following statements are equivalent:
\[
f(z)\geq f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }z\in H,
\]
\[
u\in\partial f(x),
\]
\[
f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle,
\]
and
\[
x\in\partial f^*(u).
\]
Hence a supporting affine function contacting \(f\) at \(x\) with slope \(u\) is equivalent to equality in the Fenchel–Young inequality, and the same equality expresses the reciprocal contact of \(f^*\) at \(u\) with slope \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between supporting contact, Fenchel–Young equality, and dual contact.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Boundary for Subdifferential Inversion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without lower semicontinuity, conjugate subgradient membership need not invert the original subdifferential relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\1,&x=0,\\+\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous, and
\[
f^*(u)=\begin{cases}0,&u\leq0,\\+\infty,&u>0.\end{cases}
\]
For this pair, \(0\in\partial f^*(-1)\), whereas \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\). Hence
\[
\partial f^*\ne(\partial f)^{-1}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the stated proper convex but non-lower-semicontinuous function on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial f^*(-1)\) but \(-1\notin\partial f(0)\), so \(\partial f^*\ne(\partial f)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of reciprocal subgradient membership for a proper convex function that is not lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Subdifferential Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferentials of Fenchel-conjugate functions are inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real reflexive Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\), and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous and convex. For every \(x\in X\) and \(u\in X^*\),
\[
u\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\partial f^*(u).
\]
Consequently, as set-valued relations between \(X\) and \(X^*\),
\[
\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}.
\]
The reflexive identification places \(x\) in the dual of \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the Fenchel conjugate reverses the subdifferential relation: a dual vector subdifferentiates the primal function exactly when the primal point subdifferentiates the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real reflexive Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial f^*(u)\), hence \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Inverse of the set-valued subdifferential relation.
Fenchel conjugate of f on X*.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Fenchel–Young Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient is equivalent to a Fenchel–Young gap at most epsilon, and this approximate relation is symmetric under conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\partial_\varepsilon f(x):=\{u\in H:f(z)\geq f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }z\in H\}.
\]
Then
\[
u\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x)+f^*(u)\leq\langle x,u\rangle+\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\partial_\varepsilon f^*(u).
\]
Thus an additive Fenchel–Young gap of at most \(\varepsilon\) is exactly equivalent to approximate subgradient contact in either primal-dual direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error extension of Fenchel–Young equality and subdifferential inversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient and Strong-Monotonicity Characterizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity is equivalent to a uniform quadratic subgradient lower model and to strong monotonicity of the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\mu>0\). Then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2
\]
for all \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), \(u\in\partial f(x)\), and \(y\in H\). Equivalently, whenever \(u\in\partial f(x)\) and \(v\in\partial f(y)\),
\[
\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if its subgradient models have curvature \(\mu\), equivalently \(\partial f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent Hilbert-space formulations of primal strong convexity used by the conjugacy correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is strongly convex when subtracting a positive quadratic leaves a convex function, equivalently when convex interpolation has a uniform quadratic deficit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when
\[
x\longmapsto f(x)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2
\]
is convex. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)
\leq(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.
\]
The largest admissible \(\mu\) is the strong-convexity modulus of \(f\), when such a largest value exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex exactly when \(f-(\mu/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Uniqueness of the Strongly Convex Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general optimization consequence rather than a conjugacy-regularity statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some \(\mu>0\). Then \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x_\star\), and
\[
f(x)\ge f(x_\star)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x_\star\|^2\qquad(x\in H).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed strongly convex function on a Hilbert space has a unique minimizer and grows at least quadratically away from it.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique minimizer \(x_\star\), with \(f(x)-f(x_\star)\ge(\mu/2)\|x-x_\star\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity of the Dual Gradient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient of the conjugate of a mu-strongly convex function is mu-cocoercive as well as 1/mu-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with \(\mu>0\). Then, for every \(u,v\in H\),
\[
\langle \nabla f^*(u)-\nabla f^*(v),u-v\rangle
\ge \mu\|\nabla f^*(u)-\nabla f^*(v)\|^2.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-side operator characterization induced by primal strong convexity in Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a closed, proper, strongly convex function is differentiable everywhere, and its gradient has reciprocal Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u,v\in H\), the maximizer defining \(f^*(u)\) is unique and equals \(\nabla f^*(u)\). Moreover,
\[
\|\nabla f^*(u)-\nabla f^*(v)\|\leq \frac{1}{\mu}\|u-v\|.
\]
Thus primal strong convexity makes the inverse subdifferential \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*=\nabla f^*\) single-valued and globally Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(H\), and \(\nabla f^*\) is \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space formulation with the norm induced by the inner product.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity of a closed proper convex function is equivalent to global differentiability and reciprocal-gradient smoothness of its conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following are equivalent:
\[

\]
\[
f^*\ \text{is Fréchet differentiable on }H\ \text{and}\ \|\nabla f^*(u)-\nabla f^*(v)\|\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\|u-v\|\quad(u,v\in H).
\]
Equivalently, \(\partial f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone exactly when \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\) is single-valued and \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity Does Not Imply Lipschitz Dual Gradient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even closed differentiable strict convexity is insufficient: the quartic has a differentiable conjugate whose gradient is not locally Lipschitz at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=x^4/4\). Then \(f\) is proper, closed, differentiable, and strictly convex, but it is not strongly convex with any \(\mu>0\). Its conjugate is
\[
f^*(u)=\frac34|u|^{4/3},
\]
and
\[
\nabla f^*(u)=\operatorname{sgn}(u)|u|^{1/3}.
\]
The gradient \(\nabla f^*\) is not Lipschitz in any neighborhood of \(0\), hence is not globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly but not strongly convex, and \(\nabla f^*\) is not Lipschitz near \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional sharp boundary separating strict convexity from positive quadratic curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary convexity is insufficient: simple closed convex functions have conjugates that are nonfinite or nondifferentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\equiv0\), then \(f^*=\iota_{\{0\}}\), which is not finite or differentiable on \(H\). If \(f=\iota_B\), where \(B=\{x\in H:\|x\|\leq1\}\), then \(f^*(u)=\|u\|\), which is not differentiable at \(u=0\). Both functions are closed and convex but not strongly convex. Hence ordinary convexity alone does not transfer to global smoothness of the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space.
\(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(\mu>0\), differentiability or global Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f^*\) can fail.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failures when positive strong curvature is removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Difference Lower Model
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex L-smoothness is equivalently expressed by a lower bound on the Bregman divergence in terms of the squared gradient difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable. For \(L>0\), \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth if and only if, for all \(x,y\in H\),
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)\|^2.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth exactly when its two-point first-order remainder dominates \(\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)\|^2/(2L)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent two-point formulation of global smoothness for convex differentiable functions on a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex differentiable function is L-smooth when its gradient is globally L-Lipschitz, equivalently when it satisfies the quadratic upper model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is called \(L\)-smooth when
\[
\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in H).
\]
For convex \(f\), this is equivalent to the quadratic upper model
\[
f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad(x,y\in H).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal \(L\)-smoothness means that \(\nabla f\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global first-order smoothness on the entire Hilbert space.

Dual Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of an everywhere-finite convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient is strongly convex with parameter 1/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For all \(u,v\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\), all \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\), and every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
f^*((1-t)u+tv)\leq(1-t)f^*(u)+tf^*(v)-\frac{t(1-t)}{2L}\|u-v\|^2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
f^*(v)\geq f^*(u)+\langle x,v-u\rangle+\frac{1}{2L}\|v-u\|^2.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Monotonicity of the Dual Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent operator characterization of strong convexity of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=f^*\). Then \(g\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex if and only if, for all \(u,v\in\operatorname{dom}\partial g\), \(x\in\partial g(u)\), and \(y\in\partial g(v)\),
\[
\langle x-y,u-v\rangle\geq \frac1L\|u-v\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual strong convexity is equivalent to strong monotonicity of the conjugate's subdifferential with the same modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f^*:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

Smoothness–Strong-Convexity Transfer
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global L-smoothness of a closed convex function is equivalent to 1/L-strong convexity of its Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following are equivalent:
\[
\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in H);
\]
\[
f^*-\frac{1}{2L}\|\cdot\|^2\ \text{is convex}.
\]
Under either condition, \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\), and the reciprocal constants \(L\) and \(1/L\) express the duality between the Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f\) and the strong monotonicity of \(\partial f^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient if and only if \(f^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hilbert-space equivalence for an everywhere-finite primal function.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiability alone is insufficient: the exponential has no globally Lipschitz derivative, and its conjugate has no positive strong-convexity constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is closed, strictly convex, and infinitely differentiable, but \(f'(x)=e^x\) is not globally Lipschitz. Its conjugate is
\[
f^*(u)=\begin{cases}u\log u-u,&u>0,\\0,&u=0,\\+\infty,&u<0,
\end{cases}
\]
and \((f^*)''(u)=1/u\) for \(u>0\). Since \(1/u\) has no positive global lower bound, \(f^*\) is not strongly convex with any positive constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f\) is differentiable, its derivative is not globally Lipschitz and \(f^*\) is not strongly convex with any positive constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The global Lipschitz-gradient hypothesis cannot be replaced by differentiability alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power-type uniform smoothness and dual curvature profile
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be Fréchet differentiable and convex, let \(\beta>0\), and let \(p\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hölder-gradient regime and its conjugate power-type curvature inequality on gradient images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
\[\mathsf{UCUS}_{ eta,p}(f):\quad \|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le eta\|x-y\|^p\quad( orall x,y),\] \[f^*(
abla f(y))\ge f^*(
abla f(x))+\langle x,
abla f(y)-
abla f(x)angle+ rac{p}{p+1} eta^{-1/p}\|
abla f(y)-
abla f(x)\|^{1+1/p}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The power-type uniform convexity–smoothness profile with parameters \((\beta,p)\) pairs a \(p\)-Hölder gradient bound for \(f\) with the corresponding power-type lower curvature bound for \(f^*\) along the image of \(\nabla f\). The dual exponent is \(1+1/p\), and the canonical coefficient is \(p\beta^{-1/p}/(p+1)\). This definition records the quantitative conjugate correspondence without asserting global finiteness or differentiability of \(f^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile consists of the Hölder-gradient inequality and its displayed conjugate power-curvature inequality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The primal smoothness condition implies \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\beta}{p+1}\|x-y\|^{p+1}.\]
For \(p=1\), the dual curvature term becomes \(\|\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x)\|^2/(2\beta)\).
special_cases_latex: At \(p=1\), the profile reduces to Lipschitz smoothness versus quadratic strong convexity.
For \(0<p<1\), the conjugate curvature has exponent \(1+1/p>2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The dual power exponent is Hölder-conjugate to the primal exponent \(p+1\).
The profile yields a quantitative monotonicity lower bound for \(\nabla f\).
boundary_notes: The stated dual inequality is guaranteed on points of the form \(\nabla f(x)\); extension to all of \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) needs additional hypotheses.
The case \(p=0\) is excluded because the displayed reciprocal exponent is undefined.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Minimizer and Modulus Error Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity makes an attained minimizer unique and converts objective error into a distance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), then
\[
f(x)-f(x_\star)\ge\phi(\|x-x_\star\|)\qquad(x\in H).
\]
Thus \(x_\star\) is unique when \(\phi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\). Moreover, \(f(x)-f(x_\star)\le\varepsilon\) implies
\[
\|x-x_\star\|\le\phi^{\leftarrow}(\varepsilon),
\qquad
\phi^{\leftarrow}(s):=\sup\{t\ge0:\phi(t)\le s\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the accepted uniform-convexity inequality with modulus \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f(x_\star)\ge\phi(\|x-x_\star\|)\), with the stated uniqueness and error bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence when the minimum is attained.

notation.meaning: generalized upper inverse of the modulus

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Monotonicity of the Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly convex function has a uniformly monotone subdifferential, so a common subgradient can occur at only one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), \(u\in\partial f(x)\), and \(v\in\partial f(y)\),
\[
\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge2\phi(\|x-y\|).
\]
Consequently, when \(\phi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), \((\partial f)^{-1}\) is single-valued on \(\operatorname{ran}\partial f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the accepted uniform-convexity inequality with modulus \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of the seed's subgradient-remainder convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity requires a positive, distance-dependent lower bound on every subgradient linearization error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi\) if, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), every \(u\in\partial f(x)\), and every \(y\in H\),
\[
f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|y-x\|).
\]
The requirement \(\phi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\) makes the convexity improvement uniform over all base points and directions of a fixed length.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) is convex, nondecreasing, and vanishes only at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform convexity with modulus \(\phi\) is the displayed uniform subgradient lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space subgradient-remainder formulation adapted to Fenchel duality.

Symmetric Bregman Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform smoothness bounds the symmetric Bregman divergence, equivalently the gradient monotonicity pairing, by twice the modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
D_g(v,u):=g(v)-g(u)-\langle\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle.
\]
Then for all \(u,v\in H\),
\[
0\le D_g(v,u)+D_g(u,v)
=\langle\nabla g(v)-\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle
\le2\psi(\|v-u\|).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(g\) satisfies the accepted uniform-smoothness remainder bound with modulus \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of the accepted first-order-remainder definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform smoothness bounds every first-order linearization error by a uniform modulus that is sublinear near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(g\) is uniformly smooth with modulus \(\psi\) if, for all \(u,v\in H\),
\[
0\leq g(v)-g(u)-\langle\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle\leq\psi(\|v-u\|).
\]
The estimate is uniform in the base point \(u\), and \(\psi(t)/t\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\) ensures uniform first-order differentiability.
assumptions_latex: \(g:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hölder Gradient Gives Power-Type Uniform Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hölder-gradient specialization of the uniform remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
\|\nabla g(v)-\nabla g(u)\|\le L\|v-u\|^\alpha
\]
for \(0<\alpha\le1\), then
\[
0\le g(v)-g(u)-\langle\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle
\le\frac{L}{1+\alpha}\|v-u\|^{1+\alpha}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally Hölder-continuous gradient yields a power-type uniform-smoothness remainder with the integrated constant.
assumptions_latex: \(g:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.
\(\nabla g\) is globally \(\alpha\)-Hölder with constant \(L\), where \(0<\alpha\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The uniform-smoothness modulus may be chosen as \(\psi(t)=Lt^{1+\alpha}/(1+\alpha)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power Remainder Controls Gradient Hölder Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse quantitative implication under the global convex power-remainder convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If, for some \(K>0\) and \(0<\alpha\le1\),
\[
g(v)-g(u)-\langle\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle
\le\frac{K}{1+\alpha}\|v-u\|^{1+\alpha}
\]
for all \(u,v\in H\), then
\[
\|\nabla g(v)-\nabla g(u)\|
\le K\left(\frac{1+\alpha}{2\alpha}\right)^\alpha\|v-u\|^\alpha.
\]
For \(\alpha=1\), this reduces to the usual equivalence between a quadratic remainder \(K\|v-u\|^2/2\) and a \(K\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global power-type smoothness remainder forces global Hölder continuity of the gradient; the quadratic case recovers the exact Lipschitz-gradient constant.
assumptions_latex: \(g:H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.
The displayed power remainder holds globally for \(K>0\) and \(0<\alpha\le1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Power Remainder Controls Gradient Hölder Continuity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point consequence of the immutable uniform-remainder definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For all \(u,v\in H\),
\[
0\le\langle\nabla g(v)-\nabla g(u),v-u\rangle\le2\psi(\|v-u\|).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform remainder controls the symmetric gradient increment and recovers monotonicity of the gradient.

Dual Modulus Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated remainder convention, uniform convexity with modulus phi is equivalent to uniform smoothness of the conjugate with scalar-conjugate modulus phi-star.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi^*(s)=\sup_{t\ge0}\{st-\phi(t)\}\). Then \(f\) satisfies
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|y-x\|)
\]
for all \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), \(p\in\partial f(x)\), and \(y\in H\), if and only if \(f^*\) is finite and Fréchet differentiable on \(H\) and
\[
0\le f^*(q)-f^*(p)-\langle\nabla f^*(p),q-p\rangle
\le \phi^*(\|q-p\|)
\]
for all \(p,q\in H\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is lower semicontinuous, convex, nondecreasing, supercoercive, satisfies \(\phi(0)=0\), and is positive on \((0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform convexity of \(f\) with remainder \(\phi\) is equivalent to uniform smoothness of \(f^*\) with remainder \(\phi^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space subgradient-remainder convention; the scalar Fenchel conjugate fixes the constants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space subgradient-remainder convention; scalar conjugation is taken on \([0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi^*(s)=\sup_{t\ge0}\{st-\phi(t)\}\). If
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|y-x\|)
\]
for every \(p\in\partial f(x)\), then for every \(a,b\in H\) and \(x\in\partial f^*(a)\),
\[
f^*(b)\le f^*(a)+\langle x,b-a\rangle+\phi^*(\|b-a\|).
\]
If \(\phi\) is superlinear, this yields an everywhere-finite Fréchet-differentiable conjugate with the displayed uniform remainder. Conversely, if \(f^*\) is finite and Fréchet differentiable and satisfies the corresponding upper remainder with a convex modulus \(\psi\), then
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle+\psi^*(\|y-x\|)
\]
for every \(p\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the fixed subgradient-remainder convention, conjugation transforms a uniform-convexity modulus into its scalar Fenchel-conjugate smoothness modulus, and the reverse implication uses the scalar conjugate of the smoothness modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The relevant scalar modulus is convex, nondecreasing, vanishes at zero, and is positive away from zero; superlinearity is assumed for the global differentiability conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lower remainder \(\phi\) transfers to upper remainder \(\phi^*\); a global upper remainder \(\psi\) transfers back to lower remainder \(\psi^*\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-remainder specialization with normalization \(c t^p/p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p>1\), \(q=p/(p-1)\), and \(c>0\),
\[
\left(\frac{c}{p}t^p\right)^*(s)=\frac{c^{-1/(p-1)}}{q}s^q.
\]
Consequently, a lower remainder \(c\|y-x\|^p/p\) for \(f\) transfers to the upper remainder \(c^{-1/(p-1)}\|b-a\|^q/q\) for \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-p curvature transfers to power-q conjugate smoothness with Hölder-conjugate exponents and the reciprocal power coefficient.

Nonuniform Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When quadratic curvature degenerates, quadratic transfer fails even though a nonquadratic uniform modulus may remain available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly convex and differentiable, but it is not strongly convex because \(f''(0)=0\). Its conjugate is
\[
f^*(u)=\frac{3}{4}|u|^{4/3},
\]
whose derivative is not globally Lipschitz near \(u=0\). Hence strict convexity without a quadratic uniform modulus does not yield quadratic dual smoothness; any valid dual control must retain the nonquadratic modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict convexity and differentiability alone do not ensure a positive quadratic uniform modulus or globally Lipschitz gradient for the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the quadratic transfer when curvature degenerates, while nonquadratic modulus control remains possible.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function is of Legendre type when the restriction to the nonempty interior of its effective domain is both strictly convex and essentially smooth. Essential smoothness means differentiability throughout that interior together with blow-up of the gradient norm along every interior sequence approaching the boundary. Equivalently, \(f\) is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex. This class is stable under Fenchel conjugation.

equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex}.\]
\[\partial f\text{ is one-to-one, and on }C\text{ it equals }\nabla f.\]
special_cases_latex: A finite differentiable strictly convex cofinite function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is Legendre type.
A differentiable convex function can fail to be Legendre type if its gradient does not diverge at a finite boundary point.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(f^*\) is also of Legendre type.
The gradient mapping is injective on \(C\).
boundary_notes: Strict convexity merely on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is not by itself the full essential-strict-convexity condition.
